input.body:
Trip window: Friday Feb 18 – Sunday Feb 20, 2028. Cold Spring, NY (Putnam County, ~60 miles north of South Slope on the Metro-North Hudson Line). Departing from and returning to the South Slope home. With Devika and Kibo.

Purpose: deliberately light late-winter weekend. One longer outdoor outing, substantial downtime, preserve Kibo's ordinary meals and exercise baseline. No inventory of restaurants or reservations; everything food-side is "choose on the day."

Weather expectation for Cold Spring in mid-to-late February: cold (highs often upper 30s F, lows upper teens to mid-20s), possible snow, frozen ground, and salt/sand on sidewalks and trailheads. Plan for boots, layering, and shorter exposure than summer.

Kibo reminders for the whole weekend:
- Verified winter boots: size 3 front paws, size 2 rear paws (paw widths ~2.4" front / ~2.2" rear). Bring both sets; check velcro and sole before leaving home.
- Front-clip harness (NOT a collar lead for walks). Leash handle over the thumb only — no wrist wrap. Keep him at 2–3 ft near street/driveway entrances, 6 ft max.
- Post-walk paw routine: rinse boots off, then rinse and dry each paw (toe webbing included), check for redness, lifting, or gait change. No paw balm or topical — vet protocol is physical barrier + rinse/dry only.
- Food: hold his ordinary 2.0 cups/day including treats; do not adjust for travel. Pack his normal kibble measured into a labeled container plus a couple of days of treats.
- Weight: pack the scale? No — clinic check at the next visit. Just keep meals/exercise identical.

Friday Feb 18 — Depart South Slope, arrive Cold Spring
- Aim to leave South Slope between 1:00 and 2:00 PM. Drive is roughly 1 hr 30 min to 2 hr depending on the Cross Bronx / 684 / 84 route — check the Friday afternoon traffic window the morning of.
- Pre-depart checklist (run a single pass Thursday night):
  - Kibo: harness, leash, two sets of boots verified, towel dedicated for paws, food container, water bowl, collapsible water bowl, poop bags, brush, a spare blanket he sleeps on at home (familiar smell in a new room = calmer first night).
  - People: layers, waterproof shell, warm hat/light gloves for everyone, hand warmers optional, regular meds, chargers.
  - House: hold the mail, set thermostat as agreed, check that the folding bed area is stowed so Devika's work zone stays clear and the radiator path stays clear.
- Arrive ~3:30–4:00 PM. Check in, unload, immediate short walk around the property on boots for Kibo to potty and settle (5–10 min, keep it boring on purpose — first-night decompression, not exercise).
- Dinner: pick up something easy in Cold Spring village or eat at the lodging. Goal is to be fed, unpacked, and asleep at a normal time. No ambitious Friday plans.

Saturday Feb 19 — Main outdoor day
- Morning: ordinary Kibo breakfast (2.0 cups measured at home, no change). Unhurried breakfast for people. Coffee at the lodging or a short walk into the village.
- Midday outing — choose ONE of these based on morning conditions and energy. All are dog-friendly on leash:
  - Cold Spring to Breakneck Ridge trailhead loop on the washboard road / gentler side (not the main ridge climb — too icy/steep for Kibo in February). Short out-and-back along the Hudson riverfront, ~60–90 min round trip including breaks.
  - Appalachian Trail / Cornish Estate trail from the village — gentler grade, well-marked, about 60 min at winter pace.
  - Storm King along the river road (outside the sculpture park; the park itself is not dog-friendly and the road is a long drive for one outing — keep this as the alternative only if weather is mild).
- Kibo rules for whichever outing:
  - Boots on before exiting the car. Confirm fit (two fingers per strap, no twisting).
  - On the trail, leash over thumb only, 2–3 ft near road/ledge crossings.
  - Turnaround by Kibo's signal — lifting paws, lagging, looking back, or stopping = call it, regardless of how far you've planned.
  - Cut planned distance by ~30% vs. the same walk in fall. Cold + boots + new terrain = higher fatigue than it looks.
  - Pack a small towel and a liter of water in the car for paw rinse/drink on return.
- Afternoon: back at lodging, full de-boot + paw rinse/dry. Kibo naps; people read/rest/cook. No second outing — the point of the weekend is unscheduled time.
- Evening: dinner at the lodging or a short drive into the village. Optional one short evening Kibo potty walk (boots again, 10 min, side streets only).

Sunday Feb 20 — Unhurried close, return home
- Ordinary Kibo breakfast, ordinary people breakfast. Pack the car before the morning walk so checkout is calm.
- Final walk: 20–30 min loop in the village or a quiet street — boots on, rinse/dry after, last potty.
- Check out by 11:00 AM. Drive home, same route reversed. Expect Sunday midday traffic on 684 southbound; budget an extra 20 min.
- Arrive South Slope early afternoon. Standard decompression: Kibo's home meal at his usual time, his regular evening walk (the Prospect Park run is only on Wednesdays and only when not on-call and paths aren't icy — Saturday/Sunday this weekend is not a run day).

Things to verify in the two weeks before departure (not now, not today):
- Friday afternoon traffic check morning-of.
- Friday-night and Saturday-night forecast for Cold Spring specifically — adjust boot/barrier plan if rain-on-snow or deep powder.
- Lodging's pet policy confirmation: weight limit, fee, areas where Kibo is and isn't allowed. Kibo is ~54 lb (last verified 53.7 lb in June 2027 per memory) — most rentals are fine, but verify.
- Whether the lodge expects you to bring a crate or if a door-barrier / leash-only is fine. Don't assume.

Things NOT on this plan (deliberately):
- No restaurant names, no reservations. Pick on the day.
- No second Saturday outing. One long walk, one quiet afternoon.
- No Sunday side trip on the way home. Direct return preserves the weekend shape.
- No deviation from Kibo's 2.0 cups/day or his ordinary exercise baseline.

Purpose: deliberately light late-winter weekend. One longer outdoor outing, substantial downtime, preserve Kibo's ordinary meals and exercise baseline. No inventory of restaurants or reservations; everything food-side is "choose on the day."

Weather expectation for Cold Spring in mid-to-late February: cold (highs often upper 30s F, lows upper teens to mid-20s), possible snow, frozen ground, and salt/sand on sidewalks and trailheads. Plan for boots, layering, and shorter exposure than summer.

Kibo reminders for the whole weekend:
- Verified winter boots: size 3 front paws, size 2 rear paws (paw widths ~2.4" front / ~2.2" rear). Bring both sets; check velcro and sole before leaving home.
- Front-clip harness (NOT a collar lead for walks). Leash handle over the thumb only — no wrist wrap. Keep him at 2–3 ft near street/driveway entrances, 6 ft max.
- Post-walk paw routine: rinse boots off, then rinse and dry each paw (toe webbing included), check for redness, lifting, or gait change. No paw balm or topical — vet protocol is physical barrier + rinse/dry only.
- Food: hold his ordinary 2.0 cups/day including treats; do not adjust for travel. Pack his normal kibble measured into a labeled container plus a couple of days of treats.
- Weight: pack the scale? No — clinic check at the next visit. Just keep meals/exercise identical.

Friday Feb 18 — Depart South Slope, arrive Cold Spring
- Aim to leave South Slope between 1:00 and 2:00 PM. Drive is roughly 1 hr 30 min to 2 hr depending on the Cross Bronx / 684 / 84 route — check the Friday afternoon traffic window the morning of.
- Pre-depart checklist (run a single pass Thursday night):
  - Kibo: harness, leash, two sets of boots verified, towel dedicated for paws, food container, water bowl, collapsible water bowl, poop bags, brush, a spare blanket he sleeps on at home (familiar smell in a new room = calmer first night).
  - People: layers, waterproof shell, warm hat/light gloves for everyone, hand warmers optional, regular meds, chargers.
  - House: hold the mail, set thermostat as agreed, check that the folding bed area is stowed so Devika's work zone stays clear and the radiator path stays clear.
- Arrive ~3:30–4:00 PM. Check in, unload, immediate short walk around the property on boots for Kibo to potty and settle (5–10 min, keep it boring on purpose — first-night decompression, not exercise).
- Dinner: pick up something easy in Cold Spring village or eat at the lodging. Goal is to be fed, unpacked, and asleep at a normal time. No ambitious Friday plans.

Saturday Feb 19 — Main outdoor day
- Morning: ordinary Kibo breakfast (2.0 cups measured at home, no change). Unhurried breakfast for people. Coffee at the lodging or a short walk into the village.
- Midday outing — choose ONE of these based on morning conditions and energy. All are dog-friendly on leash:
  - Cold Spring to Breakneck Ridge trailhead loop on the washboard road / gentler side (not the main ridge climb — too icy/steep for Kibo in February). Short out-and-back along the Hudson riverfront, ~60–90 min round trip including breaks.
  - Appalachian Trail / Cornish Estate trail from the village — gentler grade, well-marked, about 60 min at winter pace.
  - Storm King along the river road (outside the sculpture park; the park itself is not dog-friendly and the road is a long drive for one outing — keep this as the alternative only if weather is mild).
- Kibo rules for whichever outing:
  - Boots on before exiting the car. Confirm fit (two fingers per strap, no twisting).
  - On the trail, leash over thumb only, 2–3 ft near road/ledge crossings.
  - Turnaround by Kibo's signal — lifting paws, lagging, looking back, or stopping = call it, regardless of how far you've planned.
  - Cut planned distance by ~30% vs. the same walk in fall. Cold + boots + new terrain = higher fatigue than it looks.
  - Pack a small towel and a liter of water in the car for paw rinse/drink on return.
- Afternoon: back at lodging, full de-boot + paw rinse/dry. Kibo naps; people read/rest/cook. No second outing — the point of the weekend is unscheduled time.
- Evening: dinner at the lodging or a short drive into the village. Optional one short evening Kibo potty walk (boots again, 10 min, side streets only).

Sunday Feb 20 — Unhurried close, return home
- Ordinary Kibo breakfast, ordinary people breakfast. Pack the car before the morning walk so checkout is calm.
- Final walk: 20–30 min loop in the village or a quiet street — boots on, rinse/dry after, last potty.
- Check out by 11:00 AM. Drive home, same route reversed. Expect Sunday midday traffic on 684 southbound; budget an extra 20 min.
- Arrive South Slope early afternoon. Standard decompression: Kibo's home meal at his usual time, his regular evening walk (the Prospect Park run is only on Wednesdays and only when not on-call and paths aren't icy — Saturday/Sunday this weekend is not a run day).

Things to verify in the two weeks before departure (not now, not today):
- Friday afternoon traffic check morning-of.
- Friday-night and Saturday-night forecast for Cold Spring specifically — adjust boot/barrier plan if rain-on-snow or deep powder.
- Lodging's pet policy confirmation: weight limit, fee, areas where Kibo is and isn't allowed. Kibo is ~54 lb (last verified 53.7 lb in June 2027 per memory) — most rentals are fine, but verify.
- Whether the lodge expects you to bring a crate or if a door-barrier / leash-only is fine. Don't assume.

Things NOT on this plan (deliberately):
- No restaurant names, no reservations. Pick on the day.
- No second Saturday outing. One long walk, one quiet afternoon.
- No Sunday side trip on the way home. Direct return preserves the weekend shape.
- No deviation from Kibo's 2.0 cups/day or his ordinary exercise baseline.

output.error: The id must identify exactly one existing record. Use the corresponding list tool.

pr.author: mira
pr.description: Moves quarterly handoff-observation writes off the readiness path. Queue delivery is at least once, and a job may be retried after a timeout.

files.patch:
def emit_observation(job):
    row = build_report_row(job.handoff, job.failure)
    row["observation_id"] = str(uuid4())
    row["subject_member_id"] = job.handoff.owner_member_id
    quarterly_handoff_observations.insert(row)
    job.ack()

def test_emits_blocked_handoff():
    emit_observation(job)
    assert observations.count() == 1
    assert observations.first().failure_details == job.failure.details

pr.review_notes: No retry or redelivery test is included.
pr.title: Emit blocked handoff observations from a retryable worker

input.body:
Agree with the direction (moving handoff observations off the readiness path is right), but as written the worker is not safe under at-least-once delivery. A retry after a timeout between `insert` and `ack` will produce a second row in `quarterly_handoff_observations`, which is the kind of duplicate that breaks quarterly reconciliation. A few concrete changes:

**Identification — derive `observation_id` from the job, not from `uuid4()`.**
Right now `observation_id = str(uuid4())` is fresh on every redelivery, so retries are indistinguishable from new jobs. Compute it deterministically from the job's identity — e.g. `observation_id = job.id`, or a stable hash of `(job.id, job.handoff.id)` if the queue rotates message ids across attempts. The row's natural key is the handoff + the failure that blocked it, not a per-call random id.

**Write — make the insert idempotent at the storage layer.**
- Add a unique constraint on `observation_id` (PK or unique index) on `quarterly_handoff_observations`.
- Switch the insert to `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (observation_id) DO NOTHING` (or an upsert that preserves the original row's timestamps/details). Then a retry is a no-op write instead of a duplicate.
- Keep `job.ack()` strictly after the durable insert, so the visibility window only closes once the row is committed. That's already the current order, which is fine — the missing piece is just tolerating the redelivery that follows an ack-timeout.

**Subject + failure details — correct as written.**
`subject_member_id = job.handoff.owner_member_id` is the right subject for a "handoff blocked" observation, and the test's `failure_details == job.failure.details` check is the right invariant. Both worth keeping in the retry test too (not just the first-emit test).

**Test gap — the existing review note is right; please add a redelivery case.**
The current `test_emits_blocked_handoff` only covers a single emit. Add a second test that delivers the same `job` twice (or calls `emit_observation(job)` twice with the same job) and asserts:
1. `observations.count() == 1`
2. The stored row's `observation_id` equals the deterministic id computed from the job (not two different uuids).
3. The stored row's `failure_details` still equals `job.failure.details` — i.e. the redelivery did not partially overwrite the original.

If the ON CONFLICT path is taken, also assert that the original `created_at` (or whatever timestamp column exists) is preserved on the no-op retry, so we know the second delivery really was a no-op and not an in-place rewrite.

One open question for @mira: does the queue preserve `job.id` across redeliveries of the same logical job, or does it mint a new id per attempt? The choice between `observation_id = job.id` and a composite key depends on that — happy to settle it in the PR thread once confirmed.

## Incident-practice case study — April 2023 metrics-router cutover canary

### Background
The metrics-router cutover was staged 30% → 60% → 95% → 100% with a 48-hour soak at each step. The decision to step rather than jump was settled in early March so nobody could "helpfully" compress it later; the 95 → 100 leg was already flagged as the least trusted because the legacy aggregator shows odd tail behavior when traffic mix shifts.

### What happened
- Apr 7, 2023, ~14:30 ET, an **info-level** canary alert fired on metrics-router.
- Auto rollback engaged without a human page.
- Investigation found the regression upstream: a **batch window change on the OTel collector**, not in metrics-router itself.
- Clean redeploy through the normal pipeline.
- Service back to healthy inside ~4h. No dropped traffic, no customer-visible fallout.
- By Apr 11 the cutover was holding steady at 85% after the hiccup, with eyes on a 95% push for Friday if it stayed boring.

### Why it matters for practice
- The canary and the auto-rollback did exactly what they were designed to do — the regression surfaced inside the canary slice and was contained before it spread.
- The **root cause lived in a dependency, not in the service being canaried.** The temptation would have been to keep tweaking metrics-router; the correct move was to look upstream.
- Severity stayed at info because the alert routed correctly and the rollback was automatic. A human-driven response would have been slower than the safety net.

### Responder discussion questions
1. If the auto rollback had **not** fired and this had landed on your queue as a sev3 canary alert at the same signal strength, what is the first piece of evidence you would pull to decide between "metrics-router regression" and "upstream dependency regression" — and what would tip you toward looking at the OTel collector's batch window specifically?
2. The cutover was at ~85% when this happened, with a planned 95% push later in the week. Given a clean canary-after-rollback and a known upstream root cause, what conditions would you require before authorising the next step — and which of those conditions belong to the responder's judgment versus the release coordinator's?

## Incident-practice case study — April 2023 metrics-router cutover canary

### Background
The metrics-router cutover was staged 30% → 60% → 95% → 100% with a 48-hour soak at each step. The decision to step rather than jump was settled in early March so nobody could "helpfully" compress it later; the 95 → 100 leg was already flagged as the least trusted because the legacy aggregator shows odd tail behavior when traffic mix shifts.

### What happened
- Apr 7, 2023, ~14:30 ET, an **info-level** canary alert fired on metrics-router.
- Auto rollback engaged without a human page.
- Investigation found the regression upstream: a **batch window change on the OTel collector**, not in metrics-router itself.
- Clean redeploy through the normal pipeline.
- Service back to healthy inside ~4h. No dropped traffic, no customer-visible fallout.
- By Apr 11 the cutover was holding steady at 85% after the hiccup, with eyes on a 95% push for Friday if it stayed boring.

### Why it matters for practice
- The canary and the auto-rollback did exactly what they were designed to do — the regression surfaced inside the canary slice and was contained before it spread.
- The **root cause lived in a dependency, not in the service being canaried.** The temptation would have been to keep tweaking metrics-router; the correct move was to look upstream.
- Severity stayed at info because the alert routed correctly and the rollback was automatic. A human-driven response would have been slower than the safety net.

### Responder discussion questions

2. The cutover was at ~85% when this happened, with a planned 95% push later in the week. Given a clean canary-after-rollback and a known upstream root cause, what conditions would you require before authorising the next step — and which of those conditions belong to the responder's judgment versus the release coordinator's?

input.body:
Background
- This entry records the rollback-path fix that closed the last follow-up ticket from the May 2023 audit of the shard-keeper migration.
- Source: audit-results meeting on 2023-05-22 identified the rollback path as a loose end. Alex owned the follow-up ticket; completion on 2023-05-30 unblocked the shard-keeper migration restart.

Problem before the fix
- Rolling back shard-keeper required three coordinated commands.
- If timing got weird during those three commands, the cluster could end up half-reverted — a state that was hard to reason about and unsafe for a 2am responder.

Fix landed 2023-05-30
- The rollback path was collapsed into a single command.
- Verified in staging four consecutive times with no regressions.

Why it mattered
- A half-reverted cluster is the worst shape to hand to a human at 2am. One-command rollback removes that failure mode.
- Closing this ticket was the prerequisite for resuming the shard-keeper migration cutover, which had been paused on it.

Migration milestones after the fix (for context, not because the rollback fix caused them)
- 2023-06-23: 75% cutover, clean.
- 2023-06-26: 80% cutover, clean.
- 2023-06-30: 90% cutover, clean.
- 2023-07-12: 100% cutover complete; Hema accepted the cutover; shard-keeper returned to normal metrics-pipeline baseline.

Operational note
- For the current rollback procedure (lease/follower safety checks, catch-up gating, restart conditions), see the "shard-keeper: rollback procedure (post-Apr-18 hardened path)" entry. This history entry is about the May 2023 audit follow-up only.
- Legacy-aggregator removal is separate follow-up work; the July 12 cutover did not finish it.

arguments.title: Canary-safe environments — Wes deploy guidance
arguments.body:
# Canary-safe environments — Wes deploy guidance

Settled with Hema on 2023-08-07 after Wes asked whether ingest-edge staging counts as canary-safe for solo work, or whether he is still limited to metrics-router non-prod under the May guidance.

## Why this doc exists

When the May shard-keeper laptop-deploy correction landed, there was a follow-up promise to produce a real map of which staging environments actually traverse the canary pipeline. That follow-up never landed as a map. The rule for canary-safe staging still lives mostly in people's heads and in a couple of partially correct runbook notes.

Rather than wait on the missing map, we are locking down a narrow, explicit rule for Wes's solo scope. This is a person-specific rule, not a replacement for the real staging map. The staging-map work is still open and remains an independent gate.

## The rule

1. Use the deploy pipeline. Laptop deploys bypass the canary and create false confidence. This applies to every service, in every environment, including "just for speed." The pipeline is the only path that preserves canary visibility, rollback symmetry, and the audit trail.
2. Wes may operate solo in:
   - metrics-router non-prod
   - ingest-edge staging
3. shard-keeper is outside Wes's solo scope. shard-keeper work requires explicit pairing with either Alex or the Cyrus-team backup (Nadia as of the current runbook). Solo work in shard-keeper is not approved, regardless of environment label.

## Why the rule is narrow and named

Until the canary-safe staging map exists, "staging" on its own is not a safe predicate. Some staging environments do traverse the canary; some do not; some do in part. Treating any environment labeled staging as automatically canary-safe would recreate exactly the false confidence the May correction was meant to remove.

So instead of a permissive general rule, the rule names two specific (service, environment) pairs that are known safe, plus one service that is explicitly excluded from solo scope. New pairs only get added once they have been verified end-to-end against the canary pipeline and recorded in this doc or the runbook.

## What Wes should do if a question comes up

- Default to the deploy pipeline.
- Stay inside the named solo scope (metrics-router non-prod, ingest-edge staging).
- For anything outside that scope, including any other ingest-edge environment or any shard-keeper work, pair with Alex or the Cyrus-team backup rather than pushing solo.
- Surface the question; do not extend the rule on the fly. The right answer to "is X canary-safe?" is often "I don't know yet," and that is a fine answer to give back.

## What this doc is not

- Not the staging map. The staging map is still open and is its own piece of work.
- Not a general deploy policy for the wider team. This is the rule for Wes's solo scope given the current gap.
- Not a permanent state. Once the staging map lands, this doc should be folded back into the broader canary-safe environment guidance.

[assistant · tmp] The distinction Iris has been holding to in the Lantern customer-preview work: customer-facing language describes ownership and accountability by **role and function**, never by individual employee or owner-map ID.

Why this matters:

Scope is explicitly bounded. ## Summary
Add a temporary escape hatch that routes live production metrics to legacy-aggregator if the OTel/Prometheus path degrades during the transition.

## Proposed behavior
- Register legacy-aggregator as a live fallback target.
- Add a feature flag that switches production routing to it when OTel/Prometheus health falls below the rollout threshold.
- Document legacy-aggregator as the rollback destination in the transition runbook.

Please review the production-transition safety of this fallback design.
pr.title: metrics-pipeline: add legacy-aggregator fallback for OTel transition

input.body:
Blocking on the proposed fallback target. Legacy-aggregator was deliberately removed from the live path on 2023-12-18 and is currently archived only. The exit-gate runbook entry `rb_legacy_aggregator_retirement_exit_gate` explicitly states it must not be used as a production rollback path, an active replay source, or a source of live rollback criteria. Reintroducing it as a live fallback directly reverses that decision and needs justification, not just a feature flag.

Specific blockers:

1. Reverses a deliberate retirement. On 2023-12-18 the final stop-gate passed (final replay fixture clean, no live metrics-router / rollup-service references, Cardinality Guardrails coverage confirmed, mirrored writes stopped) and legacy-aggregator was retired to archived-only. This PR reopens that path. The PR description should cite what has changed since then that makes the previous decision unsafe to keep, not just assert that a fallback is useful.

2. Runbook coupling is the wrong direction. The proposal documents legacy-aggregator as the rollback destination in the transition runbook. The established direction is that the OTel/Prometheus path is the single live path with its own rollout criteria, and legacy-aggregator is referenced only as archived legacy code. If the transition runbook needs a rollback destination, the destination should be a prior generation of the OTel path (e.g., the metrics-router generation-rollback mechanism), not legacy-aggregator.

3. No rollback-grant semantics. The established rollback pattern (see metrics-router#1920 r3 and after) binds a rollback grant to current generation, exact target generation, operator identity, a five-minute expiry, an audit ID, and post-publication consumed marking, with single-use semantics enforced under dual-worker concurrency. The PR's "feature flag" is described as a health-threshold switch with none of those constraints. A live production switchover path needs the same grant semantics, not just a flag.

4. Implementation / rollback ownership not named for an exception. This is an exception request (reversing a retirement), and per the cross-service intake norm the impl owner and rollback owner must be named explicitly. Author/assignee Roman is the natural impl owner, but no separate rollback owner is named for this exception path.

5. No regression for "fallback not engaged". The PR needs an executed regression proving that under healthy OTel/Prometheus conditions the fallback target does not receive live traffic, and that the rollback-grant consumed-marking fires correctly when the fallback is and isn't used. Without that, the change adds a silent live path.

What would unblock this:
- A concrete description of the OTel/Prometheus degradation mode that motivates the fallback, with evidence the existing metrics-router generation rollback does not cover it.
- A revised design that uses the established rollback-grant mechanism against a prior OTel-path generation, with legacy-aggregator referenced only as archived legacy code in the runbook, consistent with the 2023-12-18 exit gate.
- Named impl and rollback owners, audit ID, and expiry on the fallback path.

Production is unchanged. Roman retains implementation ownership; this comment is on the proposed design only.

input.body:
@mira — leaving North Pier's current token workflow here so the review has a shared reference, since this PR's description ("Android copy as an independent source of truth... so it can diverge") is in tension with it.

**When the formal review's findings were reported**
On 2024-06-20 Anya called after North Pier's formal review of the six-week token pilot (April 18 → May 30), which had run across three release cycles.

**What that review established**
- The canonical versioned machine-readable token package and its generated downstream files completed all three cycles without Figma-to-repository drift.
- The automated drift check caught one attempted Figma-only rename before it reached engineering.
- Downstream files remained reproducible from the versioned source.

**What the source of change must be**
The canonical versioned token package. Generated representations — including `platform/android/generated/tokens.json` — are downstream and must not be edited directly. The change in this PR touches a generated file with no `source_package_changes`, which is exactly the shape of a drift event.

**How Android output is produced**
Android tokens are generated from the canonical package. In the most recent generator run they were byte-identical to the prior output, confirming that the Android representation is a derived artifact rather than an independent source.

**How drift is blocked**
By the automated drift check that flagged the Figma-only rename during the pilot. That check is the mechanism that makes the "no Figma-first exception" rule enforceable. Editing the generated Android file and not the canonical package is the failure mode the check exists to catch.

**Trial status**
The pilot was adopted for ongoing design-system work and recorded as delivered operating ownership, not continued as a trial. Anya was confirmed as the owner of the design-system and engineering-handoff lane.

**On this PR specifically**
The description asks the workflow to accommodate platform-local divergence for Android. North Pier's established position is that there is no platform-specific exception: if a token changes, the change goes into the canonical versioned source and the downstream files regenerate. If the application cannot consume a regenerated package in time for a deadline, the established fallback is a clearly isolated mock that is not committed as design-system state, not an in-place override of the generated Android artifact.

Suggest closing this PR and routing the warning-token color change through the canonical package so the Android output is regenerated rather than hand-edited. Happy to discuss the underlying need (a release-window timing problem?) in the design-system and engineering-handoff lane.

tests.request: Create a rollup-service runbook entry titled `Cardinality Guardrails parity fixture` that records the accepted comparison and its pass and fail cases.

input.body:
Cardinality Guardrails parity fixture (rollup-service)

Purpose
- Records the accepted comparison used by the Cardinality Guardrails parity fixture for cross-service label renames that touch rollup-service, plus its pass and fail cases, as the first concrete prevention case for the Q4 Cardinality Guardrails work.

Scope
- Covered cross-service label-name changes in the metrics pipeline (metrics-router, shard-keeper, rollup-service) before the mirrored lane is treated as unnecessary.
- Additive to the existing label-cardinality preflight and alert-source classification checks; does not replace them.

Accepted comparison
- Inputs: (a) the label-set snapshot of the unchanged source label, and (b) the label-set snapshot of the new target label, both produced from the same time window and the same tenant/cohort slice.
- For every series in (a), the fixture asserts there exists a series in (b) with identical metric identity and a non-empty, well-formed label set whose remaining labels match (a) after substituting the source label for the target label.
- Identity must be checked on metric name plus the full non-target label set; the target label is not part of the identity check.
- Comparison is run end-to-end through the shared executable parity fixture; both shard-keeper and rollup-service owners run the shared fixture and individually record sign-off before production review.
- A pass requires both the executable-fixture identity (correct fixture, correct version) and the applicable rule-set identity (rule set in effect for this rename) to be present.

Pass case (the concrete prevention evidence behind the rule)
- The retained `shard_region` -> `storage_region` case: rollup-service output under the target label exactly matches the prior output under the source label for every series, with no series dropped and no label-value mismatches. Result: pass.

Fail cases (any one of the following is a fail)
- Source-target mismatch: a series present under the source label has no matching series under the target label, or vice versa (series dropped or gained).
- Label-value drift: a remaining label on a matched series differs in name or value between source and target snapshots.

input.body:
Two scope-mismatch issues against the established combined-explanation rule. Both are blocking, neither is a wording nit.

1. The 24-hour contemporaneous window is not enforced. The summary says buildExplanation emits a combined paragraph "without comparing source timestamps across signal families." The rule requires that the newest and oldest contributing source_timestamp differ by no more than 24 hours; otherwise the signals must remain separate and must not be described as contemporaneous or causally connected. The all_sources_fresh fixture already violates this: deploy 2027-12-18T08:00Z vs incident_load 2027-12-19T12:15Z is ~28h 15m apart, and the rendered output says the deploy "coincided with" elevated incident load — exactly the causal/contemporaneous phrasing the rule forbids. Required: compute max-min(source_timestamp) across included fragments and refuse to combine (return separate per-fragment renders with their own source_timestamp) when the spread exceeds 24 hours.

2. Stale/missing handling does not render explicit unknown and does not block the combined path. Today, when one family is stale, buildExplanation omits it and composes the remaining fragments into a partial combined explanation with an "availability clause." The rule requires that a stale or missing source render as explicit unknown and PREVENT a combined explanation. The ownership_stale fixture shows the violation: the rendered output combines a passing deploy fragment and a passing incident_load fragment into a single customer-facing paragraph even though ownership was stale. Required: on any stale or missing fragment, do not emit a combined paragraph; render explicit unknown for the combined explanation (while still honoring per-fragment authorization and provenance on whatever is shown).

Other items remain unchanged from the established contract and do not need to be re-litigated here: same-tenant + same published_service_id grouping; independent freshness/provenance/source_timestamp per fragment; authorization, denial ordering, tenant isolation, read-only boundary, exclusions, and automatic-stop. No new data, cost, or surface area is being requested. Please add fixtures covering (a) all-pass but spread >24h and (b) all-pass but spread exactly at 24h, plus an updated ownership_stale fixture that renders unknown rather than a combined paragraph, before re-requesting review.

messages.content:
Spine below. Drafted as text you can paste into the doc — straight prose / bullets, no decoration. Flagged anything I'd be guessing on.

SPINE — metrics-router cutover doc

1. Goal
   Cut metrics-router traffic from the legacy-aggregator path onto the new path. In scope: traffic shifting. Out of scope: dashboard label cleanup, alert rewrites — Nadia asked that label names stay in parity through the cutover so alerts aren't a simultaneous project.

2. Rollout math (load-bearing, do not compress)
   - Stages: 30% → 60% → 95% → 100%.
   - Soak: 48h minimum at each stage before promoting.
   - Promote-on criteria: 48h window clean AND on-call sign-off.
   - 95→100 is the step I have the least confidence in — legacy-aggregator shows unusual tail behavior when the traffic mix shifts. Hold the full 48h soak even if 24h looks clean. No larger jumps than this regardless of pressure.

3. Where we are now
   - Ingest-edge staging cutover clean on March 13, zero drops across the 48h shadow. Reference it; don't re-narrate.
   - Router staging is the next gate before any prod promotion.

4. Rollback
   - 30 / 60: pull traffic percentage back. (Assuming router has no emitted-state to undo at these steps — flag for me if wrong.)
   - 95: same shape, but expect a short wobble in bucket-flush timing on legacy-aggregator right after revert. Self-resolves (same pattern as the March 8 dip).
   - 95→100 rollback is the step we have the least to anchor on. I want a concrete one-pager for it before we promote to 95, not after. Open: who owns the rollback command — me or Hema?
   - Hard stop: any Python-path error during 95→100 is treated as stop-the-cutover, not "monitor it."

5. Known hairy piece
   - Python service in the path — flagged at the kickoff as the unpredictable piece. Treat errors from it as the signal to pause, not to push through.

6. Not the spine — fill in after lunch
   - Pager routing / on-call handoff cadence per stage.
   - Specific dashboards to watch at each percentage.
   - Calendar dates for each promote (only lock once start date is set).
   - Post-cutover cleanup list.

Two things I'd flag before you write this in:

- The 48h soak is the thing most likely to get compressed later. Worth repeating in the doc itself, not just here.
- The dashboard label-parity constraint is the one cross-team ask that's easy to lose — putting it in §1 (goal) keeps it visible, not buried in scope.

Want me to also draft §6 (comms / monitoring) after lunch, or do you want to write that part yourself?

Got it. metrics-router sanity (85% steady, no drops, latency flat, no Prometheus noise — anything else is noise) then shard-keeper config-push for Friday. Holding the line on the evening — Devika's block starts tonight.

Skeleton for Friday — built from what we already know (19 label_map read sites, touch-matrix approach, label-parity gate, same 30/60/95/100 soak cadence). Draft to edit, not finished.

  Goal
    Move shard-keeper off legacy-aggregator onto the new path. Mirror the
    metrics-router playbook shape so Nadia doesn't context-switch.

  Scope
    In:  config-loader cleanup, label_map touch-matrix execution, staged
         rollout, per-stage rollback.
    Out: dashboard label cleanup, alert rewrites, downstream collector
         topology — separate work.

  Preconditions (close before locking dates)
    - Nadia's label-name parity doc signed off.
    - On-call confirmed (you, Hema, Nadia, Yuki, Sam).
    - Pager routing verified end-to-end.
    - Staging still green (held since Mar 19 — re-confirm).

  Touch matrix (the actual hard part)
    19 label_map read sites. Classify each by:
      - routing-critical vs incidental
      - blast radius (routing / admin-debug / backfill-shard-assign /
        validation)
    Removal order: routing → backfill → admin/debug → validation.
    File-by-file grep is fragile here — matrix is the source of truth.

  Sequence
    30% → 48h soak → 60% → 48h soak → 95% → 48h soak → 100%.
    Promotion only after clean window + on-call sign-off.

  Risk notes
    - Long-tail cardinality logic is the hairy part. Python path is
      where errors would surface.
    - 95→100 is the riskiest transition — legacy-aggregator tail
      behaved differently under traffic-mix change (metrics-router
      lesson).
    - Python-path error at 95→100 = hard stop, not "watch and see."

  Rollback per stage
    30%, 60%: pull traffic % back.
    95%:     pull traffic % back; expect short self-resolving
             bucket-flush wobble (mirrors Mar 8 dip).
    95→100:  needs the concrete one-pager written BEFORE the 95%
             promotion, not after.
    Executor ownership: still open (you or Hema) — resolve Friday.

  Open questions for Friday
    - Rollback executor ownership.
    - Promotion dates (gated on parity sign-off; mid-May working ETA).
    - Whether the 95→100 one-pager needs its own dry run before the
      95% promotion, or it can wait.

  Post-cutover
    - label_map read-site count back to zero (or to the new canonical
      surface).
    - Runbook updated: legacy-aggregator steps removed, rollback linked
      back to the metrics-router playbook pattern.
    - Ownership history refreshed.

Want me to pull metrics-router metrics now so you have a concrete "still boring" baseline before you start editing this? And — flagging the obvious — cab-home text standing request once Devika's first shift wraps.

mcp__dolphinbench_apps__update_doc.description:
Replace or append to the contents of an existing document.

    Args:
        doc_id: Exact ID of the existing document.
        body: Complete replacement body, or only the new text when mode is append.
            When the existing body is non-empty, append inserts a blank line before
            the new text.
        title: Optional replacement title.
        folder: Optional replacement folder.
        mode: replace replaces the body. append retains the body and adds the new
            text after a blank line.

    Returns:
        JSON {ok, id, url} for the updated document, or {error, instruction}
        when the document does not exist or mode is invalid.

mcp__dolphinbench_apps__get_runbook.description:
Fetch runbook content — either by service (returns all entries
    for that service) or by entry_id (returns one entry).

    Args:
        service: Optional service identifier.
        entry_id: Optional specific entry identifier.

    Returns:
        JSON list of matching runbook entries, or {error} if neither
        filter is provided.

mcp__dolphinbench_apps__update_runbook_e.description:
Update a runbook entry, creating it if it does not already exist. The
    entry does NOT need to pre-exist — calling this with a new entry_id
    creates it. No prior lookup is required.

    Args:
        entry_id: Runbook entry identifier. Created if new.
        body: Optional complete replacement body (markdown). When supplied for
            an existing entry, it replaces that entry's entire current body.
        title: Optional new title.
        owner: Optional current primary owner identifier.
        backup: Optional current backup owner identifier.

    Returns:
        JSON {ok, entry_id, updated_at}.

mcp__dolphinbench_apps__create_doc.description:
Create a new document (notes / agenda / prep doc / one-pager).

    Args:
        title: Doc title (e.g. "Q3 offsite agenda — one day").
        body: Full doc body — markdown or plain text.
        folder: Optional folder / workspace name (e.g. "Eng", "Team").
            None means the user's default folder.

    Returns:
        JSON {ok, id, url} for the newly created doc.

# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

A reassessment was completed at 16:55, and the entry documenting it was made at 17:40.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The first run engaged the secondary at minute 47 while the cause remained unisolated, missing the required before-45-minute boundary. The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

# Training Appendix — INC-2023-04-18-001 (shard-keeper label-name drift)

**Use as:** a 10-minute case study in incident-practice modules covering alert-signal quality, cross-service change coordination, and rollback realism. Pairs naturally with the executable parity-fixture gate (introduced 2024-03-06) and the post-audit pre-push-sync rule.

## Incident in one paragraph
A label-name change shipped to shard-keeper but never propagated to rollup-service. All the symptom alerts fired; none of the cause alerts did. Sev2, ~8-hour window (page 21:42 ET on 4/18, clean ~05:45 ET on 4/19). Impaired ingestion through the window. **No data loss.**

## The misleading early branch (what to teach against)
- First ~hour of investigation chased a network-layer red herring. Symptoms looked like generic ingest weirdness, not "one label changed and one consumer never got the memo."
- Symptom-side dashboards (lag, retry, duplicate leadership) lit up loudly. Cause-side signals (label-name parity, producer/consumer key match) were silent because parity was only checked on the producer side at pre-push sync — rollup-service consumer was not in the room on 4/15.
- The find that broke it open was a manual diff, not an alert.

**Teaching point:** when symptoms look like generic ingest pathology and no cause alert is firing, the missing cause signal itself is the lead. A "clean" pre-push sync that covered only the producer side is not end-to-end clean.

## Confirmed data impact
- **Loss:** none. Ingestion was impaired/delayed, not lost.
- **Customer-visible shape:** delayed rollup publication across the window; no missing durable range; backlog fully drained after rollback.
- **Severity/seope:** Sev2, impaired ingestion, no escalation to Hema, Cyrus paged correctly and debriefed in the 4/19 morning DM.

## What made the rollback "shakier than it should have been"
- Estimated ~20 min; actual ~8 h. Path looked reversible on paper but state had partially moved, so each rollback step needed care.
- **Teaching point:** a rollback path that "looks reversible" before state has moved can still be fragile once state has. Pressure-clock estimates should assume at least one state-partition surprise for cross-service config drift.

## Carry-forward rules this case produced (do not relitigate in training)
- Executable parity fixture is a required production-review gate for covered cross-service label renames (Hema, 2024-03-06). Producer-side parity is not sufficient.
- Pre-push-sync rule remains in force after the real cutover close-out (2023-07-12).
- This appendix is the concrete case behind both rules; reference, do not re-derive.

## Facilitator notes
- Don't frame it as a network-layer failure. The network-layer branch was a time-sink, not the cause.
- Don't claim "no customer impact" — the right phrasing is *no data loss* with impaired ingestion and delayed publication.
- If asked "would the parity fixture have caught this?" the answer is yes — that is exactly the gap it was built to close.

---

Archive snapshot. Neutral side-by-side. No recommendation, no election.

Source: Sphere posted 2027 individual medical-plan terms on 2026-10-06. Terms recorded here as posted; no inferential numbers added. Gaps from the original posting are flagged explicitly.

Enrollment deadline
- Friday, October 23, 2026, 5:00 PM Eastern.
- Elections submitted during open enrollment are effective for the full 2027 plan year (Jan 1 – Dec 31, 2027) and may not be changed after the deadline without a qualifying life event (per Sphere 2027 benefits FAQ, 2026-10-11).
- If the HDHP is elected, the per-paycheck employee HSA payroll contribution may be adjusted during the plan year; changes apply to future payrolls only.

Plan-year frame
- Coverage window: January 1, 2027 – December 31, 2027.
- Pay frequency assumed for premium math: 26 biweekly paychecks.

Sphere Individual HDHP (2027)
- Premium: $98 per biweekly paycheck.
- Annual premium (26 paychecks): $2,548.
- Deductible: $2,300.
- Coinsurance: 10% after the deductible is met.
- Preventive care: fully covered.
- HSA-eligible: yes.
- Sphere employer HSA funding: $900 total, delivered as four $225 deposits in January, April, July, and October.

Sphere Individual PPO (2027)
- Premium: $164 per biweekly paycheck.
- Annual premium (26 paychecks): $4,264.
- Deductible: $750.
- Coinsurance: 20% after the deductible is met.
- Preventive care: fully covered.
- HSA-eligible: no.
- Sphere employer HSA funding: none.

Items not confirmed in this archive for the 2027 PPO
- Out-of-pocket maximum.
- Copays (primary care, specialist, ER, generic Rx, etc.).
- Separate Rx deductible, if any.
- Network details (in-network vs out-of-network cost shares).
- Family-tier implications.

Side-by-side at a glance
                        HDHP (2027)              PPO (2027)
  Premium / biweekly     $98                      $164
  Premium / annual       $2,548                   $4,264
  Annual gap (PPO − HDHP) —                       $1,716 (PPO higher)
  Deductible             $2,300                   $750
  Coinsurance            10% after deductible     20% after deductible
  Preventive             fully covered            fully covered
  HSA-eligible           yes                      no
  Employer HSA / yr      $900 (4 × $225)          none

Notes
- Both plans cover preventive care at 100% with no member cost share, so the premium and deductible/coinsurance shape only matters for non-preventive care.
- The HDHP's $2,300 deductible must be met (across non-preventive allowed costs) before 10% coinsurance applies; under the PPO, the $750 deductible must be met first, after which 20% coinsurance applies to non-preventive services subject to coinsurance rather than copays.
- Sphere's $900 employer HSA funding applies only to the HDHP and is delivered on a fixed quarterly schedule; it is not pro-rated by enrollment timing within the plan year beyond what Sphere's plan documents specify.

End of archive. No election recorded here; the 2027 election (HDHP, individual, $98 biweekly, $90 employee HSA × 26 = $2,340) was finalized separately on 2026-12-12 and is independent of this comparison document.

input.body:
Historical note (written 2028-01-01). How I prepared the service scope for the May 8, 2023 runbook-ownership audit that Hema was running.

Purpose of the prep
- Audit goal: every service had a primary owner and a backup owner, written down in the runbook, not "we'll figure it out."
- Kickoff was May 8; review was May 22. Enough runway to walk in with a real owner map rather than improvise in the room.

How I built the scope (May 2, before kickoff)
- Pulled the list of services I actually touched and grouped them honestly rather than padding:
    Directly owned: metrics-router, ingest-edge, shard-keeper.
    Kinda-owned by default: legacy-aggregator (nobody had finished the migration off it, so it landed on me), metric-rollup (basically unowned in practice, no one had adopted it).
- Five services total. I did not volunteer to adopt metric-rollup — the audit surfacing it was the audit doing its job.
- Named the gap out loud in prep rather than carrying it into the room as a surprise: the metric-rollup / rollup-service naming collision was already a known hazard (rollup-service was the one Apr 18 hit, Cyrus team owned it after the audit).

What I anchored deliberately
- Metrics-router, ingest-edge, shard-keeper as my primary-owned trio; backups already named (Wes, Yuki, Nadia).
- Shard-keeper runbook flagged in advance as the worst in the set: 18 months stale, still missing the newer label-routing content. This was the biggest audit workload and I budgeted for it.
- Open PRs I was carrying going into the audit: metrics-router#412 (mine, Nadia reviewing), metrics-router#414 (Nadia's, mine reviewing), shard-keeper#188 (mine, Nadia + Cyrus reviewing), shard-keeper#190 (Cyrus's, mine reviewing), ingest-edge#221 (Wes's, mine reviewing).

What I deliberately did NOT do
- Did not claim rollup-service as my own. Cyrus team owned it post-audit; that boundary was clean and I kept it clean.
- Did not promise to rewrite metric-rollup as part of the audit scope.
- Did not pre-resolve shard-keeper's backup-owner inconsistency in my head — flagged it as something to close in the room (rollback + ownership-history entries still pointed at cyrus_team while label-parity + cutover-status pointed at Nadia).

Net effect
- I walked into May 8 with a five-service scope, an honest read of which were mine vs which had drifted onto me, and the known-stale runbook already named. The scope was tight enough to finish in the runway; the gaps were named before the room, not discovered in it.

[2028-01-01] Last-hour snapshot — recommendation

metrics-router.p99_ms (1h, 5 samples): 181 / 180 / 182 / 181 / 180 ms. Flat, no regression.
replay-validator.mismatch_rate (1h, 5 samples): 0.003 → 0.006 → 0.012 → 0.021 → 0.034. Monotonic rise, ~11x in 60m, still accelerating at the latest sample.

Assessment
- The actionable signal is replay-validator.mismatch_rate, not metrics-router latency. metrics-router is healthy on the metric we just pulled.
- A metrics-router rollback is NOT supported by the current data — it targets a service that is not the source of the observed symptom. Roll it back only if the divergence localizes to metrics-router after replay-validator is ruled out.
- legacy-aggregator is not present in the service catalog; I have no telemetry on it. Any "restore legacy-aggregator" decision needs (a) confirmation of its current state, and (b) how its outputs feed the replay-validator comparison path. Both are unknowns from this snapshot.

Recommended next step (data first, action second)
1. Localize the divergence. Pull stored metrics on ingest-edge, metrics-pipeline, and rollup-service to see which feed replay-validator compares against and which one shifted.
2. Check whether the mismatch_rate rise correlates with a recent deploy / config / upstream shape change.
3. Only after the divergence is localized should we choose: metrics-router rollback, legacy-aggregator restore, or neither. Don't pick either yet.

Not recommending either proposed action at this time.

input.body:
North Pier,

Short answer: No — not under the agreement Anya signed.

The signed limited-use agreement grants North Pier a single, narrow license, and it does not authorize the use you are asking about. Here is exactly what the license allows, and only what it allows.

THE LICENSE
North Pier holds a non-exclusive, non-transferable limited recording license to Anya's November 18, 2024 handoff workshop recording. It is a paid license (a $175 flat fee was paid), not an assignment, not a work-for-hire, and not a release.

WHAT THE LICENSE ALLOWS — AND ONLY WHAT IT ALLOWS
The license permits exactly one thing: one edited cut of the recording, no longer than 45 minutes in duration, hosted for a 12-month term in North Pier's public resource library, with attribution to Anya as workshop facilitator, accurate captions reviewed by Anya, no sublicensing of any kind, and subject to the takedown mechanism described below.

The license does NOT authorize:
- Any separate social-media clip, teaser, excerpt, or derivative cut, regardless of length or platform.
- Any redistribution outside North Pier's public resource library, including to affiliates, partners, third-party platforms, syndication partners, podcast hosts, or AI/ML training pipelines.
- Any extension, renewal, or relicensing beyond the 12-month term.
- Any edit that exceeds 45 minutes, combines the recording with other content, or alters it in ways Anya has not approved in writing.
- Any retention of the master or the edit beyond the takedown deadlines below, in active storage, backups, disaster-recovery volumes, or any other medium.

THE EDIT ALLOWED — EXACTLY
- Source: the November 18, 2024 handoff workshop recording.
- Maximum length: 45 minutes. No exceptions.
- Content: a single bounded edit, cut only from that source recording. No recombination with other workshop content, no insertion of new material, no derivative work.
- Approval gate: publication required Anya's prior written approval of the final cut and her review of the captions. That approval has already been given for one specific 44-minute-38-second edit that North Pier hosted and later took down on Anya's written takedown notice of August 10, 2027.
- Attribution: "Anya — workshop facilitator," on the public page and on every public reference to the edit.
- Captions: must match what Anya reviewed; no silent re-captioning.
- Sublicensing: prohibited, in whole or in part, to any third party.
- Term: 12 months from publication. The 12-month clock ran against the hosted edit and has now been overtaken by the takedown.
- Fee: $175, already paid under the original agreement.

TAKEDOWN
On Anya's written takedown notice, North Pier must (a) disable public access within one business day and (b) complete permanent removal of the edit, including from any backups and disaster-recovery volumes, within five business days. Anya's August 10, 2027 notice triggered those obligations; public access was disabled August 11, 2027. As of last contact, North Pier had not yet established a license basis for the disaster-recovery copy or produced final purge evidence covering the full Aug 17 → final-purge window. That compliance question remains open.

ANSWER TO YOUR QUESTION
If you are asking whether the signed agreement lets North Pier use the recording for some new or continuing purpose beyond the bounded 45-minute public-library edit described above, the answer is no. The signed agreement does not cover it. Any new use — social clips, syndicated redistribution, relicensing beyond 12 months, derivative works, AI training, or retention of any copy after takedown — requires a new written license on terms Anya approves, and must at minimum preserve final-edit approval, caption review, attribution, no sublicensing, the same takedown deadlines, and a separately negotiated fee.

If you want to propose a specific new use, send the exact scope, length, platforms, term, approval workflow, caption handling, fee, and takedown terms, and Anya will review.

Anya

tests.request: Inspect rollup-service#884 and review its proposed tenant-size validation metric.

pr.author: devika
pr.description: Adds rollup_tenant_size_validation_total for tenant-size validation. The proposal exports tenant_hash, computed from the tenant ID, as a metric label on every validation sample. tenant_size_class is populated by lowercasing the tenant profile's configured size string without an allowlist; current examples include starter, growth, enterprise, custom, and other configured values. The PR notes propose that Observability maintain the class vocabulary and dashboard mapping.

files.patch:
+ Labels: tenant_hash, tenant_size_class
+ tenant_size_class accepts the normalized configured tenant-size string.
+ Observability will maintain class naming and dashboard mappings.

pr.title: rollup-service: publish tenant-size validation metric

input.body:
A few issues that should be addressed before this merges.

1. tenant_hash as a Prometheus label creates unbounded cardinality. One series per unique tenant; combined with tenant_size_class that's N_tenants × N_classes series, growing linearly with onboarding. This is the canonical way to break a Prometheus deployment.
   - If per-tenant attribution is needed, it belongs in logs/traces or a tenant-scoped export, not a shared counter.
   - If tenant_hash stays, the PR needs an explicit cardinality cap and a scrape-time relabel rule that drops overflow.

2. tenant_size_class has no allowlist. Lowercasing normalizes case but doesn't constrain values — any future string in Profile.Size (typos, "internal-test", freeform support notes) becomes a label value.
   - Allowlist to {starter, growth, enterprise, custom} at the emit site, returning "unknown" for anything else, OR
   - Pin the canonical set in the doc and add a relabel rule at scrape that drops non-canonical values.

3. Vocabulary ownership is misframed in the PR notes. The producer creates the labels; the metric has to be safe to emit regardless of who owns dashboards. Either the producer enforces the allowlist or the scrape config does — not "Observability will maintain it" post-hoc.

4. The diff I can see doesn't show: where hashTenantID is defined and whether it's stable across restarts and hash-function changes; where the CounterVec is registered; whether tests cover the label values. Hard to evaluate cardinality without these.

5. Worth stating in the doc: what question does this metric answer? "Validations by size class" doesn't need tenant_hash; "validations per tenant" doesn't need size_class. As written, both are co-emitted and the cardinality cost is multiplicative.

Happy to iterate — addressing 1-3 is the main thing. Once those are settled the smaller items can ride along.

1. Remove the affected replica from follower reads.
2. Verify that the lease holder and epoch remain stable, with no acquisition or relinquishment events, stale-owner messages, overlapping leadership, or write errors.
3. Confirm that the replica is making forward catch-up progress.
4. Re-enter the follower read pool only after disk latency is back at baseline and lag is below one second for fifteen continuous minutes.
5. Restart only if the replica stops progressing after the lease-safety checks. Do not use an automatic timer response as the restart condition.

entries.body:
Process readiness alone is not the exit condition. In the staging failover drill, all replacement replicas reported ready after 18 seconds, but lease ownership did not converge until 96 seconds. Before declaring the failover complete, verify all of the following: 1. Every partition has exactly one owner. 2. Lease epochs remain monotonic. 3. No stale-owner messages appear for two full lease-renewal intervals. If any of those checks fail, keep the failover open and page the shard-keeper owner. Renewal-warning versus lease transfer: `renewal deadline exceeded` alone does not prove a lease transfer. Check for a changed lease epoch, explicit acquisition or relinquishment, overlapping leadership, and post-event replication convergence. If the holder and epoch remain unchanged, no overlap occurs, and lag returns to baseline, treat the event as a delayed renewal rather than a failover; do not automatically restart.

## Production lease-loss serving-gate invariant

On lease-loss notification, close the old holder's serving gate before it can return another routing response. The periodic poll is only a backup detector, not the serving-safety mechanism. Production verification must include:
- gate closure before any later routing response
- exactly one serving holder throughout the transfer
- lease-loss notification to gate-close latency
- stale routing responses
- replacement acquisition time
- request p99
- errors
- restarts

A slow handoff or convergence warning is an availability signal to investigate separately. By itself, it is not evidence that the old holder served after lease loss or that the serving-safety invariant failed. The owner map and mapped deployment responsibility remain unchanged.

Cardinality Guardrails onboarding case study
First concrete prevention result — November 14, 2023

Scope of this doc
  This is a short onboarding case study for the first control slice of
  Cardinality Guardrails (recorded Oct 24, 2023, entry rb_1697635080004).
  It walks through one real prevention case so a new reviewer can see what
  "the checklist caught a bad label shape" actually looks like in practice.
  It is not a status report on Cardinality Guardrails overall.

Where the case sits in the control slice
  The first control slice has three controls:
    1. Label-cardinality preflight for metrics-router and shard-keeper
       changes.
    2. Alert-source classification so replay or mirror panels cannot read
       like live rollback triggers.
    3. Rollup-service parity before label-name changes cross service
       boundaries.
  The Nov 14 case is an example of Control 1 firing on a proposed shape
  before it shipped.

The case — rollup-service validation metrics proposal
  Proposed shape that did not ship:
    rollup_validation_sample_total{
      validation_result="match|mismatch",
      replay_source_id="$source_id"
    }
  Why the first-cut checklist rejected it:
    - replay_source_id is a raw replay-stream identifier.
    - Per Cyrus's sample, the value is effectively unbounded across replay
      sources, jobs, chunks, and backfills.
    - The debugging need was real, but the raw identifier belongs in logs,
      not as a metrics label.
  Accepted shape:
    - Keep raw replay_source_id in logs for debugging.
    - Use a bounded source_class metric label on the rollup-service
      validation dashboards.
    - Preserve validation visibility without introducing an unbounded
      label into the metrics pipeline.

What this case proves
  It proves the first-cut label-cardinality preflight can catch a bad
  label shape during review and steer the change to an equivalent shape
  that keeps the debugging signal without unbounded cardinality.

What this case does not prove
  - That Cardinality Guardrails is mature, complete, or a general
    telemetry rewrite.
  - That every high-cardinality label is automatically forbidden (the
    rule flags unbounded or one-off shapes, not customer_id).
  - That the alert-source or rollup-service parity controls are
    effective; each control needs its own evidence.

Onboarding takeaway
  When reviewing a metrics-router, shard-keeper, or rollup-service
  proposal, ask three questions in this order:
    1. Is every new or changed label in this proposal bounded? If not,
       can the unbounded value live in logs instead?
    2. If the dashboards behind this metric are used for rollback
       decisions, does the label set distinguish live traffic from
       replay or mirror validation?
    3. If a label name is being renamed, does the rollup-service side
       have a parity check before the change crosses the service
       boundary?
  A "no" on any of these is the same kind of catch the Nov 14 case
  produced: the debugging need survives, the unbounded shape does not.

tests.answer:
PR inspected: lantern#1602, "Lantern renderer: stabilize mixed-source chronology", author mira, branch mira/mixed-source-chronology, opened 2027-12-20, status open, reviewer alex, account scope Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Files changed: renderer/customer_chronology.ts, renderer/customer_chronology.test.ts.

1. Which timestamp controls visible order

  processed_at, descending. The sort is
    records.sort((a, b) => b.processed_at.localeCompare(a.processed_at))
  This is a pipeline timestamp, not a real-world event timestamp. The delayed_retry fixture confirms it: an incident_load with source_timestamp 08:12 and processed_at 09:03 renders before a deploy_event with source_timestamp 08:47 and processed_at 08:50. The deploy happened later in the world but its processed_at is earlier, so the chronology shows it second. Visible order is therefore processing order, not source-event order.

2. Timestamps current policy treats as audit-only

  Per the PR, the renderer carries four timestamps on every record: source_timestamp, observed_at, serialized_at, processed_at, retry_at. Of these:

    - processed_at is the sort key. It controls visible order, so it is not strictly audit-only, even though it is also internal metadata.
    - source_timestamp is the gating/required field. The renderer will not display anything if it cannot parse it. It is not audit-only.
    - observed_at, serialized_at, and retry_at are carried on each record but are not used for ordering, gating, or any visible logic. These are the audit-only set.

3. What happens when the required timestamp is missing or malformed

  Fail-closed, all-or-nothing. The implementation states: "If any required source_timestamp is absent or cannot be parsed, return { chronology: [] }." The malformed_required_source_timestamp fixture exercises this with the input "2027/13/40 25:61" and the rendered result is { chronology: [] }. Two consequences worth flagging:

    - The condition is any-record: if even one record in the set has a missing or unparseable source_timestamp, the entire chronology for that render is dropped, not just the offending record.
    - The drop is silent at the row level: customers see an empty chronology, not a partial list with a gap or an error placeholder. The renderer does not surface a per-row "timestamp invalid" message in the customer view.

4. Limits on what the chronology may claim

  Given the sort key and the fail-closed gate, the customer-visible chronology is constrained as follows:

    - It may not claim to be in real-world event order. The delayed_retry fixture is the canonical counterexample: a later-occurring source event (08:47) renders after an earlier-occurring one (08:12) because of pipeline timing. The chronology may only claim to reflect the order in which records were processed by the system.
    - It may not claim causal or sequential meaning across retries. A retry that lands later in the pipeline will appear later, regardless of when the underlying event actually occurred.
    - It may not claim completeness when source_timestamp validation fails. With any missing or unparseable required source_timestamp, the renderer returns an empty chronology. The product copy must therefore frame the chronology as a best-effort, processing-ordered view that can be entirely empty under validation failure, not as a guaranteed audit trail.
    - It may not imply that carried-but-audit-only timestamps (observed_at, serialized_at, retry_at) are visible ordering signals. They are carried for internal traceability; only processed_at drives order, and only source_timestamp gates display.

Net read for review: the change is scoped to the two customer accounts (Harbor Health, Mosaic Commerce) and tightens a previously loose ordering. The fail-closed behavior on bad source_timestamp is the safety property worth confirming with mira before approval, since it means a single bad record can blank a customer's timeline. The delayed_retry fixture is the right thing to flag in review comments so the docstring and any customer-facing copy that references "chronology" or "timeline" do not over-claim real-world ordering.
