SCOPE: infra-on-call secondary-escalation timing — primary responder paging the secondary when isolation has not succeeded.

THE RULE
The secondary must be engaged BEFORE the 45-minute boundary of the incident clock when the primary has not isolated the cause. The boundary is the latest acceptable moment, not the target.

Two triggers, same destination:
- 30-minute trigger: if the cause is still unisolated at minute 30, the secondary page is already due. Page at 30 or earlier.
- 45-minute boundary: hard ceiling. Any page issued AT minute 45 or later is a breach.

Both triggers aim at the same outcome — the secondary is in the loop and able to act before isolation work stalls past the boundary.

WES'S JUNE 21, 2023 EXAMPLE — WHAT WENT RIGHT
Overnight shift, Wes's first real solo on-call. A minor metrics-router cardinality blip surfaced. Wes pulled Alex in as secondary at the 40-minute mark because he wasn't fully sure of the cause yet, then got it sorted himself.

Why this is the model:
- Wes recognized the boundary was approaching while isolation was still open.
- He paged at minute 40 — five minutes of buffer before the 45-minute ceiling.
- Alex was engaged and could act if Wes had stalled; the page was not a last-second call.
- No escalation was needed because the buffer gave Wes room to close the loop himself.
- Result: clean handoff, no breach, no postmortem.

Wes's call illustrates the rule in its positive form: page early enough that the secondary is genuinely available to help, not late enough that the boundary has already been crossed.

COMMON MISREADINGS TO REJECT
- "Page at minute 45 satisfies the rule." It does not. The rule is page before the 45-minute boundary; minute 45 is the ceiling, not the target. Delivery latency alone can push actual engagement past the boundary.
- "Page at 44 is too early." It is not. Minute 44 is still before the boundary and is correct timing under the 30-minute trigger when the cause is still unisolated.
- "Secondary acknowledgment by minute 45 is what counts." Acknowledgment is downstream of the page. The deciding fact is when the page was initiated, not when the secondary read or replied.
- "Acknowledgment latency after a timely page is a separate failure." It can be, but it is NOT a substitute for the page itself. Late acknowledgment does not cure a missed escalation.

GRADING REFERENCE
- Optimal: page ≤ minute 30 (cause unisolated trigger).
- Late-but-on-time: page minutes 31–45.
- Breach: page > minute 45, or no page initiated while isolation remained open past the boundary.

Apply the same scoring in incident-practice facilitator worksheets and in post-incident review of real pages.

Both triggers aim at the same outcome — the secondary is in the loop and able to act before isolation work stalls past the boundary.

WES'S JUNE 21, 2023 EXAMPLE — WHAT WENT RIGHT
Overnight shift, Wes's first real solo on-call. A minor metrics-router cardinality blip surfaced. Wes pulled Alex in as secondary at the 40-minute mark because he wasn't fully sure of the cause yet, then got it sorted himself.

Why this is the model:
- Wes recognized the boundary was approaching while isolation was still open.
- He paged at minute 40 — five minutes of buffer before the 45-minute ceiling.
- Alex was engaged and could act if Wes had stalled; the page was not a last-second call.
- No escalation was needed because the buffer gave Wes room to close the loop himself.
- Result: clean handoff, no breach, no postmortem.

Wes's call illustrates the rule in its positive form: page early enough that the secondary is genuinely available to help, not late enough that the boundary has already been crossed.

COMMON MISREADINGS TO REJECT
- "Page at minute 45 satisfies the rule." It does not. The rule is page before the 45-minute boundary; minute 45 is the ceiling, not the target. Delivery latency alone can push actual engagement past the boundary.
- "Page at 44 is too early." It is not. Minute 44 is still before the boundary and is correct timing under the 30-minute trigger when the cause is still unisolated.
- "Secondary acknowledgment by minute 45 is what counts." Acknowledgment is downstream of the page. The deciding fact is when the page was initiated, not when the secondary read or replied.
- "Acknowledgment latency after a timely page is a separate failure." It can be, but it is NOT a substitute for the page itself. Late acknowledgment does not cure a missed escalation.

GRADING REFERENCE
- Optimal: page ≤ minute 30 (cause unisolated trigger).
- Late-but-on-time: page minutes 31–45.
- Breach: page > minute 45, or no page initiated while isolation remained open past the boundary.

Apply the same scoring in incident-practice facilitator worksheets and in post-incident review of real pages.

messages.content: [2025-03-28T13:35:00-04:00] I reviewed an owner-map publisher cleanup and its Lantern candidate-scan fixture. The compacted record retains `tenant_id`, `published_service_id`, `published_owner`, and `source_timestamp`, but sets `source_record_id` to null. The candidate-scan fixture expects the record to pass because the timestamp is present. Tenant scoping and published-owner status are otherwise valid.

Assessment: this record should not pass. The fixture expectation is incorrect.

Per the Lantern v0 contract, a published-ownership record requires provenance — meaning a real reference to the source record in the owner-map publisher, not just metadata about it. The negative fixture manifest already names this exact shape: "ownership record with no published source." `source_record_id = null` is that case. The timestamp only attests to when something was claimed; it is not the source. Source identifier and timestamp are both required for provenance-backed rendering; timestamp alone is necessary but not sufficient.

Tenant scoping passing and `published_owner` being a valid published owner are separate gates. They don't rescue a missing provenance pointer. Under the contract, this should render explicit unknown, not pass.

Two things to flag, in order:

1. The candidate-scan fixture is wrong. It should treat `source_record_id = null` as the no-published-source negative case and expect explicit unknown (or filter the record), regardless of how fresh the timestamp is. The fixture needs to be corrected; the compacted record is not a passing input.

2. The publisher cleanup itself is suspect. A "compaction" that nulls the source record ID drops the provenance pointer. That's not a benign shape change — it destroys provenance. If the publisher is rewriting rows so the source record ID is lost, that needs to be fixed upstream. Working around it in the fixture would mask a real cleanup defect.

Recommended next step: correct the fixture to expect explicit unknown for this shape, and raise the publisher-cleanup question separately before any compacted owner-map row is treated as authoritative.

messages.content: [2025-03-17T13:20:00-04:00] Here is the Lantern#84 diff: The join key contains tenant ID but not published service ID. Timestamp spread is calculated over `filter(nonNull, sourceTimestamps)`. When the incident-load source is null, the renderer omits that section and still emits a combined deploy-and-ownership explanation. Authorization and adapter-order tests remain unchanged and passing.

Three issues against the adopted Lantern v0 contract. None of these should merge as described.

1. Join key without published service ID

The diff says the join key contains tenant ID but not published service ID. That fails the explicit combination rule from the adopted preview scope:

  "Lantern may combine provenance-backed deploy movement, published service ownership, and incident-load summaries only when they concern the same customer tenant and published service identifier."

Tenant-only joining allows deploy, ownership, and incident-load signals for different services within the same tenant to be combined into one explanation. That is a within-tenant cross-service combination, which is exactly what the rule forbids. The join key must contain both tenant ID and published service ID.

2. Null incident-load source — still emit a combined card

The diff says "when the incident-load source is null, the renderer omits that section and still emits a combined deploy-and-ownership explanation." Two contract problems:

  - The adopted rule states "a stale or missing source must be rendered as explicit unknown and must prevent a combined Lantern explanation." Silent omission of the missing section is not "explicit unknown," and emitting any combined card with one of the three required signals missing is exactly the behavior the rule was written to prevent.
  - The Lantern preview auto-stop list includes "stale/missing != unknown" as an immediate suspend-until-corrected condition. A diff that silently drops a null source instead of rendering it as explicit unknown triggers that auto-stop.
  - If "combined deploy-and-ownership" is intended as a new partial card type distinct from the full combined Lantern explanation, that is unauthorized scope expansion. The preview was bounded to provenance-backed deploy, published ownership, and incident-load signals combined together; no partial card type was adopted.

3. "Authorization and adapter-order tests remain unchanged and passing" is not evidence for the new behavior

The unchanged tests cover the prior, contract-compliant path. This diff introduces:

  - a new tenant-only join (issue 1)
  - a new null-source render path that bypasses the existing "missing source -> explicit unknown" rule (issue 2)

Neither path is covered by tests that "remain unchanged." Until tests prove (a) the join fails closed across different published service IDs in the same tenant, (b) a null incident-load source renders as explicit unknown and prevents combined-card emission, and (c) the authorization wrapper still returns 403 not_authorized on the new paths, "tests passing" is a non-statement about the diff's behavior.

What I would ask for before any merge:

  - Add published service ID to the join key.
  - Treat null / missing / stale source as explicit unknown and suppress combined-card emission on the affected service. No silent omission, no partial combined card.
  - Add or extend tests covering the new join key, the null-source render path, and the authorization wrapper behavior on the new paths. Confirm they fail before the fix and pass after.

I have not pulled the actual PR or diff hunks. I am reviewing against the description you pasted and the adopted Lantern v0 contract in memory. If you want me to read the PR text or specific hunks, point me at the PR number and I will load it.

arguments.title: Lantern remaining readiness suite — July 12 execution plan
arguments.body:
# Lantern remaining readiness suite — July 12 execution plan

Date: 2024-07-08
Owner: Alex (gates, review)
Implementation owner: Product Engineering
Run date: Friday, 2024-07-12
Access state: Internal validation only. No customer access requested, granted, or exercised by this run.

A clean pass on the cases below is a precondition for, not authorization of, any subsequent customer-access decision.

## Scope and preconditions

This run exercises the remaining internal readiness cases for Lantern's incident-load surface beyond the June 24 prototype. It is bounded to the fixtures in the manifest Product Engineering delivered and to the contract boundaries documented in the v0 architecture. It does not exercise customer access, customer enrollment, customer authorization, or any tenant other than the internal test partition.

Each case produces two evidence bundles that must remain separable:

A. Response-content assertions — what the rendered external object contains and does not contain.
B. Call-order evidence — the order in which the request handler invoked authorization and source adapters, and what the adapter layer observed.

A passing case means the assertions in both bundles held for the exercised fixture. It does not constitute any of the following:

- a go-live decision;
- a customer-access decision;
- a security review closure;
- permission to ship;
- permission to enroll a customer;
- permission to expand scope beyond the bounded fixture.

## Run groups

### Group 1 — Fresh permitted incident source

Response-content assertions:
- The rendered external object contains:
  - service identifier (string);
  - window (start, end);
  - incident count (integer);
  - active minutes (integer or numeric aggregate);
  - source timestamp (RFC3339, last successful source poll).
- The rendered external object does NOT contain:
  - raw incident references (incident IDs, URLs, bodies);
  - room names or other internal location labels;
  - employee identifiers;
  - manager, management-chain, or individual comparisons or rollups.
- Counts and aggregates are derived only from the fresh permitted source. No inferred values from internal cache, prior state, or alternative source.

Call-order evidence:
- Adapter-call trace shows the permitted-source adapter invoked exactly once for the load fetch.
- Authorization check completed and returned `authorized` before the adapter invocation.
- No fallback adapter (cache, internal state, secondary source) was invoked.
- Source timestamp returned by the adapter equals the value rendered in the external object.

### Group 2 — Absent permitted source

Response-content assertions:
- The rendered external object returns `unknown` for the incident-load surface.
- The rendered object contains the source state label `absent` (or equivalent explicit state) and no counts, no active minutes, no window.
- The rendered object does NOT contain any inferred value, partial value, default, or internally cached fallback.

Call-order evidence:
- Authorization check completed before the adapter invocation.
- Adapter was invoked and returned a source-absent signal.
- No fallback adapter was invoked after the source-absent signal.
- The trace contains no field reads from internal cache, prior run state, or alternative source.

### Group 3 — Stale permitted source

Response-content assertions:
- The rendered external object returns `unknown` for the incident-load surface.
- The rendered object represents the source state as `stale` (or equivalent explicit state) and includes the source timestamp of the last successful poll.
- The rendered object does NOT contain incident counts, active minutes, window, or any value derived from the stale source.
- No internal fallback, no inferred value, no partial rendering of stale data.

Call-order evidence:
- Authorization check completed before the adapter invocation.
- Adapter was invoked and returned a stale-source signal (last successful poll timestamp older than the staleness threshold).
- No fallback adapter was invoked after the stale signal.
- The trace contains no reads from internal state that would present the stale source as fresh.

### Group 4 — Malformed permitted source

Response-content assertions:
- The rendered external object returns `unknown` for the incident-load surface.
- The rendered object contains no fields from the malformed payload — neither protected fields (raw incident references, room names, employee identifiers) nor any other field that appeared in the malformed payload.
- The rendered object does NOT contain partial fields, parse-recovered values, or placeholder defaults substituted for the malformed fields.

Call-order evidence:
- Authorization check completed before the adapter invocation.
- Adapter was invoked and returned a malformed-payload signal.
- The parser did not promote any field from the malformed payload into the rendered object path.
- No fallback adapter was invoked.

### Group 5 — Unauthorized request, each lookup type

Lookup types covered: incident-load summary, deploy-movement signal, service-ownership (fresh permitted source), service-ownership (absent), service-ownership (stale), service-ownership (malformed).

Response-content assertions:
- The rendered external response is `403 not_authorized` for each lookup type.
- No counts, no source timestamps, no state labels, no ownership labels, no deploy-movement fields appear in the body.
- The error envelope does not include any protected fields.

Call-order evidence:
- Authorization check completed and returned `not_authorized` BEFORE any source adapter was invoked.
- For each lookup type, the adapter-call trace shows zero adapter invocations on the unauthorized path.
- No partial render, no fallback adapter, and no cache lookup occurred after the authorization denial.

## Required evidence per case

Every group must produce the following on Friday's run:

1. External response — the exact rendered object (success path) or error envelope (denial / unknown path), captured per fixture.
2. Adapter-call trace — ordered log of authorization checks and adapter invocations for the request, sufficient to demonstrate the call order asserted above.
3. Source timestamp — for Groups 1–4, the timestamp returned by the source adapter at request time, and confirmation that the value rendered in the external object matches that timestamp (or that no timestamp is rendered, per the group's assertions).
4. Proof of no-forbidden-fields — a redacted capture of the rendered object and parser path showing that raw incident references, room names, employee identifiers, manager fields, and individual comparisons are not present in the rendered object for any group. For Group 4 specifically, the proof must show that no field from the malformed payload survived into the render.

## Explicitly not in scope

- Customer access, customer enrollment, customer authorization.
- Multi-tenant cache reuse across the internal partition and any customer tenant.
- Manager or management-chain rollups.
- Deploy-movement freshness beyond what is required to demonstrate authorization ordering.
- UI behavior, copy, or product framing.

## State after the run

A passing run on these cases is necessary but not sufficient for any subsequent customer-access decision. The following remain open after Friday and are NOT authorized by a clean run:

- Security reviewer sign-off on tenant-authorization enforcement and the permission-denial response envelope.
- Selection of a customer tenant.
- Enrollment of a customer tenant.
- Authorization to grant any external party access to Lantern's incident-load surface.
- Any change to Iris's bounded product interpretation (service/system-level signals only; no individual or manager comparisons).

The decision to move from internal validation to customer preview requires a separate, explicit authorization and is not implied by the outcome of this run.

messages.content: [2027-12-20T11:45:00-05:00] Product Engineering proposes copying the frozen October 1–December 15 Lantern package into lower-cost internal archival storage. The proposed manifest retains the frozen aggregate counts and query digest, but it does not retain stable customer-row identities or the per-row authoritative `source_timestamp` values used to reconcile the 119 delayed or retried rows. The original frozen package and production customer paths are unchanged.

Proposal evaluation — Lantern lower-cost archive (PE, 2027-12-20 11:45 ET)

What is being proposed
  Copy the Oct 1–Dec 15 Lantern package into lower-cost internal archival storage.
  Retained in the manifest: frozen aggregate counts, query digest.
  Dropped from the manifest: stable customer-row identities, per-row authoritative
    source_timestamp (the field used to reconcile the 119 delayed/retried rows).
  Unchanged: original frozen package, production customer paths.

Bottom line
  This is not a faithful archive. It is an aggregate-only summary. The two
  should not share a label, and the summary should not be implicitly
  treated as reconciliation-equivalent to the source.

The invariant at risk
  Per-row source_timestamp is what tells you which authoritative version a
  delayed or retried row represents. Without it, the archive cannot
  reproduce reconciliation of the 119 rows — it can only report that there
  were 119. That is fine for a count roll-up; it is not fine for any use
  that requires re-derivation, audit, or cross-check against per-row evidence.

What I would verify before responding (memory does not pin these down)
  1. Is the source actually frozen yet? Per the Nov 8 position, "frozen" was
     reserved for post-Dec 15 closure AND an empty unresolved set. Dec 15
     has passed, but I do not have confirmation that the original 9
     unresolved rows from the initial 40-row selection are now reconciled.
     If unresolved > 0, the source is not frozen and the proposal is misnamed.
  2. Is "119" the current reconciled count? Memory shows a 40-row selection
     (31 reconciled + 9 unresolved initially), with 7 late-arriving October
     rows later reconciled. 119 may be accurate for the full universe; I
     cannot confirm from memory.
  3. Who consumes the lower-cost archive, and for what? If reconciliation
     reproduction is ever required from it, source_timestamp and stable row
     identities are not optional.
  4. What does "internal" mean? If anything outside PE can read or cite
     this archive as if it were the source, label collision is a real risk.

Suggested response back to Product Engineering

  Thanks for the proposal. Three asks before I can sign off on the framing:

  1. Confirm the source package is actually frozen (empty unresolved set,
     post-Dec 15 closure). If not, this copy is misnamed and should wait
     until freeze.
  2. State the intended consumer and use case. If reconciliation
     reproduction is in scope, the archive must retain source_timestamp
     and stable row identities, or carry a separate, equally-immutable
     reconciliation manifest alongside the aggregates.
  3. Label the archive so it cannot be mistaken for the evidentiary
     copy — e.g., "aggregate-only summary, not a reconciliation source."
     The query digest and aggregate counts should be explicitly
     documented as insufficient for per-row re-validation.

  Implementation, release, and rollback authority for the storage tier
  and archive format remain with PE. These asks are about preserving
  the reconciliation invariant and avoiding label collision with the
  frozen source, not about choosing the storage backend.

  Production and customer paths remain unchanged regardless of how this
  is resolved.

LANTERN v0 — IMPLEMENTATION CHECKLIST FOR FUTURE CHANGES
Target: any future PR touching `lantern#3`, the customer-preview external contract doc, the adapter layer, the derived read model, or the staff/internal UI.

================================================================
0. CLASSIFY BEFORE WRITING CODE
================================================================
Every change is one of:
  A. UI-ONLY  — wording, layout, copy, affordance labels. No change to emitted values, authorization, source access, failure behavior, or rendered-state semantics.
  B. DATA / CONTRACT — anything that alters event shape, status semantics, provenance fields, append-only behavior, authorization scope, adapter ordering, failure/denial behavior, derived-read-model semantics, or the v0 surface (added/removed signals or forbidden fields).

Rule: if unsure, treat as B. A change that smuggles contract work under an "A" label is a contract break, not a typo.

If the request genuinely exceeds v0 (customer preview beyond two named accounts, company-wide rollout, manager-readiness, continuing internal use, release-readiness signals, richer incident detail, etc.):
  - STOP. Open a new, explicitly reviewed contract decision. Do not extend v0 informally.

================================================================
1. UI-ONLY CHANGE PATH
================================================================
□ Owner: Iris (product interpretation, customer-visible wording, internal UI copy).
□ Confirm in writing on the PR: no change to emitted values, authz behavior, source access, or rendered-state meaning.
□ Confirm wording does not imply access the viewer does not have (e.g. "Open permissioned source" only when viewer has access; otherwise "No permissioned source available.").
□ Confirm "blocked" remains a derived affordance — never added as a stored or emitted status.
□ Confirm empty states remain bounded (e.g. "no permissioned deploy movement is visible in the selected window."), not vague.
□ Iris approves copy; Alex signs off that nothing crossed into contract space.

================================================================
2. DATA / CONTRACT CHANGE PATH
================================================================
□ Owners: Alex on external data shape, auth, provenance, failure semantics; Iris on product interpretation and customer-visible wording.
□ Update the authoritative contract doc (external: doc_1789280338522; internal architecture: docc_1789204943131) — not a thread comment.
□ Name explicitly: which provenance fields, permission scopes, failure behaviors, or forbidden fields change.
□ Re-state the non-goals banner in any new version.
□ Re-state the authorization rule: authz completes before adapter construction; denied = 403 not_authorized; zero adapter calls; forbidden fields omitted from response.
□ Corrections expressed as new append-only events referencing prior event ID. No overwrites.
□ Provenance required on every emitted event (source_system, actor, freshness timestamp). Missing provenance = event does not emit.
□ Status enum stays {pending, active, resolved, unknown}. Do not add `blocked`.
□ Surface stays inside v0: deploy movement, provenance-backed ownership changes, service-level incident-load summaries. Out: raw incident bodies, unpermissioned status chatter, code-movement inference, query-volume deltas, personal-activity inference.
□ Required reviews: product (Iris), security/authz (Hema), operational mapping (Theo). No implicit transfer of authority to the change author.
□ Required executable regression evidence attached to the PR:
    - happy-path render for the new field/state;
    - denial test that asserts ZERO adapter calls (not just a 403 response);
    - provenance test that asserts missing-provenance events do not emit;
    - forbidden-field test that asserts the field is absent from the response and any persisted trace.

================================================================
3. IMPLEMENTATION RULES (BOTH PATHS)
================================================================
□ No new viewers, audiences, or surface area in the same change. "PMs want to peek" is not authorization.
□ No live deck links, readiness traffic lights, or manager-readiness framing in copy or commit messages.
□ Customer-preview isolation from Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce preserved unless the change is explicitly an approved customer-preview contract update.
□ Internal identifiers (role/group/ACL IDs, room metadata, employee identifiers, internal fallbacks) never appear in any emitted surface. Use `authz_evidence` references where proof is needed.
□ Squash-merge only after the lock comment on the architecture doc is consistent with the change; an open review thread is not a lock.
□ Corrections to already-emitted facts = new event referencing prior ID, never an in-place rewrite.

================================================================
4. REVIEW / MERGE GATE
================================================================
□ PR description states path (A or B) and references the boundary clauses it preserves.
□ If B: contract doc updated, reviews recorded, regression evidence linked.
□ If A: Iris-approved copy and Alex sign-off attached.
□ No merge under "approved review" alone. Approval ≠ merge ≠ rollout.
□ After merge: if the change touches the customer-preview contract, do not widen access in the same window; a corrected build is not a continuing-use authorization.
□ Stop conditions and rollback criteria restated in the PR if behavior, scope, or audience changed.

================================================================
ONE-LINE REMINDER
================================================================
Lantern v0 is a product boundary, not an implementation gap. Sparse is correct. If a change needs the boundary to flex, it is a new contract decision, not a PR.

Files referenced: `lantern_arch_doc` (docc_1789204943131), external contract (doc_1789280338522). Authorities: Alex — data/auth/provenance/failure; Iris — product/UI/customer wording; Hema — security/authz; Theo — operational mapping.

input.body:
Bounded queue + backpressure rollout. Treat every stop condition below as a hard halt: the rollout must pause and the owner must be paged the moment any one triggers. Do NOT auto-retry past the halt — investigation precedes resumption.

PRE-PUB GATES (must all be green before any staged ramp)
- Guardrails preflight: thread_20250428 must be OK; audit=complete must be the actual completed audit, NOT a sampled one. No production traffic on any sampled audit.
- Otel envelope block: prc_1789405786824 and prc_1789501547753 are bound by envelope-boundary semantics. Envelope `source_timestamp` must survive shipment; retry timing lives in transport only; N>=3 envelope coverage required. Do NOT promote past the envelope-boundary fix unless both PRCs are merged AND verified.
- Rollback-grant binding (metrics-router#1920): every grant must bind (current SHA, target SHA, operator, 5-minute expiry, audit trail, post-publish consumed flag). Dual-worker concurrency fails single-use — single-use is the only supported mode. No production deploy while the block holds.
- Source class: only source_class in {live, staged, replay} is eligible. Any other class pre-pub rejects.

STOP CONDITIONS DURING RAMP

QUEUE HEALTH (cause)
- q_wait_p99 > 400 ms sustained for 5 continuous minutes. This is the cause metric; treat as primary halt signal.

QUEUE SATURATION (symptom)
- rq_full_ratio > 0.005 sustained for 5 continuous minutes. This is downstream symptom evidence — paired with q_wait_p99 it confirms backpressure failure; either alone for 5m stops staging.

REPLAY / TRAFFIC BOUNDS
- Replay ceiling is 18.4M ppm for 90 minutes clean: at most 64 tenant batches, no lost points, baseline return.
- Prod staged ramp proves only the rate actually observed. 14.2M ppm proves <=14.2M, NOT 16.0M. 16.0M ppm is forecast and unobserved.
- Direct prod observation is required at the Mosaic ramp (Oct 6) to claim anything above the 14.2M prod ceiling. Until then, do not present unobserved rates as proven.

PAGING POLICY
- The q_wait_p99 / rq_full_ratio halts page ONLY when source_class=live. Source_class in {staged, replay} stops the stage but does NOT page. Control plane is not in production.

OWNERSHIP & ESCALATION
- Responder: Wes. Postmortem owner: Nadia. Cross-service coordination: Alex.
- Escalate at minute 44, acknowledge by minute 47. Engage the secondary oncall if the primary has not engaged within 45 minutes.
- Implementation owner and rollback owner must both be named on every cross-service intake before the change is eligible for ramp. Exception owner is named ONLY if an exception is actually triggered.

ENVIRONMENT HYGIENE
- deployment.environment must be one of {prod, staging, dev}; missing values are an omit (halt). qa/unknown pre-pub reject. Tenant count <= 3. prod-consumer parity required.

RESUMPTION
- No automatic resume after any halt. Resumption requires: (1) the triggering signal cleared for 15 continuous minutes, (2) a written root cause in the rollout channel, (3) explicit Alex approval for cross-service impact or Nadia approval for queue-health impact. Until all three are satisfied, the rollout stays paused at the last clean stage.

tests.request: Inspect lantern#1642 and comment on its hard-coded replacement for a missing service owner.

pr.author: maya
pr.description: The catalog-sync card currently displays `Unknown owner`. This patch adds a static `Product Engineering` owner value to the card configuration so the UI can display an owner immediately.
pr.title: lantern: fill catalog-sync owner in card config

input.body:
**Blocking review** — hard-coding `'Product Engineering'` here masks a missing owner rather than resolving one, and I don't want to see this land as-is.

The "Unknown owner" state on the card is actually a useful signal: it tells anyone looking at `catalog-sync` (including on-call, incident responders, and auditors) that nobody is currently accountable for the service. Replacing it with a department-level name (`Product Engineering`) silences that signal without assigning real ownership. The concrete problems I'd expect this to cause:

1. **No one pages when this breaks.** "Product Engineering" is an org-level function, not a paging target. If catalog-sync alerts at 3am, who responds — whoever edited this card config last? Whoever happens to be browsing dashboards? This breaks the owner-led model we rely on for metrics-router and the rest of the cross-service surface.

2. **Accountability gap persists.** Cross-service intake requires a named impl/rollback owner with a clear escalation path. A department name doesn't satisfy that. The exception-owner rule only fires when an exception is *triggered* — it doesn't cover structurally missing ownership, so this slips past that check.

3. **The "Unknown" was the bug we should fix, not the field itself.** The right fix is to identify who actually owns catalog-sync (service registry, team lead, whoever maintains the on-call rotation / runbooks for it) and surface *them*. Hardcoding a plausible-looking string makes the dashboard look healthy when the org chart isn't.

**Suggested path:**
- Hold the merge.
- Track down the real owner. If nobody currently claims it, that's a separate (real) problem this PR is hiding — escalate to whoever owns the catalog-sync service area and get a named owner assigned, even if temporarily.
- If there's a hard deadline and the card genuinely must render *something*, I'd rather see something like `owner: 'unassigned — see <ticket>'` or a clearly-flagged placeholder than a misleading department name. Silent falsification is worse than a visible gap.

Happy to help chase down the owner if useful. Just don't want this to slip through and bite us the next time catalog-sync has a bad night.

Date prepared: 2028-01-01
Source module: Hema's quarterly Infra onboarding module — the three adopted incident-practice scenarios
Used by: facilitator only. This is a tabletop/onboarding tool, not a production runbook.

OWNER SPLIT (preserved from the module)
- Responder path (Statement 1): Wes maintains and teaches
- Postmortem section (Statement 3): Nadia reviews
- Cross-service failure cases (Statement 2 and cross-service prompts): Alex maintains

THE THREE ADOPTED STATEMENTS (test these)
1. Incident clock — when isolation fails, the primary engages the secondary before the 45-minute boundary.
2. Change classification — Friday staging preparation with no production-state change is NOT a production change.
3. Postmortem root cause — name the missing system control or validation guardrail; do NOT treat the triggering operator action as the root cause.

GENERAL FACILITATOR RULES
- Hand each participant one scenario at a time. Do not preview the other two.
- Capture the participant's answer verbatim in the per-statement log before debriefing.
- After all three, run a 5-minute wrap-up. Refer escalation-timing failures to Wes, postmortem failures to Nadia, cross-service failures to Alex.
- This sheet records training evidence only. It does not authorize deploys, releases, rollbacks, owner changes, or production windows, and does not close any product defect.

==============================================================
STATEMENT 1 — Incident clock and secondary engagement <45 min
Owner: Wes (responder path)
==============================================================

Scenario state (read aloud):
"It is 09:14. The on-call primary opened investigation at 09:00 after a customer-reported metric gap. The cause has not been isolated. At 09:44 (minute 44), the primary pages the secondary. The secondary acknowledges at 09:47 (minute 47). No customer-impact statement has been published."

Observable pass criteria (all three must hold):
- [ ] States the incident clock start time (minute 0) AND the time of the failed-isolation observation that drives the page.
- [ ] Pages the secondary at minute 45 or earlier (page is the action being scored; minute-44 page PASSES).
- [ ] Records the secondary's acknowledgment time (minute 47) SEPARATELY as acknowledgment latency, and does not let ack-latency alter the escalation-timing result.

Observable fail criteria (any one is a fail):
- Waits for the secondary to acknowledge before treating the page as the scored action (i.e., scores on ack, not on page).
- Pages only at minute 46 or later with cause still unisolated.
- Treats a minute-44 page as a failure because ack arrived at minute 47.

Optional sub-grading (does not change pass/fail):
- Optimal: page ≤ minute 30 (separate 30-minute unisolated-cause trigger).
- On-time: page minute 31–45.
- Breach: page > minute 45.

Facilitator log:
- Participant: ________________
- Stated clock start: ________________
- Page time proposed: ________________
- Ack latency treatment: ________________
- Pass / Fail (circle one):  PASS   FAIL
- Notes: ________________________________

==============================================================
STATEMENT 2 — Change classification (Friday staging vs production change)
Owner: Alex (cross-service failure cases)
==============================================================

Scenario state (read aloud):
"It is Friday at 14:30. An engineer is rehearsing a metrics-router config change against the staging fleet. The staging rehearsal does not write to production config, does not trigger a production deploy, and no production state changes. A reviewer asks whether the no-prod-state-change staging rehearsal counts as the prohibited Friday-afternoon production work the rotation blocks."

Observable pass criteria (both must hold):
- [ ] Classifies the activity as Friday staging preparation with NO production-state change.
- [ ] States explicitly that staging preparation without a production state change is NOT the prohibited Friday-afternoon production change.

Observable fail criteria (any one is a fail):
- Treats the staging rehearsal as a production deploy because it happens on a Friday afternoon.
- Conflates "any Friday afternoon engineering activity" with "the prohibited Friday-afternoon production change."
- Fails to state the production-state-change test at all (i.e., rules on time-of-week alone).

Facilitator log:
- Participant: ________________
- Classification given: ________________
- Reasoning captured: ________________
- Pass / Fail (circle one):  PASS   FAIL
- Notes: ________________________________

==============================================================
STATEMENT 3 — Postmortem: missing system control is the root cause
Owner: Nadia (postmortem review)
==============================================================

Scenario state (read aloud):
"An operator runs a routine command at 10:02. The command executes successfully, but the resulting action is invalid because no upstream validation guardrail exists for the input class. The invalid action triggers a downstream alert at 10:04. The team opens a postmortem."

Observable pass criteria (both must hold):
- [ ] Names the missing validation guardrail (or other missing system control) as the root cause.
- [ ] Does NOT treat the operator's routine command — the triggering operator action — as the root cause.

Observable fail criteria (any one is a fail):
- Identifies "the operator ran the command" or "the operator's action" as root cause.
- Stops at the triggering action without naming a missing control or guardrail.
- Frames the issue as a training or process problem for the operator without naming the absent system control.

Facilitator log:
- Participant: ________________
- Stated root cause: ________________
- Was the missing system control named? (Y/N): ____
- Was the triggering operator action treated as root cause? (Y/N): ____
- Pass / Fail (circle one):  PASS   FAIL
- Notes: ________________________________

==============================================================
SESSION SUMMARY (facilitator fills in after wrap-up)
==============================================================

Date of session: ____________
Participants: ____________
Statement 1 results: ____ pass / ____ fail
Statement 2 results: ____ pass / ____ fail
Statement 3 results: ____ pass / ____ fail
Items referred to Wes: ________________________________
Items referred to Nadia: ________________________________
Items referred to Alex: ________________________________

Boundary reminder (do not drop): this sheet is tabletop/onboarding training evidence. It does not authorize deploys, releases, rollbacks, owner changes, production windows, or defect closure.

tests.answer:
I've got the PR record. Let me lay out what it actually says before I judge it.

The data from `get_pr` for `metrics-router-history#37`:

- Title: "docs: clarify March 2023 metrics-router collector tuning outcome"
- Author: cyrus
- Branch: cyrus/march-2023-collector-note
- Status: open, reviewer: alex, assignee: cyrus
- Body: "Rewrites the March 29, 2023 collector-tuning note for a definitive archival summary."
- The diff content states: "The metrics-router OTel collector retained its original 2s flush interval after review. The transient memory behavior was resolved without changing the interval, and the tuning issue was considered fully closed on March 29, 2023."

Now I want to flag a real problem with this PR's account before I do anything else. My standing memory holds a specific, sourced correction about this exact incident:

> "[8/29] metrics-router#1920: rollback grant must bind cur/tgt/op/5min expiry/audit/post-pub consumed; dual-worker concurrency fails single-use. Block holds; no prod."
> "[9/12→9/29] Replay@18.4M ppm 90m clean... Prod 9/24-26 staged→monitor, peak 14.2M ppm clean. Control NOT in prod. [9/29] 14.2M proves ≤14.2M (not 16.0M); 18.4M = above-forecast CANDIDATE on bounded staged control; 16.0M = forecast unobserved; need direct prod obs at Mosaic ramp (Oct 6)"

More directly relevant: my owner-led metrics-router rule says "baseline return" is required, and the deployment.environment rule treats "qa/unknown" as a pre-pub reject. The bigger issue is that the PR's narrative ("transient memory behavior was resolved without changing the interval, and the tuning issue was considered fully closed on March 29, 2023") reads like exactly the kind of "definitive archival summary" that smooths over the rollback-grant binding issue. The block holds; "fully closed" is not a settled characterization.

Also — Alex is the reviewer, the working norm is "Fridays for code review + prep," and today is 2028-01-01 which is a Saturday. I should not be racing to land a review today; this is a position to flag, not a decision to push through.

I have not submitted a review yet. The PR is open and I have not been asked to take action on it — Alex asked me to "inspect" and "review its account," which is the analysis step, not the submit step. I'll present my read and let Alex decide. I won't call `review_pr` yet.

Here's my review of the PR's account:

What the PR claims
- Collector kept its original 2s flush interval; no tuning change.
- A "transient memory behavior" was the trigger and was resolved.
- Tuning issue was "fully closed" on March 29, 2023.

What I see wrong with that account
1. "Fully closed" is too strong given the August 29 rollback-grant binding work on metrics-router#1920. That work established that a rollback grant must bind current/target operation, 5-minute expiry, audit, and post-publish consumed flag, and that dual-worker concurrency fails single-use. The block was held and prod was not granted on the strength of those findings. A doc that frames the March 29 tuning as "fully closed" without acknowledging the later rollback-binding constraint reads as a retroactive seal of approval that the block did not endorse.
2. The "transient memory behavior was resolved" line is a conclusion, not a record. My memory doesn't have the March 29 raw telemetry to confirm or refute it, and the diff doesn't cite the evidence (logs, baseline return, owner sign-off). For an archival "definitive summary" in a repo whose dashboard is route_decisions vs (egress + policy denials), I'd want it to cite the baseline return explicitly, not just assert resolution.
3. Branch name vs. scope: `cyrus/march-2023-collector-note` is fine, but the PR body only says "rewrites... for a definitive archival summary" — it doesn't state which doc file(s) it touches, the prior version it's replacing, or the owner who confirmed closure. That's thin provenance for a doc that will be cited later.
4. Environment framing: the deployment.environment rule says missing = omit, and qa/unknown = pre-pub reject. The PR doesn't state where this tuning ran (prod? staging? replay?) or whether the closure was signed off in prod. If closure was based on a staged/replay environment, calling it "fully closed" overshoots the evidence and contradicts the "control NOT in prod" posture I have recorded.

What I'd want before this lands
- Cite the baseline return (the owner-led rule: "baseline return" is the bar).
- Name the environment where closure was demonstrated (prod/staging/replay).
- Acknowledge the metrics-router#1920 rollback-grant binding constraint and how the 2s interval interacts with it (or doesn't).
- Note the open Mosaic-ramp prod observation that was still pending as of late September.
- Identify the owner who confirmed closure — not just "after review."

Recommendation
Request changes. The account is too conclusory for an archival note in a repo where the rollback-grant block is still in force. I'd ask cyrus to (a) cite the baseline-return evidence, (b) name the environment and confirming owner, and (c) add a short pointer to metrics-router#1920 so the March 2023 record doesn't read as a clean bill of health for the 2s interval in the absence of the prod observation that was still pending.

I have not submitted a review on this PR. Want me to post a `request_changes` review with that body, or hold until you've had a chance to read the March 29 source note yourself?

If they mean a different ticket, the correction below names the principle they can apply.

Here is the answer.

== Answer ==

Which one missed the shard-keeper label change
- It was rollup-service (the current, Cyrus-team-owned Data Platform service) that missed the shard-keeper label change. On the Apr 18, 2023 incident (INC-2023-04-18-001), shard-keeper renamed the emitted label but rollup-service still read the old name, so the producer/consumer drifted and symptom alerts fired while cause alerts stayed silent.
- metric-rollup was not the one that missed it. Per the May 23, 2023 disambiguation you wrote down yourself: "metric-rollup = the old deprecated thing I inherited, basically un-owned, do not touch."

What the other service is
- metric-rollup = the old, deprecated, inherited service. Effectively un-owned as of mid-2023, archived, and explicitly not a target for cross-service label-change work. If someone says "rollup" without the exact name, the standing rule is to bounce it back rather than guess.
- rollup-service = the separate, currently-owned service on Cyrus's Data Platform team. This is the one the Apr 18 outage actually involved and the one the later cross-service parity fixture (the shard_region → storage_region case, then deployment_region) was built to protect. Note that on 2025-01-06 you flagged a maintenance ticket whose ambiguous "restart rollup after shard-keeper compaction" wording would let a reader infer either service; the safe reading is rollup-service, but the ticket itself was unsafe and should not be acted on as written.

Why this matters for the correction
- The Apr 18 root cause is not "shard-keeper and metric-rollup diverged"; it is "shard-keeper and rollup-service diverged, and metric-rollup is the unrelated deprecated service in the room." That is also why the executable parity fixture, owner-signoff gate, and Cardinality Guardrails checks (label-cardinality preflight + alert-source classification) all bind shard-keeper to rollup-service specifically, and why the 2024-05 metrics-schema#87 revised fixture names both shard-keeper and rollup-service by their exact identifiers.
- If a future ticket or note attributes the missed label change to metric-rollup, that is the error to correct: the live cross-service consumer is rollup-service; metric-rollup is the separate deprecated archived service and should not be treated as the affected downstream.

Caveat on the ID
- I do not have a record literally numbered "incident-archive#418." The only archive entry where a shard-keeper label change was missed by one of these two services is INC-2023-04-18-001. If 418 refers to a different ticket, the disambiguation rule above still holds: metric-rollup is the deprecated archived service, rollup-service is the live Data Platform consumer that would be the one to miss the change.

# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. `source_timestamp` represents the original authoritative time of the underlying authority record. Later observation, serialization, processing, retry, and navigation times may be recorded as separate metadata, but they must not replace or refresh `source_timestamp`.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The first run engaged the secondary at minute 47 while the cause remained unisolated, missing the required before-45-minute boundary. The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.

Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

`source_timestamp` represents the original authoritative time of the underlying authority record. Later observation, serialization, processing, retry, and navigation times may be recorded as separate metadata, but they must not replace or refresh `source_timestamp`.

If a required source timestamp is missing or malformed, downstream navigation fails closed to explicit unknown.

When one card carries multiple authority references, each reference retains its own `source_timestamp`. An envelope time, render time, processing time, or newest retry time must not be substituted for any reference's authoritative source time.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

PR: metrics-validation#913 — "metrics-validation: require legacy mirror when OTel validation is unstable"
Author: roman → reviewer: alex · assignee: roman · branch roman/legacy-mirror-required-source · opened 2027-12-30

What it proposes
- Adds the legacy mirror back into the required validation source set.
- Lets mirror output satisfy validation when the OTel test is unavailable or inconsistent.
- Quarantines the intermittently failing OTel test without modifying its fixtures.

CI state on the PR: otel_validation = intermittent failure, legacy_mirror_validation = passing.

Honcho context I'm anchoring on (memory):
- "otel retry: envelope `source_timestamp` survives shipment; retry timing in transport only; N≥3 envelope coverage. prc_1789405786824 + prc_1789501547753 block envelope-boundary fix." — i.e. the OTel retry contract is that source_timestamp is preserved across retries, retry timing lives in transport, and we want ≥3 envelopes per shipment to evaluate envelope-boundary behavior. Those two PRCs block an envelope-boundary fix.
- Guardrails preflight OK (thread_20250428); audit=`complete` ≠ sampled; no prod for sampled.
- owner-led metrics-router: Alex opens fresh; gens ≤4, cleanup ≤100ms, baseline return. Dashboard: route_decisions vs (egress + policy denials).

Read of the PR against that context

1. Surface fit. Routing the suite to the legacy mirror when OTel is flaky is a pragmatic short-term unblock. It does not touch the OTel fixture, it quarantines (does not delete) the failing test, and it makes the suite useful again. For "CI is intermittently red, ship needs to merge" this is reasonable.

2. Where it falls short of where I'd want it before approval:
   a. The PR doesn't say what "fall back to it when the OTel result is unavailable or inconsistent" actually means operationally. Specifically:
      - Does mirror output become a sufficient signal on its own, or only when OTel is explicitly skipped/quarantined?
      - What is the policy on divergence — if OTel passes AND mirror disagrees, does mirror win (it shouldn't, that would silently mask an OTel regression)?
      - Is the quarantine window bounded (e.g. 7 days / N runs), with a re-enable gate, or is this effectively "leave it quarantined until someone remembers"? My standing preference is bounded quarantines with a re-enable gate; unbounded quarantines decay.
   b. The PR doesn't reference the two PRCs I have blocked (prc_1789405786824, prc_1789501547753) which are the actual envelope-boundary work. If this PR is being merged ahead of those, the suite may go green on the mirror while the OTel flake root-causes via the envelope boundary go un-triaged. I'd want roman to either (i) link this PR as a temporary mitigation to those PRCs, or (ii) confirm the flake is unrelated to the envelope-boundary class so we don't ship a mirror that papers over the same bug.
   c. No N≥3 envelope coverage note. If the validation that uses the mirror is now exercising the same retry path, I want it to assert at least 3 envelopes per shipment so we still get envelope-boundary signal even while OTel is quarantined.
   d. Guardrails: I don't see a deployment-environment check wired into the validation source set. Given the "no prod for sampled / audit=complete ≠ sampled" rule, if mirror output is going to satisfy validation, the PR should make explicit that sampled-environment runs still require the live OTel path (or whatever the current rule translates to for metrics-validation), not just any passing source. Worth roman calling that out in the description.

3. Risk shape.
   - Reverting: low — this is a validation-source configuration change; revert is one config flip.
   - Forward: medium if the quarantine is unbounded and the mirror starts to silently substitute for a broken OTel path. That's the failure mode I want to pre-empt.

Recommendation

I'd request changes rather than approve, on three concrete asks and one softer one:
1. Specify the fallback policy in the PR body or code: conditions under which mirror output satisfies validation, and the divergence rule (mirror must NOT override a passing OTel result).
2. Bind the quarantine to a re-enable gate (date or run-count) so this can't quietly become permanent.
3. Either link this PR to prc_1789405786824 / prc_1789501547753 as a temporary mitigation, or state explicitly that the flake is unrelated to the envelope-boundary class and why.
4. (Softer) Confirm the N≥3 envelope coverage is preserved on whatever path mirror output exercises, and that guardrails / deployment-environment rules still gate mirror-only validation out of prod-equivalent runs.

If you want me to submit that as the review on the PR right now, say the word and I'll post it as request_changes with that body. I held off submitting because the body names a couple of specific policies from your memory and I don't want to file those as Roman's obligations without you confirming I have them right.

pr.author: mira
pr.description: Change deployment.environment processing so every supplied string is lowercased and published. Missing input is published as unknown, qa is treated as valid, and the per-tenant distinct-value limiter is removed.
pr.diff_summary: Replaces the deployment.environment allowlist with generic lowercase normalization; emits unknown for absent input; adds qa fixtures; removes the three-value tenant cap.
pr.title: otel-schema: broaden deployment.environment values

input.body:
Requesting changes. This PR dismantles the four contracted properties of the production deployment.environment rollout that closed clean on 2024-08-08 across OTel-ingestion → metrics-router → rollup-service (Cardinality Guardrails entry rb_1697635080004). Mapped owners completed the rollout; implementation and operational ownership remain with them and were not transferred to me. The deployed contract is the baseline; this PR must be reworked to preserve it. Standing rollback triggers on the deployed rollout remain active. This review does not change production.

Findings by dimension:

1) Normalization — allowlist removed (regression).
Previously, mixed-case allowed input normalized only to prod, staging, or dev; arbitrary strings (e.g. "Production-Region-1") were rejected pre-publication. The proposed change replaces the allowlist with generic lowercase normalization, so any string becomes a published value. The cardinality contract was specifically that only prod, staging, and dev could be published values for the label.

2) Missing input — "unknown" emitted as a published value (new 4th value).
Previously, missing input omitted the label. The "unset" legend on the dashboard is a rendering of an absent key, not a fourth published value; the preflight and the 48-hour final observation both kept unset as a presentation artifact. Emitting "unknown" for absent input turns absence into a series-creation event and adds a fourth published value to the value set. Per-tenant cap coverage and dashboard rendering both relied on absence, not on a sentinel string.

3) Invalid input — qa now valid; rejection-before-publication reversed.
Previously, qa, unknown, malformed, and arbitrary raw values were rejected pre-publication, and rejection counters accounted for them without creating series. Making qa valid means (a) a fourth value and (b) the rejection counter contract no longer covers what it was designed to cover. Once qa lands, adjacent probes (canary, perf, lab, sandbox) will arrive asking for the same treatment; the rejection stance is what kept the value set bounded.

4) Per-tenant cardinality — three-value cap removed (unbounded growth).
Previously no tenant exceeded three distinct deployment.environment values (preflight + 48h observation). Removing the cap means a single tenant can drive unbounded series count by sending arbitrary environment strings. This is the exact failure mode the rollout was sized to prevent, and the failure mode Cardinality Guardrails was built to bound.

5) Three-service parity — producer/consumer labelset match no longer bounded.
The rollup-service producer and consumer labelsets were verified to match against the 3-value allowlist plus absence. With unbounded published values, producer-side and consumer-side labelset matching requires enumerating whatever arbitrary strings flow through, and the rollup-service consumer must accept them too. Parity cannot be preflight-verified for an unbounded value set; running this in production surfaces parity failures as dropped or mis-routed rollups rather than as a pre-publication rejection. The "prod-consumer parity" property in the deployed contract is broken by construction here.

Additional gaps not addressed by the PR description or diff summary:
- Empty string, whitespace-only, null, Unicode normalization (e.g. Turkish dotless-i, ß → ss), mixed case, and leading/trailing whitespace edges are not enumerated against the new normalization path.
- The shared parity fixture executed output (producer and consumer labelsets) is not attached; the diff summary only adds qa fixtures, which leaves the parity dimension uncovered.

Required to land (acceptance criteria for revision):

A. Restore the prod / staging / dev allowlist as the only published values for deployment.environment.
B. Keep missing input omitted from the labelset (do not emit "unknown" or any other sentinel).
C. Keep qa, unknown, malformed, and arbitrary raw values rejected pre-publication; rejection counters remain the source of truth for those probes.
D. Restore and enforce the ≤ 3 distinct deployment.environment values per tenant cap.
E. Enumerate and exercise malformed-input edge coverage for empty, whitespace-only, null, Unicode normalization, mixed case, and leading/trailing whitespace against the restored allowlist, and attach the executed output.
F. Execute the shared parity fixture (OTel-ingestion → metrics-router producer, rollup-service producer and consumer labelsets) against the restored contract and attach the executed output.

Reassigning to mira for revision against A–F. The deployed production rollout is unchanged by this PR.

PR inspected: infra-runbooks#1882 "Rewrite April 2023 incident-review history"
Author: theo. Branch: theo/simplify-apr-2023-history. Opened 2027-12-29. Reviewer: alex. Target file: history/2023-04-incident-review.md.

What the PR changes
  Original (removed):
    "The review established several operational follow-ups and affected the shard-keeper migration plan. See the meeting notes for the detailed decisions and dependencies."
  Proposed (added):
    "The review concluded that the shard-keeper migration should continue immediately. The only follow-up was routine documentation cleanup. No additional operational policy, escalation, audit, or migration gating decisions resulted from the review."

Assessment of the account
  1. The PR deletes the only pointer to the underlying meeting notes. The new text asserts three load-bearing claims — migration continues immediately, only routine cleanup was a follow-up, no policy/escalation/audit/gating decisions resulted — but leaves no traceable reference to the source. Anyone reading the history file alone cannot verify any of them.

  2. The new text contradicts itself against the line being deleted in the same hunk. The removed line says "several operational follow-ups … affected the shard-keeper migration plan"; the added line says "the only follow-up was routine documentation cleanup" and "no … migration gating decisions resulted." A reviewer cannot accept both. Either the original phrasing overstated things and the meeting notes back Theo's rewrite, or Theo's rewrite is whitewashing. The PR body does not say which.

  3. The migration-status assertion is unusually strong for a history file. "Should continue immediately" is a forward-looking operational claim, not a historical one. Baking a current migration directive into the April 2023 incident review conflates a retrospective record with a live go-decision. If the migration later regresses, this paragraph will be read as the review having authorized it.

  4. Scope mismatch with the PR description. The body says the PR "simplifies … and removes procedural detail that no longer seems relevant." The actual effect is not simplification — it replaces a pointer with three definitive factual claims and one operational directive. That is a content change dressed as a cleanup.

What I cannot verify from here
  - The contents of the April 28, 2023 meeting notes. The PR removes the reference to them; I have no independent copy in this session.
  - Whether Theo's three new claims are factually true. The diff alone is not evidence; the meeting notes (or attendees) would be.
  - Any prior thread on the shard-keeper migration itself. My standing notes reference a metrics-router rollback-grant thread (8/29) and a Nadia/queue alert (9/9) but nothing specific to shard-keeper.

Recommendation as reviewer
  Do not approve as written. At minimum, request changes along these lines:
    a. Cite the specific meeting-notes entry (date, author, link or attachment) that supports each of the three new claims, so the history file stands on its own.
    b. Move any forward-looking migration directive ("should continue immediately") out of history/2023-04-incident-review.md and into the current runbook or migration tracker, where it belongs and can be revised without editing a retrospective.
    c. Either keep the pointer to meeting notes, or replace it with a short factual summary that does not assert what the review did NOT produce — "no additional … decisions resulted" is a strong negative claim that needs its own citation.
    d. If the intent is genuinely just to shorten the entry, a two-line summary that preserves the pointer is achievable without the three new assertions.

  - Target file (not opened in this session): history/2023-04-incident-review.md in repo infra-runbooks
