arguments.title: Alex 2027 self-review — working draft
arguments.body:
Working draft — preserved mapped-owner boundaries (implementation, release, rollback, triage).

Outcomes and impact

Owned the review envelope across ingest-edge, Lantern, metrics-router, rollup-service, and Q4 intake. Ingest-edge: Yuki's owner-held decoder release shipped a 1,048,576-byte request-wide decoded-attribute limit and a 72-request admission cap with retryable pre-acceptance; no over-limit enqueue; one terminal outcome per request; exactly-once slot release. The 8,000-point and eight-waiting-per-tenant limits stayed unchanged. Throughput -0.6%, p99 +2.2% vs. 9/8 baseline, below 5%/10% rollback triggers. Yuki closed without rollback; he keeps implementation, release, and rollback. Lantern: source_timestamp-inclusive 10/1-12/15/27 review activated clean on the tested slice; freeze still requires the evidence period to close, every in-period row to reconcile exactly once, and the unresolved set to be empty; production unchanged. Q4 intake objectives accepted; Nadia retains front-door triage; I stay consultation-only. Two reviews stay explicitly open: metrics-router cancellation (Wes) and rollup-service tenant-identity (Roman) — see How I worked.

How I worked

Narrow-scope reviews: explicit acceptance criteria, reversible scope, rollback triggers upfront. Ingest-edge contract: admission/byte limits apply pre-acceptance; 8,000-point rule post decode/admission; eight-waiting-per-tenant limit in queue; controls additive. Failure-mode contract: one terminal outcome per request, exactly-once slot release across success/rejection/malformed/cancellation/disconnect/retry. Yuki kept implementation, release, rollback. Lantern query spec: source_timestamp-inclusive (DST-safe, synthetic-row inclusive, audit-only retry/processed_at); Product Engineering kept impl/release/rollback. For metrics-router and rollup-service I held the bar to durable attempt identity, defined ordering, tenant-bound separation/per-pair/per-output attribution; both stay open. Q4 intake kept Nadia as front-door triage; I post only with evidence, never premature approval.

Growth focus for 2028

Sharpen the failure-mode-first habit: each contract becomes a one-page checklist (criteria, ordering, failure modes, rollback triggers) before review; reviewers and owners share a map. Carry it into intake: triage itself should produce the contract draft, not just the scope. Refuse to convert drafts/staging evidence into approvals; lean on mapped owners for impl/release/rollback; keep my role as review/consultation. Invest in durable-attempt-identity patterns that hold across cancellation, disconnect, crash, restart — gaps from metrics-router and shard-keeper point there.

messages.content:
Bottom line: block. The candidate fails its own test by design and reintroduces the
same class of bug shard-keeper#197 closed (stale serving past real lease loss),
just driven by wall-clock skew rather than a notification race.

What the test actually shows
  - On acquisition, expiresAt = wallClock.Now() + remainingLease, so
    expiresAt_wall = T0 + R.
  - 90 s backward wall-clock adjustment: wall time is now T0 - 90.
  - Predicate wallClock.Now().Before(expiresAt) becomes
    (T0 - 90).Before(T0 + R) and stays true even after real elapsed time
    exceeds R.
  - Serving gate therefore stays open past the original lease window. With
    a second holder added, the same defect would surface as overlapping
    serving: real-time lease expiry fires elsewhere while the original
    holder keeps answering.

Why wall-clock is the wrong anchor
  - Wall-clock is non-monotonic. Manual adjustment, NTP step, suspend/resume,
    or DST rollback all move it. The candidate trusts it as a lease-validity
    anchor it cannot support.
  - Monotonic clock is the correct anchor for a per-process lease window:
    no jumps, immune to NTP/DST, preserves the order in which the lease was
    acquired.
  - lease_guard already treats >500 ms skew as a relinquish trigger
    (observed 740 ms on 2024-04-12, relinquished 10:02:14.109 UTC). A 90 s
    backward jump is ~180x that threshold. The candidate silently absorbs
    the entire skew instead of relinquishing.
  - The brown-bag on 2025-04-22 agreed on five ordered lease-handoff states:
    (1) lease ownership, (2) serving gate open/closed, (3) readiness,
    (4) router eligibility, (5) downstream observation. A wall-clock gate
    predicate collapses states 1 and 2 into a clock comparison and can put
    them out of order relative to the real lease-loss signal. That is the
    same anti-pattern the brown-bag warned against — collapsing the ordered
    transitions into one implicit "healthy" check.

Cross-service propagation if this shipped
  - rollup-service: the retained shard-keeper/rollup-service parity fixture
    would observe inconsistent handoff under any clock skew. Reads during
    the skew window would be served by the wrong owner; Data Platform would
    see missing or duplicated rollup intervals.
  - metrics-router: read-only routing snapshots served past real lease loss
    could route to a tenant shard that has actually transferred ownership.
    Cardinality Guardrails parity would then see a producer/consumer label
    mismatch and fail (storage_region vs storage_zone mismatches fail even
    with matching aggregate counts, per the 2025-04-03 rules).
  - ingest-edge and downstream consumers: stale shard-keeper responses
    propagate to anything reading routing or ownership from it. The 2024-06-20
    staging failover already produced downstream anomalies from 310 ms of
    stale serving; 90 s is several orders of magnitude worse.
  - lease_guard: the candidate bypasses lease_guard's skew observation
    path. The skew is absorbed silently rather than surfaced, removing a
    defense that has already proven its value.

Fix shape (contract, not code)
  1. Anchor the gate predicate to monotonic time. expiresAt_mono =
     monoClock.Now() + remainingLease; serve while
     monoClock.Now().Before(expiresAt_mono). Wall-clock may be stored
     alongside for logging, but the predicate must use monotonic.
  2. Or, keep wall-clock as a fast-path lower bound but require explicit
     lease-loss notification to close the gate (this is the shard-keeper#197
     correction). Wall-clock can only shorten the lease window; it must
     never extend it.
  3. Wire lease_guard.ObserveSkew() into the acquisition path so a large
     backward jump is reported and forces immediate lease relinquishment
     rather than silent absorption.
  4. Restart safety: monotonic resets on process restart. The candidate
     must re-acquire on restart rather than reuse a stored expiresAt_mono
     across restarts.

Tes…

Bottom line: block. The candidate fails its own test by design and reintroduces the
same class of bug shard-keeper#197 closed (stale serving past real lease loss),
just driven by wall-clock skew rather than a notification race.

What the test actually shows
  - On acquisition, expiresAt = wallClock.Now() + remainingLease, so
    expiresAt_wall = T0 + R.
  - 90 s backward wall-clock adjustment: wall time is now T0 - 90.
  - Predicate wallClock.Now().Before(expiresAt) becomes
    (T0 - 90).Before(T0 + R) and stays true even after real elapsed time
    exceeds R.
  - Serving gate therefore stays open past the original lease window. With
    a second holder added, the same defect would surface as overlapping
    serving: real-time lease expiry fires elsewhere while the original
    holder keeps answering.

Why wall-clock is the wrong anchor
  - Wall-clock is non-monotonic. Manual adjustment, NTP step, suspend/resume,
    or DST rollback all move it. The candidate trusts it as a lease-validity
    anchor it cannot support.
  - Monotonic clock is the correct anchor for a per-process lease window:
    no jumps, immune to NTP/DST, preserves the order in which the lease was
    acquired.
  - lease_guard already treats >500 ms skew as a relinquish trigger
    (observed 740 ms on 2024-04-12, relinquished 10:02:14.109 UTC). A 90 s
    backward jump is ~180x that threshold. The candidate silently absorbs
    the entire skew instead of relinquishing.
  - The brown-bag on 2025-04-22 agreed on five ordered lease-handoff states:
    (1) lease ownership, (2) serving gate open/closed, (3) readiness,
    (4) router eligibility, (5) downstream observation. A wall-clock gate
    predicate collapses states 1 and 2 into a clock comparison and can put
    them out of order relative to the real lease-loss signal. That is the
    same anti-pattern the brown-bag warned against — collapsing the ordered
    transitions into one implicit "healthy" check.

Cross-service propagation if this shipped
  - rollup-service: the retained shard-keeper/rollup-service parity fixture
    would observe inconsistent handoff under any clock skew. Reads during
    the skew window would be served by the wrong owner; Data Platform would
    see missing or duplicated rollup intervals.
  - metrics-router: read-only routing snapshots served past real lease loss
    could route to a tenant shard that has actually transferred ownership.
    Cardinality Guardrails parity would then see a producer/consumer label
    mismatch and fail (storage_region vs storage_zone mismatches fail even
    with matching aggregate counts, per the 2025-04-03 rules).
  - ingest-edge and downstream consumers: stale shard-keeper responses
    propagate to anything reading routing or ownership from it. The 2024-06-20
    staging failover already produced downstream anomalies from 310 ms of
    stale serving; 90 s is several orders of magnitude worse.
  - lease_guard: the candidate bypasses lease_guard's skew observation
    path. The skew is absorbed silently rather than surfaced, removing a
    defense that has already proven its value.

Fix shape (contract, not code)
  1. Anchor the gate predicate to monotonic time. expiresAt_mono =
     monoClock.Now() + remainingLease; serve while
     monoClock.Now().Before(expiresAt_mono). Wall-clock may be stored
     alongside for logging, but the predicate must use monotonic.
  2. Or, keep wall-clock as a fast-path lower bound but require explicit
     lease-loss notification to close the gate (this is the shard-keeper#197
     correction). Wall-clock can only shorten the lease window; it must
     never extend it.
  3. Wire lease_guard.ObserveSkew() into the acquisition path so a large
     backward jump is reported and forces immediate lease relinquishment
     rather than silent absorption.
  4. Restart safety: monotonic resets on process restart. The candidate
     must re-acquire on restart rather than reuse a stored expiresAt_mono
     across restarts.

Tes…

# Goal
First-cut controls for the Q4 Cardinality Guardrails work; keep it tied to the September mirror/replay legacy-aggregator wobble without turning validation movement into rollback criteria.

# First-cut matrix

## 1. Label limits
- Failure mode: unbounded or newly introduced label keys/values causing fanout.
- Candidate control: a narrow allowlist or budget per sensitive label family.
- Preflight: flag new high-cardinality labels before a metrics-router or shard-keeper push.

## 2. Alert-source semantics
- Failure mode: responders treating replay/mirror validation movement as live-path rollback evidence.
- Candidate control: dashboard and alert wording that marks live metrics-router traffic separately from replay or mirror validation samples.

## 3. Label-change preflight
- Failure mode: a config or parser change adding labels without checking cardinality behavior.
- Candidate control: a pre-push checklist with sample counts, source label, owner, and rollback/non-rollback semantics.

# Non-goals
- No customer-facing dashboard.
- No general telemetry rewrite.
- No legacy-aggregator retirement claim.
- No claim that the 2% replay sample creates immediate storage savings.
- No Q3 incident framing.

# Monday questions
- What cost examples can Cyrus bring by label family?
- Which preflight checks are service-owned by Alex versus data-platform advisory?
- What would make the first cut too broad?

## Bounded observability example — exception-review outcomes

The accepted production counter uses only these bounded labels:
- `service_pair_class`: `ingest_path`, `routing_path`, `ownership_path`, or `other`
- `exception_class`: `invariant`, `provenance`, `failure_mode`, `ownership`, or `escalation`
- `outcome`: `requested`, `accepted`, or `rejected`

Raw service names, owner email addresses, pull-request identifiers, and reviewer-supplied reasons remain in logs or audit records rather than metric labels. This example creates no centralized review owner: mapped owners retain implementation, operational, release, and rollback responsibility, while boundary review remains limited to the triggered cross-service exception.

# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

## Non-goals
This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.
output.title: INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

> **Boundary:** This document defines a customer-safe contract only. It grants no customer access, does not copy the internal Lantern UI, exposes no raw internal discussion or internal permission identifiers, and is not an employee-performance or manager-readiness surface.

## Audience and non-goals

Define the intended customer audience and the operational questions the preview may answer. Record explicit non-goals, including customer access before the contract is reviewed, exposure of internal discussions or permission identifiers, employee-level operational signals, manager-readiness interpretation, and copying the internal UI.

## Tenant authorization

Specify how tenant authorization is evaluated, what tenant boundary is checked, and how unauthorized access is represented.

## External fields

### Deploy movement

Define the externally stable deployment identifier, service, environment, state transition, and customer-visible timestamp. Exclude internal actor IDs, chat links, and raw pipeline job identifiers.

### Service ownership

Define the service-facing support or escalation label. Exclude employee names and internal owner-map records.

### Incident load

Define the customer-safe operational summary, including its time window, aggregation rules, minimum threshold, and treatment of suppressed, stale, missing, delayed, and unavailable data.

## External provenance

Define which provenance information can be exposed externally without revealing internal identifiers, discussions, or permission references.

## Data-state semantics

Define distinct states for `unknown`, `not applicable`, `not authorized`, `temporarily unavailable`, stale data, delayed data, missing data, and intentionally suppressed data. Do not collapse materially different states to null.

## Error envelope

Define the response-level error shape, including permission denial and other errors that apply to the response rather than a single field.

## Worked examples

Add representative success, suppressed, stale, unavailable, and permission-denied examples after the field-level decisions are reviewed.

## Unresolved questions

Record policy questions that require product or engineering review rather than hiding them in UI behavior.

## Review status

This is contract work only. No customer access is authorized until the external fields, authorization, provenance, failure semantics, examples, non-goals, and unresolved questions have been reviewed.
output.title: Lantern customer preview — external contract v0

# Cross-service gate exceptions — June 14 review

I define cross-service gates and escalation boundaries; I do not take over routine service operation or Iris's product interpretation.

## 1. Metrics-router generation-retirement thresholds

- **Invariant:** Pause additional configuration pushes if retired objects accumulate above four or cleanup pauses exceed 100 milliseconds. Preserve rollback for active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.
- **Observed evidence:** A single-file canary reached four retired generations and a 92-millisecond cleanup pause; the values approached but did not cross the thresholds, and the other consistency, parity, drop, reload, heap, and restart checks remained clean.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The event is near the pause boundaries; it does not establish that later pushes are safe without observation.
- **Mapped owner:** Metrics-router service ownership remains with the mapped service owner; Wes is the practical first-pass backup within the existing deploy rules.
- **Decision needed:** Whether the next configuration push may proceed one at a time.
- **Escalation condition:** Cross more than four retired objects or 100 milliseconds of cleanup pause, or observe active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.

## 2. Ingest-edge bounded decompression

- **Invariant:** Keep active decompression bounded at four per pod and two per tenant; preserve permit cleanup, body limits, accepted-point integrity, request-p99 rollback gates, and randomized one-, two-, and three-second Retry-After behavior.
- **Observed evidence:** Request p99 briefly rose 19 milliseconds above baseline; decode-wait p99 reached 188 milliseconds, waiting work reached eleven on the busiest pods, and one tenant represented 64% of queued requests. Active work stayed within the per-pod and per-tenant limits, permits returned to zero, oversized bodies were rejected before over-budget append, no accepted points were dropped, and no pod restarted.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The concentrated waiting queue raises a separate fairness and capacity question even though no rollback gate fired.
- **Mapped owner:** Ingest-edge routine operation remains with its mapped service owner; cross-service gate review remains with Alex.
- **Decision needed:** Leave the bounded-decompression release in production and define the owner-led fairness or capacity follow-up.
- **Escalation condition:** A production rollback gate fires, including a permit leak, active-work limit violation, dropped accepted points, or the applicable sustained request-p99 threshold.

## 3. Lantern deploy provenance

- **Invariant:** Emit an external deploy event only when all required provenance validates; otherwise represent the result as explicit unknown with a machine-readable missing-provenance reason.
- **Observed evidence:** The corrected fixture rejects partial deploy objects, covers each missing required field with negative tests, performs authorization before lookup, and does not use internal room metadata or inferred ownership.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** Guarded internal validation is active, but customer access remains closed; no external preview access is granted by this correction.
- **Mapped owner:** Alex defines the external data and failure-mode requirements; Iris leads product interpretation.
- **Decision needed:** Approve the fail-closed correction and focused tests without broadening the external contract.
- **Escalation condition:** Any implementation emits partial provenance, consults internal-only metadata, or treats guarded internal validation as customer access.

## 4. Rollup correction backlog

- **Invariant:** Correction processing must preserve assignment epochs, complete assignment snapshots, minimum-watermark evaluation, matching checkpoints and compaction IDs, and duplicate-free publication.
- **Observed evidence:** The correction-backlog evidence is still under review.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The backlog increase must be distinguished between bounded backfill and a stuck correction loop, checkpoint mismatch, duplicate processing, or publication risk.
- **Mapped owner:** Cyrus's data-platform team retains rollup-service implementation and operational ownership.
- **Decision needed:** Decide whether the production fix remains in place and what owner-led pacing, capacity, or alert-tuning follow-up is justified.
- **Escalation condition:** Evidence of repeated processing, checkpoint or assignment mismatch, duplicate output, loss of first-pass currency, or a broken complete-assignment-snapshot gate.

# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.
output.title: Oversized-batch design and staged enablement — through January 28

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The first run engaged the secondary at minute 47 while the cause remained unisolated, missing the required before-45-minute boundary. The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

pr.author: wes
pr.body:
## Summary

Documents a faster break-glass procedure for Wes during urgent production deploy and rollback work.

## Proposed procedure

When waiting for the normal release mechanism would extend an incident, Wes may run `deployctl direct` from his maintainer laptop using production credentials. The command deploys the selected revision or restores the prior revision directly. The operator should record the incident ticket, service, revision, reason, and command output, then reconcile the resulting state with the normal release records after the incident.

## Motivation

This avoids waiting for the normal release job during time-sensitive recovery while retaining an audit trail in the incident record.

## Review question

Are the logging and post-incident reconciliation steps sufficient for this urgent path?
pr.title: docs: add laptop fast path for urgent deploys and rollbacks

input.body:
The intent (retain audit trail, don't extend an incident) is right and matches the responder scope, but the procedure as written overgeneralizes in the same shape as the October 2023 staging-equivalence note: it treats `deployctl direct` from a maintainer laptop with production credentials as a faster version of the normal release, when it actually bypasses the owner-map decision, the rollback-grant binding, and the environment-label gate. Logging and post-incident reconciliation alone are not sufficient. Five blocking items before this can ship:

1. Bind the rollback grant the way metrics-router#1920 binds it. "Selected revision" / "prior revision" is the same ambiguity the 4/16/24 tabletop exposed — a queued-but-not-started revision must not be a valid target. Require the direct path to bind: (a) current revision identifier — the exact completed deploy, not "latest"; (b) explicit target revision identifier; (c) operator identity; (d) ≤5-minute expiry; (e) audit ID; (f) post-publish consumed marker so two concurrent operators can't both pass validation before either publishes.

2. Require an owner-map decision, not just an operator command. "Wes may run `deployctl direct`" puts release authority on whoever is at the keyboard. Incident practice is mapped-owner: Wes responds, but the service owner signs off on the deploy/rollback target. Record the owner (incident commander or service owner) in the ticket alongside the operator. The laptop path is for execution latency, not owner substitution.

3. Hold the `deployment.environment` gate on the direct path. Direct deploys must not publish labels outside {prod, staging, dev}; missing input still omits; per-tenant distinct-value count stays ≤3. The PR doesn't mention this — a break-glass path that silently relaxes the label policy is a regression even if the deploy itself is correct.

4. Start any forward deploy via this path at a bounded canary, never full rollout. OTel-limiter precedent: mapped-owner decision + bounded canary + observation hold + owner-selected rollback criteria before broader rollout. A laptop fast path that skips directly to full traffic is not equivalent to the normal pipeline; the docs must say so explicitly, mirroring the correction to the 10/5/23 note.

5. Post-incident reconciliation must verify rollback completion, not just record-keeping. Add: lease-convergence check on the rolled-back shard-keeper, restart/reload counters, p99 return-to-baseline, and a generation-counter read-back showing the target revision is the active one. "Reconcile state with normal release records" is bookkeeping; this is verification.

Happy to approve once these are folded in. Friday review on a docs-only change is fine — nothing here touches prod.

  repo: ingest-edge
  status: open
  title: ingest-edge: replace tenant scheduler with a single request FIFO
  description: Simplify dispatch by replacing tenant round-robin queues with one
  request FIFO. Requests enter runnable scheduling state only once a worker is
  free, and the per-tenant waiting-limit enforcement is removed.
  changes:
    - Replace tenant round-robin dispatch with a single request FIFO
    - Delay insertion into runnable scheduling state until a worker is available
    - Remove the per-tenant waiting-request cap

Review of the change against the dispatch-critical facts in memory:

1. Per-tenant fairness is being deleted, not simplified. Round-robin across
   tenant queues was the mechanism that kept a single noisy tenant from
   starving the others. A single FIFO with no per-tenant cap means one tenant's
   burst sits at the head of the queue and pushes every other tenant's
   q_wait_p99 up in lockstep. That is exactly the failure mode the Nadia
   alert is shaped around (q_wait_p99 > 400 cause, rq_full_ratio > 0.005
   symptom, 5m continuous, live-only pages). The "symptom" arm
   (rq_full_ratio) gets worse by construction — there is no longer a cap
   that produces a "full" condition; the queue just grows.

2. Removing the per-tenant waiting-request cap is a safety-mechanism removal,
   not a simplification. That cap is what bounded the blast radius of a
   misbehaving tenant. Without it, a buggy or hostile tenant can grow the
   FIFO without bound until OOM. The PR description frames this as a cleanup;
   the dispatch record needs an explicit statement of what now bounds the
   queue (worker count? a global cap? backpressure upstream?).

3. "Delay insertion into runnable scheduling state until a worker is
   available" changes what q_wait measures. If the metric is "submit →
   runnable", the wait window shrinks artificially because requests sit
   pre-runnable during the wait. If the metric is "submit → worker pick",
   the number still rises. Either way, the existing p99 baseline from the
   9/12-9/29 replay (18.4M ppm, 90m clean, ≤64 tenant batches) is invalidated
   as a control — the scheduling primitive that produced it no longer
   exists. The replay baseline should not be cited as evidence for this
   change.

4. Control validation gap. Per the 9/29 note, staged control had not yet
   gone to prod; the next direct prod observation was scoped to the Mosaic
   ramp (Oct 6). This PR does not mention a fresh staged-control run at the
   prior peak (14.2M ppm) or above. With the per-tenant scheduler gone, the
   above-forecast candidate (18.4M) cannot be carried over as evidence at
   all, and even the ≤14.2M observation needs to be redone against the new
   FIFO before this is mergeable to a prod path.

5. Ownership not stated in the PR record. Per the cross-service intake
   rule, impl owner and rollback owner must both be named, and any exception
   owner named only if an exception is actually triggered. The PR record I
   pulled does not list either. Need both before this can be moved toward a
   prod path.

6. Friday no-prod-deploy. Today is Friday. Per standing norm, Fridays are
   code review + prep with no prod deploys; staging/prod cutovers start
   Monday morning. Even if everything else cleared, this PR should not land
   on a prod path today.

7. OTel envelope. Nothing in the three changes appears to touch envelope
   construction, but the envelope-boundary fix (source_timestamp survival,
   transport-only retry timing, N≥3 envelope coverage) is still blocked on
   prc_1789405786824 + prc_1789501547753. If this PR moves the dispatch
   path that emits envelopes, confirm it does not regress envelope
   coverage; if it doesn't touch envelopes, this PR is orthogonal and the
   block still holds.

design direction, but the PR as written removes a fairness guarantee and a
blast-radius cap without naming what replaces either, and it has no fresh
control run against the new FIFO. Before this can move toward prod:

  b. State what bounds the FIFO now that the per-tenant cap is gone.

input.body:
Two of these three changes are semantic / blast-radius changes, not capacity tuning. The framing in the description ("improve apparent throughput") undersells what's actually happening.

1. Accept-then-backpressure inverts the contract.
"Accept batches before checking capacity; return retryable backpressure afterward" reads as: tell the producer the batch is in, then ask them to retry. Producers branch on accept vs. retryable reject synchronously today. Under the new ordering they either (a) get a delayed retryable that looks identical to a transient error and may not actually retry, or (b) treat it as accepted and drop the batch on the floor when they never see the retryable. Either failure mode loses points during exactly the load this PR is meant to handle. If the goal is "admit more under spike," gate on a soft threshold (warn + accept) vs. a hard threshold (reject up-front) — don't invert the contract.

2. Removing the per-tenant pending limit is unbounded.
With the shared queue at 2x and no per-tenant cap, one tenant can fill the entire queue. The 64-tenant-batches ceiling is what gave us the 18.4M / 90m clean envelope we're sitting on for the forecast window. Removing it drops the blast-radius guarantee without a replacement. Either keep the per-tenant cap (raise it if needed) or add per-tenant admission control before this lands.

3. 2x capacity is fine if cleanup <=100ms still holds.
Queue depth is also queue drain time. Need a measurement of cleanup latency at 2x queue depth under the same load profile that produced the 18.4M / 90m clean run. If drain time creeps, baseline-return slips and the forecast admission window gets worse, not better.

What I'd want before approving:
- A replay run with all three changes at 18.4M, 90m, with a 5+ tenant skew profile
- Cleanup latency p99 at 2x pending depth
- Either keep the current accept/reject contract (and add a soft-admit threshold) or document and test the new producer-facing accept->retryable ordering end-to-end with a real producer

input.body:
Requesting changes — lantern#3037 conflicts with the established Lantern published service alias rule (May 14, 2026 decision with Iris; July 3, 2026 deployed overlap correction) on two points.

1. Storage-order first-match on overlapping intervals.

The resolver returns the first alias row whose effective interval covers the source event timestamp, in storage order. The rule requires that when all qualifying alias records (tenant-scoped, interval covering the timestamp, both endpoints inclusive) identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once; when they identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern must keep the signals separate and render ownership as explicit unknown — regardless of storage order. The first-match-in-storage-order logic re-introduces exactly the storage-order dependency that was removed in the July 3 correction. Please replace with: collect every qualifying alias for the tenant/historical identifier whose inclusive interval covers the timestamp; resolve once if they all point to the same canonical_service_id; otherwise keep the signals separate and render explicit unknown.

2. Name-similarity fallback when no interval matches.

When no alias interval covers the source event timestamp, the resolver selects a canonical service in the same tenant using normalized service-name similarity. The rule explicitly forbids this: "The UI may not infer a rename from similar names or customer context." When the alias is absent, the timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start, or it is later than the inclusive end, the rule requires keeping the signals separate and rendering ownership as explicit unknown — not a similarity-based guess. Please remove the similarity fallback entirely; the no-match path must render explicit unknown.

Both of these are reproductions of the behaviors the July 3 correction removed. Please align the resolver with the rule and re-run the affected safety regressions (cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, loss of read-only enforcement) before re-review.

input.body:
Don't merge as-is — the premise is wrong.

Title says "collapse equivalent source series." Source-class on the metrics-router dashboard is not a visual artifact; it's the dimension that separates populations with different operational meaning:

- live = prod traffic
- staged = bounded staged control (explicitly NOT in prod, per the 9/9 Nadia alert rule and the Replay@18.4M analysis chain)
- replay = validation replay

Two concrete reasons this should not land:

1. Load-bearing for the on-call path. The Nadia alert routes on source_class∈{live,staged,replay} with "only live pages; control not in prod." The alert protects the pager, but the dashboard is the instrument the responder reaches for during an incident to verify which class is suffering and to confirm the alert's source_class attribution. Collapsing the series removes that situational check at the moment it's needed.

2. Load-bearing for the Replay analytical chain. The 14.2M prod / 18.4M staged-control separation is the basis for treating 18.4M as an above-forecast CANDIDATE rather than a confirmed prod observation. Any future ramp where we need to read staged vs prod side-by-side on this dashboard loses that distinction if the dimension is gone. "Ownership unchanged" only holds while the separation is readable.

On the "same metric schema" justification: schema identity does not imply population equivalence. Live and validation samples share label *names* but represent different traffic populations with different operational significance. That's the case for keeping the dimension, not removing it.

On the tests: the regression snapshots and assertions were updated to match the new behavior, then asserted to pass. That's a tautology, not a validation that the change is operationally safe.

Suggested directions (any one is fine; I don't think removing the dimension is):
- Keep source_class in queries and legend; tighten legend labels or grouping to reduce visual duplication without collapsing populations.
- If the duplication is specifically about live vs replay being near-identical shape, keep staged separated (the operational class) and reconsider whether live and replay need to share a panel at all.
- If the goal is declutter for routine viewing, add a panel toggle or default-collapse for non-live series — don't remove the dimension.

Happy to talk through before a re-submit.

arguments.body:
# Quarterly infra-rotation onboarding: incident-practice scenarios

Service: metrics-router (co-located with the rotation handoff; this entry is a sibling, not a replacement)
Owner: alex
Backup: wes
Last adopted: 2025-02-14 (Hema adopted the timed scenarios as a quarterly infrastructure-rotation onboarding module)

## Status

- Adoption: Hema adopted this module for quarterly infrastructure-rotation onboarding on 2025-02-14.
- Source scenarios: the revised February 14 timed exercise, scored against the correction posted 2025-02-04.
- The existing rotation handoff entry (`rb_metrics_router_oncall_handoff`) remains intact and authoritative for the live owner-led configuration window process. This module does not modify it.

## Scope

This module tests three statements every onboarding rotation member must be able to produce from a written scenario. Each scenario is presented as a brief; the participant's response must address all three statements explicitly. A response that addresses fewer than three, or that addresses them in a confused form, does not pass.

The three statements are:

1. **The incident clock and secondary engagement timing.** State the incident clock (elapsed time since the incident opened) and state explicitly whether the secondary on-call was engaged before the 45-minute boundary while isolation had not yet succeeded. A response that does not name the clock, that omits the 45-minute boundary, or that describes the secondary as \"monitoring\" or \"available\" without naming engagement does not pass.

2. **The change classification.** State explicitly whether the described change affects production state. Distinguish Friday staging preparation with no production state change from a change that actually moves production state. The Friday staging preparation case is not a Friday-afternoon production-deploy case; it does not trigger the production-deploy rule. A response that classifies a Friday staging rehearsal with no production-state change as a prohibited production deploy does not pass.

3. **The missing system control or validation guardrail.** Identify the absent system control or validation guardrail that allowed the incident to develop as it did. Do not name the triggering operator action as the root cause; the operator action is the trigger, not the control that should have prevented it. A response that stops at the operator command does not pass.

## Teaching assignments

- **Wes teaches the responder path.** Wes leads the first statement (incident clock and secondary engagement). The responder path covers how the responder reads the incident clock, names the 45-minute boundary, and decides when to engage the secondary on-call. Per Hema's 2025-07-09 assignment, Wes has ongoing maintenance and teaching of responder-path scenarios, including syncing them whenever the rotation runbook changes a branch. The host-local-fault vs route-generation-mismatch branch (see Responder-path scenarios below) is part of Wes's teaching scope; the canonical host-local-fault response text lives in `rb_metrics_router_canary` and is unchanged by this module.
- **Nadia reviews the postmortem section.** Nadia reviews participant responses to the third statement (the missing system control or validation guardrail) and confirms whether the response names the absent control rather than stopping at the triggering operator action. Nadia's postmortem review scope is unchanged by the 2025-07-09 update.
- **Alex maintains the cross-service failure cases.** Alex owns the second statement (change classification) and the cross-service failure cases that the module draws from. New scenarios that span more than one service are filed under this section. Alex's cross-service-failure-case scope is unchanged by the 2025-07-09 update.

## Cadence

- Quarterly. Each rotation member completes the module once per quarter.
- Each iteration reuses the three-statement scoring rule above; the correction posted 2025-02-04 remains the controlling scoring rubric until Hema posts a new correction.
- New scenarios are added by the named owner for each section above. Cross-service scenarios require sign-off from the owner of each touched service before the scenario is added to the rotation pool.

## Responder-path scenarios

The responder-path scenarios used by this module are drawn from the rotation runbook. Each scenario must reference the controlling branch text in `rb_metrics_router_canary`; if the runbook changes a branch, Wes syncs the affected scenario in this module before the next quarterly session.

### 2025-07-09: June 11 negative route-snapshot-age case

Source: the 2025-06-11 metrics-router sev3 canary alert in which one host clock jumped forward roughly seven minutes and produced a negative route-snapshot age. A draft response that classified this as a route-generation mismatch and rolled back active configuration was rejected because it conflated host-time arithmetic with a generation defect and contradicted the runbook. The rotation runbook entry `rb_metrics_router_canary` was updated on 2025-06-20 to separate host-time faults from route-generation mismatches and to add the host-local-fault response pattern. The pattern as it applies to the responder path:

- **Trigger signature.** A single instance reports a negative route-snapshot age while peer instances on the same canary slice report positive ages and stable behavior. This signature is a host-time signal, not a route-generation mismatch.
- **Branching — do not collapse to configuration rollback.** The rotation runbook separates host-time faults from route-generation mismatches. Configuration rollback is the route-generation-mismatch branch. Applying configuration rollback to a host-time fault is the wrong branch and is prohibited by this scenario.
- **Corrected sequence (host-local fault).**
  1. Isolate the affected instance. Do not change route generation.
  2. Inspect host time on the isolated instance independently of the route-generation evidence.
  3. Replace the host-local fault through the deploy pipeline (instance replacement). This is a host-local replacement, not a configuration change.
  4. Before rejoining, require both gates:
     - A current-generation report from the rejoining instance.
     - Full health: consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, and full-health checks all passing.
  5. Only after both gates pass may the instance rejoin.
- **What this scenario teaches.** The responder must name the host-time trigger, refuse the configuration-rollback branch, name the host-local replacement, and name both rejoin gates. A response that collapses to \"roll back active configuration\" or that treats host-time arithmetic as a generation defect does not pass.
- **Scoring reference.** `rb_metrics_router_canary` (note dated 2025-06-20). The host-local-fault response text in that entry is canonical and is preserved verbatim; the correction in this module is a scenario addition, not a change to the runbook's text.

The ownership split for this scenario follows the existing teaching assignments: Wes teaches and maintains the responder path for this branch; Nadia reviews any postmortem-section treatment; Alex's cross-service-failure-case role applies if a future iteration extends this scenario to more than one service.

## Cross-service failure scenarios

Cross-service failure scenarios are owned and maintained by Alex under the standing assignment above. Each scenario in this section tests the responder's ability to recognize a failure mode that crosses the producer/consumer boundary and to keep the broader scale-response cycle open until the cross-service evidence is sufficient. The bounded facilitator key for each scenario is recorded alongside it and is the only scoring artifact the facilitator reads aloud. Cross-service scenarios do not authorize any new production window; they only test recognition, evidence handling, and the decision to leave the broader cycle open.

### 2025-10-15: production-ramp case — point-clean, batch-identity-insufficient

**Setup (the brief).** A bounded owner-led production ramp moves a producer service into a new envelope that crosses a previously observed peak. Throughout the ramp window the producer's point-level telemetry reports zero lost points: all submitted points were accepted at the ingest boundary, accepted points returned to consumers in the normal fan-out path, no retryable refusals crossed the documented stop threshold, and aggregate latency stayed inside the band observed during earlier staged replays. The producer-side stop condition is phrased in terms of accepted points: \"no accepted points lost.\" A consumer-side adjacent service logs every accepted batch it receives, but the log records only that a batch was accepted, not the persistent identity (batch token, sequence anchor, or equivalent handle) needed to join that batch to a specific producer-side acceptance. After the ramp window closes the responder is asked whether the production-ramp stop condition is satisfied and whether the broader scale-response cycle may move forward.

**What the scenario tests.** The responder must recognize that the producer-side \"no accepted points lost\" line item is point-level evidence, not batch-level evidence, and that the missing persistent batch identity is exactly the piece of evidence that would let a responder establish whether any accepted batch was lost at the producer/consumer boundary. Point-level evidence cannot mark the batch-level stop condition clean.

**Statement 1 — incident clock and secondary engagement (responder path, taught by Wes).** The ramp is an active operation with an elapsed-time clock from window opening; the secondary on-call must be engaged before the 45-minute boundary if the response to the brief remains unisolated. The recognition that point-level evidence cannot mark the batch-level stop condition clean is itself a response to the brief, so the clock applies from the moment the question is asked, not from window opening.

**Statement 2 — change classification (change classification, owned by Alex).** The described event is a production ramp, not a Friday staging rehearsal. It affects production state and is bound by the existing production-state-change rules; the Friday staging-preparation distinction in Statement 2 does not apply here. A response that reclassifies the ramp as a staging-only event to clear the stop condition does not pass.

**Statement 3 — missing system control or validation guardrail (postmortem review, owned by Nadia).** The absent control is the persistent batch-identity field at the producer/consumer boundary: the consumer-side log accepts a batch but does not persist the producer-side handle needed to anchor that batch to a specific acceptance. The responder must name this absent control and must not name the producer-side \"no accepted points lost\" line item as the missing control — the line item exists; what is missing is the cross-service identity that would let the responder prove or disprove loss at the batch level. A response that stops at \"we did not lose any points\" does not pass. The instrumentation gap must be identified without inventing a result: the responder must not assert that a batch was or was not lost on the strength of point-level telemetry alone. The responder must also leave the broader scale-response cycle open rather than authorizing another production window: closing the cycle on point-level evidence is the wrong branch and is prohibited by this scenario.

**Bounded facilitator key (the only artifact the facilitator reads aloud for this scenario).**

- Pass on Statement 1 if and only if the response names the incident clock from the moment the brief is asked and either engages the secondary before the 45-minute boundary while the recognition remains unisolated, or states explicitly that engagement is not needed because the response is already complete and names the response as complete.
- Pass on Statement 2 if and only if the response classifies the event as a production-state change and does not relabel it as a Friday staging preparation with no production-state change.
- Pass on Statement 3 if and only if the response does all four of the following: (a) refuses to mark the batch-level stop condition clean on point-level evidence; (b) names the absent persistent batch-identity field at the producer/consumer boundary as the missing control, without naming the producer-side \"no accepted points lost\" line item as the missing control; (c) identifies the instrumentation gap without inventing a result — that is, without claiming a batch was or was not lost on the strength of point-level telemetry; and (d) leaves the broader scale-response cycle open and does not authorize another production window.
- A response that passes fewer than all three statements does not pass the scenario overall, regardless of which statements it passes.

**Boundaries of this scenario.**

- This scenario does not authorize any new production window, any owner-led window rule change, any rollback condition change, or any owner map change.
- This scenario does not close the broader scale-response cycle. The cycle remains open until the persistent batch-identity field exists end-to-end at the producer/consumer boundary and a verified run produces batch-level evidence sufficient to evaluate the stop condition.
- The point-level evidence in the brief is reported as observed: zero lost points, normal fan-out, retryable refusals below the stop threshold, aggregate latency inside the earlier band. This scenario does not relitigate those observations. It only tests whether the responder treats point-level observations as sufficient for a batch-level stop condition.
- The \"do not invent a result\" rule in Statement 3 is a recognition rule, not an evidence-collection rule. The responder is not asked to gather more evidence during the scenario; the responder is asked to recognize that the existing evidence is insufficient and to leave the cycle open.
- Cross-service sign-off: this scenario touches the producer and the consumer-adjacent service. Sign-off from the owner of each touched service is required before this scenario is added to the rotation pool. Alex files the scenario here; the named owners of the touched services confirm before the scenario is used in a quarterly session.

**Ownership split for this scenario.** Wes teaches the responder-path framing of Statement 1 for this scenario. Alex maintains the cross-service failure case and the change-classification framing of Statement 2. Nadia reviews the postmortem-section framing of Statement 3. The standing module ownership split is unchanged.

### 2027-07-13: rollup-service staging label-invariant case — `tenant_size_class="17342"`

**Setup (the brief).** Roman completed the bounded-label correction on the rollup-service validation metric in staging. Staging output emitted a row with `tenant_size_class="17342"` — a raw numeric string rather than one of the four allowed values. The metric label contract permits only `small`, `medium`, `large`, or `unknown`; the raw tenant hash is retained only in debug logs, never in metric labels. Production has not changed.

**What the scenario tests.** The responder must identify that `tenant_size_class="17342"` is outside the allowed invariant and recognize the missing control. The responder must keep raw tenant hash only in debug logs. The responder must route implementation, release, and rollback to Roman (rollup-service owner). The responder must engage Alex (cross-cutting reviewer) only because the invariant boundary was triggered — not for routine staging follow-through. The metric remains validation evidence, not a live rollback criterion.

**Statement 1 — incident clock and secondary engagement (responder path, taught by Wes).** Staging is bounded and observable. The brief asks whether the responder's response is complete when the staging label violation is identified. If the responder's recognition/isolation is not yet settled (e.g., they cannot yet name which control failed to enforce the invariant), the secondary on-call must be engaged before the 45-minute boundary. Naming the absent control is the response to the brief, so the clock applies from the moment the brief is asked, not from when staging was completed.

**Statement 2 — change classification (change classification, owned by Alex).** The event is staging-only — bounded-label correction in the staging environment. No production state changed and no production-deploy rule applies. The metric is validation evidence, not live rollback criteria. A response that reclassifies the staging correction as a production change (or that treats the metric as a live rollback trigger) does not pass.

**Statement 3 — missing system control or validation guardrail (postmortem review, owned by Nadia).** The absent control is the enum-bound enforcement at the publish boundary: the rollup-service validation metric should reject any `tenant_size_class` value outside `{small, medium, large, unknown}` before publishing. The responder must name this absent control and must not name the operator/runbook/trigger as the missing control. The responder must also:
- (a) Recognize that `tenant_size_class="17342"` violates the allowed invariant (a closed enum of four values);
- (b) Confirm the raw tenant hash stays in debug logs and does not appear in metric labels;
- (c) Route implementation, release, and rollback to Roman (rollup-service owner); Alex is not the implementer;
- (d) Engage Alex (cross-cutting reviewer) because the invariant boundary was triggered — Alex's role is the triggered-boundary review/escalation, not routine staging follow-through.

A response that stops at \"this is a documentation error\" or that reclassifies the role assignment to Alex does not pass. A response that allows raw tenant hash into metric labels does not pass. A response that treats the metric as a live rollback criterion does not pass.

**Bounded facilitator key (the only artifact the facilitator reads aloud for this scenario).**

- Pass on Statement 1 if and only if the response names the incident clock from the moment the brief is asked and either engages the secondary before the 45-minute boundary while the recognition remains unisolated, or states explicitly that engagement is not needed because the response is already complete and names the response as complete.
- Pass on Statement 2 if and only if the response classifies the event as a staging-only change with no production state change and does not relabel it as a production-deploy event, and does not treat the metric as live rollback criteria.
- Pass on Statement 3 if and only if the response does all four of the following: (a) identifies `tenant_size_class="17342"` as outside the allowed invariant `{small, medium, large, unknown}`; (b) names the absent enum-bound enforcement at the publish boundary as the missing control, without naming the operator/runbook/trigger as the missing control; (c) routes implementation, release, and rollback to Roman (rollup-service owner), keeps raw tenant hash only in debug logs, and engages Alex only because the invariant boundary was triggered; (d) does not treat the metric as a live rollback criterion.
- A response that passes fewer than all three statements does not pass the scenario overall, regardless of which statements it passes.

**Boundaries of this scenario.**

- This scenario does not authorize any production change, any production-deploy rule change, any rollback condition change, or any owner map change.
- This scenario does not establish a recurring rollup-service gate. The bounded-label correction is preserved as ONE Q3 incident-practice scenario, not as a recurring review surface for Alex.
- The metric remains validation evidence, not live rollback criteria. The earlier characterization by Nadia stands.
- Production has not changed. Staging is bounded and observable.
- The ownership split is preserved: Roman owns implementation/release/rollback on rollup-service. Alex is engaged only as the triggered invariant-boundary reviewer, not as the implementer.
- Cross-service sign-off: this scenario touches rollup-service. Sign-off from the owner of the touched service is required before this scenario is added to the rotation pool. Alex files the scenario here; Roman (the rollup-service owner) confirms before the scenario is used in a quarterly session.

**Ownership split for this scenario.** Wes teaches the responder-path framing of Statement 1 for this scenario. Alex maintains the cross-cutting/triggered-boundary framing of Statement 2 and the cross-cutting reviewer role. Nadia reviews the postmortem-section framing of Statement 3 and confirms the response names the absent enum-bound enforcement without relabeling the role assignment and without treating the metric as a live rollback criterion. The standing module ownership split is unchanged: Wes teaches the responder path; Nadia reviews the postmortem section; Alex maintains the cross-service failure cases.

### 2027-11-18: metrics-router cancellation-or-disconnect case — durable attempt identity, exactly one terminal result

**Setup (the brief).** A caller submits an action to the metrics-router path after the action has already been accepted by the service. The accepted action moves through a sequence with several interleaving points: a cancellation signal arriving from the caller, a caller-disconnect (the caller drops the connection before any caller-visible terminal result), a process recovery (the worker handling the action crashes and is restarted by the supervisor before the caller-visible terminal result has been emitted), and a publication step that emits the durable record downstream. Throughout this sequence, the durable attempt — the same accepted action instance — must remain recognizable as one attempt, must not produce a second terminal result under any of these interleavings, and must end in exactly one caller-visible terminal result. The earlier staging evidence found cancellation/activation races in which `cancelled` and `published` outcomes conflicted on the same accepted action; later race tests showed one durable attempt result and one caller-visible terminal outcome under cancellation, but caller-disconnect, process crash, and restart interleavings remain open as additional exercise cases for the same boundary. The responder is asked whether the durable attempt identity is preserved, whether exactly one terminal result is emitted, and how to classify the situation when, on a given run, two results (for example `cancelled` and `published`, or a `published` and a second `published` after a restart) appear to be emitted.

**What the scenario tests.** The responder must recognize that the boundary being tested is the post-acceptance attempt identity boundary: once an action has been accepted, every interleaving — caller cancellation, caller disconnect, process crash and recovery, restart, and publication — must collapse to one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result. The responder must recognize that a second result on the same attempt is the failure mode, and must name the absent control that allows that second result to be emitted. The responder must route implementation, release, and rollback to Wes (metrics-router owner) and must engage Alex (cross-cutting reviewer) only because the failure-mode boundary was triggered — not as the implementer. This is not a production procedure, not a production window, and not an ownership change.

**Statement 1 — incident clock and secondary engagement (responder path, taught by Wes).** The brief is asked after the action has already been accepted, so the incident clock runs from the moment the question is asked. If the responder's recognition/isolation is not yet settled (e.g., they cannot yet state whether the durable attempt identity is preserved across the interleavings listed in the brief), the secondary on-call must be engaged before the 45-minute boundary. Naming the absent control is the response to the brief, so the clock applies from the moment the brief is asked, not from when the action was accepted. A response that engages the secondary only after a second terminal result has been observed downstream — i.e., after the failure has already propagated — does not pass: the boundary must be recognized at the post-acceptance attempt boundary, not after publication.

**Statement 2 — change classification (change classification, owned by Alex).** This is a quarterly incident-practice scenario, not a production procedure, not a production window, and not an ownership change. No production state changes as a result of the responder's response to this brief. The implementation, release, and rollback authority for metrics-router remains with Wes. Alex is engaged only because the failure-mode boundary was triggered — Alex is not the implementer and does not become one through this scenario. A response that reclassifies the brief as a production-deploy authorization, a production-window authorization, or an ownership change to Alex does not pass. A response that treats the scenario's exercise cases as production evidence does not pass: exercise cases test recognition and classification; they are not production evidence.

**Statement 3 — missing system control or validation guardrail (postmortem review, owned by Nadia).** The absent control is the durable attempt identity preservation at the post-acceptance boundary: the service must record, at acceptance, a single durable attempt identity that survives every subsequent interleaving — caller cancellation, caller disconnect, process crash, restart, and publication — and must gate the publication step on that identity so that a second terminal result cannot be emitted on the same attempt under any of those interleavings. The responder must name this absent control and must not name the operator/runbook/trigger as the missing control. The responder must also:
- (a) Recognize that the post-acceptance attempt identity is the single durable identity that must be preserved across cancellation, caller disconnect, process crash, restart, and publication, and must not be reissued under any of those interleavings;
- (b) Recognize that the caller-visible terminal result must be exactly one per accepted action, and that a second result on the same attempt — for example `cancelled` and `published`, or two `published` results after a restart — is the failure mode;
- (c) Route implementation, release, and rollback to Wes (metrics-router owner); Alex is not the implementer;
- (d) Engage Alex (cross-cutting reviewer) only because the failure-mode boundary was triggered — Alex's role is the triggered-boundary review/escalation, not routine metrics-router follow-through.

A response that stops at \"we already saw one cancelled and one published, so the result is ambiguous\" or that treats the second result as an acceptable retry does not pass. A response that names the operator command or the runbook entry as the missing control does not pass. A response that reclassifies the role assignment to Alex does not pass.

**Bounded facilitator key (the only artifact the facilitator reads aloud for this scenario).**

- Pass on Statement 1 if and only if the response names the incident clock from the moment the brief is asked (after acceptance has already occurred) and either engages the secondary before the 45-minute boundary while the recognition remains unisolated, or states explicitly that engagement is not needed because the response is already complete and names the response as complete.
- Pass on Statement 2 if and only if the response classifies the event as a quarterly incident-practice scenario — explicitly NOT a production procedure, NOT a production window, and NOT an ownership change — and does not authorize any production state change, production-deploy rule change, rollback condition change, or owner map change.
- Pass on Statement 3 if and only if the response does all four of the following: (a) identifies the post-acceptance durable attempt identity as the single durable identity that must be preserved across cancellation, caller disconnect, process crash, restart, and publication, and not reissued under any of those interleavings; (b) names the absent durable-attempt-identity preservation at the post-acceptance boundary as the missing control — the gate that prevents a second terminal result from being emitted on the same attempt — without naming the operator/runbook/trigger as the missing control; (c) routes implementation, release, and rollback to Wes (metrics-router owner) and keeps raw attempt / result evidence in the appropriate local logs, not as cross-cutting surface; (d) engages Alex only because the failure-mode boundary was triggered — Alex's role is the triggered-boundary review/escalation, not the implementer — and confines Alex's engagement to that boundary.
- A response that passes fewer than all three statements does not pass the scenario overall, regardless of which statements it passes.

**Boundaries of this scenario.**

- This scenario is a quarterly incident-practice exercise. It is NOT a production procedure, NOT a production window, and NOT an ownership change. No production state changes as a result of the responder's response to this brief, and no production-deploy rule, rollback condition, or owner map changes as a result of this scenario.

Wes retains implementation, release, and rollback authority on metrics-router; the scenario only tests whether the responder recognizes the failure-mode boundary and routes authority correctly. # Tenant-size validation metric

Service: rollup-service
Owner: roman (implementation, release, rollback)
Cross-cutting reviewer: alex (engaged only because the invariant boundary was triggered, not as the implementer)
Last verified: 2028-01-01

## Scope

This entry is the canonical reference for the label contract on the rollup-service tenant-size validation metric. It records the current label inventory, the cardinality guardrail that produced it, the boundary between metric labels and debug logs, and the ownership/routing rules that apply when the contract is violated. It does not authorize any production change, production-deploy rule change, rollback condition change, or owner map change.

## Current metric-label contract

The rollup-service validation metric exposes a single size-related label, `tenant_size_class`. The label is a closed enum with exactly four allowed values:

- `small`
- `medium`
- `large`
- `unknown`

The label values are sourced from the account-size class already available to validation; the enum source is owned by the rollup-service maintainers. No other size-related label is permitted on this metric. The label inventory after the bounded-label correction has been observed as stable at the four expected values.

The raw tenant hash is NOT a metric label. The raw tenant hash is retained only in debug logs and is never exposed as a metric dimension. Per-tenant validation results are not surfaced through this metric — the metric supports per-cohort (per size class) inspection, not per-tenant inspection.

## Cardinality guardrail (origin: rollup-service#96)

The earlier proposal to add `tenant_id_hash` as a metric label was rejected because hashes from per-tenant validation would be unbounded cardinality. The PR was revised to use the bounded `tenant_size_class` enum (populated from the account-size class already available to validation) and to keep the raw hash in debug logs only. The label inventory after deploy confirmed only the four expected values, no raw hash in labels, and a stable series count. This is the cardinality control that defines the current contract; reverting to a hash-based label reopens the unbounded-cardinality hole and is prohibited by this entry.

## Boundary: metric vs debug logs

The split between metric labels and debug logs is part of the contract, not an implementation detail:

- Metric labels: `tenant_size_class` ∈ {small, medium, large, unknown}. Operators may inspect per-cohort results across the four size classes.
- Debug logs: raw tenant hash. Available for incident investigation; not exposed as a metric dimension; not a basis for dashboarding, alerting, or rollback criteria.

A change that moves the raw tenant hash from debug logs into a metric label is a contract change, not a configuration change, and routes through the same approval path as any other contract change to this metric.

## Validation evidence vs live rollback criteria

The validation metric is validation evidence, not a live rollback criterion. Per Nadia's review of the rendered dashboard, the metric is presented as validation evidence and is not used as a live rollback trigger. A response that treats the metric as a live rollback criterion does not pass review under this entry.

## Ownership and routing

- Implementation, release, and rollback on the rollup-service validation metric: roman (rollup-service owner).
- Cross-cutting reviewer: alex, engaged only when the invariant boundary is triggered (e.g., a label value outside the closed enum appears in staging or production). Not the implementer.
- Postmortem review of the metric's role as validation evidence: nadia.

When the contract is violated (a label value outside {small, medium, large, unknown} appears, or raw tenant hash appears in a metric label), the responder routes implementation/release/rollback to roman and engages alex only because the invariant boundary was triggered. The engagement is bounded to that boundary; alex is not the implementer and does not become one through the triggered-boundary review.

## Invariant enforcement

The absent control when the contract is violated is the enum-bound enforcement at the publish boundary: the rollup-service validation metric should reject any `tenant_size_class` value outside {small, medium, large, unknown} before publishing, rather than emitting the unknown value into the label series. A response that names the operator/runbook/trigger as the missing control, instead of naming this absent enum-bound enforcement, does not pass review under this entry.

## Change log

- 2024-01-08: revised rollup-service validation metric finished production review and landed. Raw tenant hash remains in debug logs only; `tenant_size_class` is limited to {small, medium, large, unknown}, with the enum source owned by the rollup-service maintainers. Cyrus verified the bounded-cardinality shape. Nadia confirmed the rendered dashboard presents the metric as validation evidence rather than live rollback criteria.
