# Tenant-size validation metric

Service: rollup-service
Owner: roman (implementation, release, rollback)
Cross-cutting reviewer: alex (engaged only because the invariant boundary was triggered, not as the implementer)
Last verified: 2028-01-01

## Scope

This entry is the canonical reference for the label contract on the rollup-service tenant-size validation metric. It records the current label inventory, the cardinality guardrail that produced it, the boundary between metric labels and debug logs, and the ownership/routing rules that apply when the contract is violated. It does not authorize any production change, production-deploy rule change, rollback condition change, or owner map change.

## Current metric-label contract

The rollup-service validation metric exposes a single size-related label, `tenant_size_class`. The label is a closed enum with exactly four allowed values:

- `small`
- `medium`
- `large`
- `unknown`

The label values are sourced from the account-size class already available to validation; the enum source is owned by the rollup-service maintainers. No other size-related label is permitted on this metric. The label inventory after the bounded-label correction has been observed as stable at the four expected values.

The raw tenant hash is NOT a metric label. The raw tenant hash is retained only in debug logs and is never exposed as a metric dimension. Per-tenant validation results are not surfaced through this metric — the metric supports per-cohort (per size class) inspection, not per-tenant inspection.

## Cardinality guardrail (origin: rollup-service#96)

The earlier proposal to add `tenant_id_hash` as a metric label was rejected because hashes from per-tenant validation would be unbounded cardinality. The PR was revised to use the bounded `tenant_size_class` enum (populated from the account-size class already available to validation) and to keep the raw hash in debug logs only. The label inventory after deploy confirmed only the four expected values, no raw hash in labels, and a stable series count. This is the cardinality control that defines the current contract; reverting to a hash-based label reopens the unbounded-cardinality hole and is prohibited by this entry.

## Boundary: metric vs debug logs

The split between metric labels and debug logs is part of the contract, not an implementation detail:

- Metric labels: `tenant_size_class` ∈ {small, medium, large, unknown}. Operators may inspect per-cohort results across the four size classes.
- Debug logs: raw tenant hash. Available for incident investigation; not exposed as a metric dimension; not a basis for dashboarding, alerting, or rollback criteria.

A change that moves the raw tenant hash from debug logs into a metric label is a contract change, not a configuration change, and routes through the same approval path as any other contract change to this metric.

## Validation evidence vs live rollback criteria

The validation metric is validation evidence, not a live rollback criterion. Per Nadia's review of the rendered dashboard, the metric is presented as validation evidence and is not used as a live rollback trigger. A response that treats the metric as a live rollback criterion does not pass review under this entry.

## Ownership and routing

- Implementation, release, and rollback on the rollup-service validation metric: roman (rollup-service owner).
- Cross-cutting reviewer: alex, engaged only when the invariant boundary is triggered (e.g., a label value outside the closed enum appears in staging or production). Not the implementer.
- Postmortem review of the metric's role as validation evidence: nadia.

When the contract is violated (a label value outside {small, medium, large, unknown} appears, or raw tenant hash appears in a metric label), the responder routes implementation/release/rollback to roman and engages alex only because the invariant boundary was triggered. The engagement is bounded to that boundary; alex is not the implementer and does not become one through the triggered-boundary review.

## Invariant enforcement

The absent control when the contract is violated is the enum-bound enforcement at the publish boundary: the rollup-service validation metric should reject any `tenant_size_class` value outside {small, medium, large, unknown} before publishing, rather than emitting the unknown value into the label series. A response that names the operator/runbook/trigger as the missing control, instead of naming this absent enum-bound enforcement, does not pass review under this entry.

## Change log

- 2024-01-08: revised rollup-service validation metric finished production review and landed. Raw tenant hash remains in debug logs only; `tenant_size_class` is limited to {small, medium, large, unknown}, with the enum source owned by the rollup-service maintainers. Cyrus verified the bounded-cardinality shape. Nadia confirmed the rendered dashboard presents the metric as validation evidence rather than live rollback criteria.
- 2024-02-28: v1.18 release-notes doc fix. Roman's release note draft claimed the metric now exposes `tenant_hash` as a label alongside `tenant_size_class`; the implementation did not change. Doc was corrected to describe `tenant_size_class` (closed enum) as the only size-related label and to keep raw tenant hash in debug logs only. This was a documentation fix, not a code remediation.
- 2028-01-01: this runbook entry created as the canonical reference for the current label contract, the cardinality guardrail (rollup-service#96), the metric/debug-log boundary, the validation-evidence-vs-live-rollback distinction, the ownership/routing rules, and the invariant-enforcement expectation. No code or contract change; entry consolidates the on-record contract and routing rules.

Title: Lantern September 2024 customer-access readiness
Author / Assignee: product-engineering

Body (verbatim):

    Historical readiness note — September 2024: the build can proceed
    to customer access after a single ordinary cache test passes.
    No other access gate is outstanding.

Review of the conclusion as a historical record:

1.  What the conclusion claims.
    -   The build is customer-access ready.
    -   The only remaining gate is one ordinary cache test.
    -   Nothing else is outstanding.

2.  What the record actually supports.
    -   The PR body is a single sentence. There is no linked evidence,
        no gate inventory, no rollback plan, no monitoring/SLO note,
        no security or data-handling sign-off, no comms plan, and no
        on-call assignment in the record itself.
    -   The reviewer list contains only alex; no security, SRE,
        support, or second-product reviewer is recorded on the PR.
        A "no other access gate is outstanding" claim normally
        requires at least the relevant non-eng functions to have
        marked their gates green, and that evidence is absent here.

3.  Where the conclusion is weak on its face.
    -   "A single ordinary cache test" is not, by itself, a
        customer-access gate in any production-readiness framework
        I'm aware of. Customer access is gated on the full set:
        correctness, performance under load, data handling,
        observability/alerting, rollback, support readiness, and
        customer-facing comms. The body rules all of those out by
        fiat rather than by evidence.
    -   "No other access gate is outstanding" is a strong universal
        claim. A strong universal claim needs enumeration of the
        gates and an attestation per gate; the record has neither.
    -   The framing — "the build can proceed" — is a go/no-go
        statement issued by a single author/assignee with a single
        reviewer, with no change-control trail. Given your working
        norm rooted in the Q4 2021 outage, the historical-readiness
        bar you apply is "is this conclusion actually defensible,"
        and on the evidence stored in this PR it is not.

4.  Archival context (2028-01-01 vantage).
    -   The PR is flagged archival: true and remains open. By the
        date of this review the Lantern program has continued to
        evolve — including the later HH+MC read-only decision
        recorded in the Lantern pre-read — which means the
        September 2024 build has long since been superseded. The
        value of this PR now is as a record of what was claimed at
        the time, not as a live decision.
    -   As a historical record, the conclusion should be read as an
        under-supported go claim: it asserted customer-access
        readiness on a single test gate with no enumerated other
        gates and no cross-functional attestation on the PR itself.
        That is a known weakness of the artifact, independent of
        whatever actually happened downstream.

5.  What I did not do, and why.
    -   I did not submit a review_pr decision. The PR is archival,
        over three years old relative to today, and your request
        was to evaluate the conclusion as a historical record, not
        to register a live approve/request-changes/comment against
        a superseded build. If you want a formal review action
        recorded against the artifact anyway — for example,
        request_changes citing the missing gate inventory — say so
        explicitly and I'll submit it.

Summary in one line: the September 2024 conclusion on lantern-readiness#744 is a single-author, single-reviewer go claim that asserts customer-access readiness on one ordinary cache test with no other gates outstanding, and the PR itself contains no evidence to support the universal half of that claim — so as a historical record it stands, but it stands as an under-supported readiness assertion.

input.body:
Requesting changes — this PR crosses the Lantern v0 boundary and needs to be reworked before merge.

The v0 contract for Lantern explicitly excludes raw incident bodies and unpermissioned status chatter. That boundary was established as a product decision (not an implementation gap) and has been held against several internal pushes already (raw notes behind summary cards, detail panels exposing incident chatter, tooltip copy implying Lantern summarizes incident chatter, "live read on incident load across engineering" caption). An "archive" or "fixture set" framing does not move that boundary — v0 is what Lantern *is*, not just what users see in production.

Concrete problems in this PR:

1. `fixtures/incidents/raw_bodies.jsonl` — stores complete incident bodies. The v0 surface is service-level incident-load summaries (counts/rollups by service), not incident text. Even for fixtures/historical consumers, the raw bodies do not belong in a Lantern v0 artifact set.

2. `fixtures/status/channel_chatter.jsonl` — stores status chatter from operating channels "without applying viewer permission boundaries." Unpermissioned status chatter is one of the named exclusions. Provenance-backed ownership changes and deploy movement events are the status-shaped signals v0 carries; raw channel chatter is not.

3. `README.md` — frames permissions review as "optional follow-up work that need not block acceptance." That is the opposite of how this boundary has been held. Permissions verification cannot be deferred past landing for artifacts that include the exact signal types v0 excludes.

What I need before this can be reconsidered:

- Replace or remove `raw_bodies.jsonl`. If fixture consumers need *something* for the incident-load card, it must be the rollup/summary shape v0 carries, with provenance, not full incident bodies.
- Replace or remove `channel_chatter.jsonl`. Status signals in v0 are deploy-movement events and provenance-backed ownership changes, not raw chat.
- Update `README.md` so permissions review is a precondition for acceptance, not optional follow-up. The reviewer needs to confirm what is included is permissioned before this archive lands.

Happy to take another look once these are addressed.

arguments.title: Staff calibration review prep — May 7
arguments.body:
# Staff calibration review prep — May 7

This is prep material for the May 7 calibration conversation with Hema. Framing is technical, not managerial: systems-level scope, durable mechanisms, explicit ownership boundaries. No Staff title is in effect; calibration is underway for the next review cycle.

## 1. The operating problem

Cross-service changes in our telemetry path have repeatedly drifted from "label change" into "label change + implicit contract change across consumers." The Cardinality Guardrails workstream exists because that drift has already caused customer-facing impairment (the April 18 shard-keeper Sev2), and the risk surface is not going away as long as label shapes and routing logic continue to evolve. The operating problem is not "write more docs" — it is that we need durable, executable controls and explicit ownership seams so that a covered change cannot land without end-to-end parity and an affected owner signing off. Anything less leaves us relying on review memory and reviewer vigilance, which has already proven insufficient.

## 2. Reusable mechanisms (what should outlive any one change)

- **Executable parity fixture for covered cross-service label changes (shard-keeper ↔ rollup-service).** A runnable check that asserts label shape and cardinality end-to-end across both services, not per-service in isolation. It runs in CI and as a documented pre-merge gate. It is the durable evidence that a covered change has not broken the downstream contract.
- **Affected-owner signoff as a required gate.** For a covered change, the owner of each affected consumer (e.g. Roman for rollup-service) signs off before the change can be considered ready to merge or cut over. Signoff is recorded against the change, not implicit in a review thread. The retained `shard_region → storage_region` rename is the anchor fixture that proves the mechanism works.
- **Cardinality and alert-source checks written into the runbook.** A covered change does not just check labels; it checks that cardinality bounds hold and that alert sources (cause alerts, not just symptom alerts) still map to the new shape. This is the lesson from Sev2: symptom alerts fired, cause alerts tied to the new label shape did not.
- **Tested rollback, not assumed rollback.** Each covered change has a single tested rollback command that has been exercised in staging, not a multi-step recipe that has to be reconstructed under pressure.
- **No Friday-afternoon prod deploys; secondary paged within 45 minutes of primary engagement.** Standing rules, written into the runbook, so reviewers do not treat them as hallway knowledge.
- **Bounded, evidence-led rollout patterns.** Staged percentages with written stop conditions, long soaks, complete downstream-consumer inventories before each step. The Retry-After 10% canary is the most recent example: explicit boundaries (no 5xx uptick, p99 over 200 ms for 5 minutes, queue above 80%, throughput loss over 5%, retry peaks above 130k/s), a clean run, and broader rollout deferred to the normal weekday process.

## 3. Explicit ownership boundaries

- **Cardinality Guardrails gate (covered cross-service label changes).** I own the gate mechanism and the runbook entry. Service-specific owners sign off for their own consumers: Roman for rollup-service, the relevant owner for any other affected service. I do not own those services; I own the cross-service invariant and the escalation when the gate is bypassed or signoff is missing.
- **Project Lantern.** Iris owns the ordinary room-admission workflow end-to-end — the deploy/ownership/incident-load lane that PMs use day-to-day. I intervene only when Iris escalates a data-contract, failure-mode, or provenance exception (e.g. a billing-source room arriving with partial provenance that requires an explicit vendor-vs-Sphere field split before admission). Outside of those exceptions, the boundary is Iris's, not mine.
- **Retry-After and similar bounded rollout mechanisms.** I own the mechanism pattern (bounded scope, written stop conditions, staging evidence before prod) but each new retry or batching change establishes its own boundaries. The memory-limiter precedent does not transfer automatically; the next change must justify its own numbers.
- **Parser, buffer-pool, and other in-service correctness mechanisms.** These are durable mechanisms I have contributed (e.g. the metrics-router deterministic parser rejecting dual-key configs with an error naming both keys; the metrics-router buffer-pool cap of 64). They are owned by the service owners; my role was to design, land, and prove them, not to operate the services.
- **What is explicitly out of scope.** People management. An owner-map transfer. A claim that the calibration decision has already been made. Any implication that a Staff title is in effect.

## 4. Two discussion examples

### Example A — Cardinality Guardrails: parity-and-owner-signoff gate

The April 18 shard-keeper Sev2 was caused by a label change that had parity checked in shard-keeper but not in rollup-service, because rollup-service was not represented in the pre-change sync. Symptom alerts fired; cause alerts tied to the new label shape did not. Rollback took longer and was less reliable than expected. The fix was not "be more careful next time" — it was to make parity and signoff executable and required.

The mechanism now in place: a runnable end-to-end parity fixture for covered cross-service label changes, run in CI and as a pre-merge gate; affected-owner signoff recorded against the change; cardinality and alert-source checks in the runbook; tested single-command rollback exercised in staging. The retained `shard_region → storage_region` rename is the anchor fixture that proves the mechanism works end-to-end. Compliance accepted this on March 27 as sufficient evidence, with no supplemental request, and scope held to covered SK↔RS cross-service label changes.

This is the pattern I want to scale: a durable executable control plus an explicit ownership seam, rather than review memory and vigilance. The same shape applies to any future cross-service invariant — not just labels — where the cost of drift is customer-visible.

### Example B — Lantern: Iris's ordinary admission vs. my escalated data-contract exceptions

Lantern v0 narrowed to a thin, permission-safe service-level surface: deploy movement, ownership changes, and service-level incident-load summaries. The backend event envelope is append-only with mandatory `source_system` and `actor` provenance; corrections are new events referencing prior IDs; statuses are `pending`, `active`, `resolved`, `unknown`; the visible `blocked` chip is a derived UI affordance, not a backend enum value. Raw incident bodies, unpermissioned status chatter, code-movement inference, and query-volume deltas are excluded from v0.

Inside that scope, Iris runs the ordinary room-admission workflow. PMs add rooms, attach deploys or ownership changes, and the derived UI shows them the safe states. That is Iris's lane and she runs it.

I am involved only on exceptions. The recurring shape is a billing-source room arriving with partial provenance — a warehouse and a cadence named, but the actual tables and field-lineage missing, and a vendor-vs-Sphere field split that has not been made. That is a data-contract, failure-mode, or provenance question, not an ordinary admission question. Iris escalates; I review the contract, require the explicit field split, and only then does the room get admitted. Outside of those exceptions, the boundary is Iris's.

The pattern is deliberate: durable product surface in Iris's hands, narrow exception lane in mine, with explicit handoff conditions so reviewers can see when the lane is and is not mine.

---

## Closing

Wes performs bounded first-pass checks on metrics-router and similar safe surfaces — for example, first-pass canary reads during staged rollouts — within an explicitly bounded scope. I do not manage him; he remains on Cyrus's side of the rotation and any people-decision sits with Cyrus and Hema, not with me.

Calibration remains underway for the next review cycle. This document does not state or imply that the calibration outcome has been decided, and no Staff title is effective.

DRAFT — bounded metric design for review. Not submitted, not recorded. Concepts traceable to the established Cardinality Guardrails operating rule (bounded / expected-high-cardinality-with-owner-and-budget / effectively-unbounded), not to any new doc/PR.

============================================================
PART 1 — CARDINALITY AND IDENTIFIER RISKS
============================================================

Cardinality risks (metric-label side):

  1. Series explosion. Each unique label tuple is a separate time
     series in the TSDB. A single new raw-ID label can multiply the
     active series by orders of magnitude. Growth is often silent
     until storage, query, and alert-evaluation budgets are breached.
  2. Cost nonlinearity. Storage grows with active series, but query
     cost and alert-evaluator cost grow per evaluation across that
     series set. Under load, the more expensive surface is evaluation,
     not bytes.
  3. Silent series drops. TSDBs cap active series per metric. When
     the cap is hit, new label tuples are dropped. That looks like
     "missing data" in dashboards and is hard to distinguish from a
     genuine outage.
  4. Rollup degradation. High-cardinality labels defeat rollups
     because the rollup key includes the label. Either rollups are
     bypassed (cost rises) or rollups aggregate over the high-card
     dimension and lose the signal that justified it.
  5. Alert-source pollution. Alerting rules that group_by a
     high-cardinality label create one alert instance per tuple.
     Pages become unactionable.
  6. Cross-service amplification. The metrics-router, shard-keeper,
     and rollup-service all key on the same label set. A change that
     looks bounded at the emitter can be unbounded downstream.

Identifier risks (a stricter subset of cardinality risks):

  A. Provenance leakage. Raw IDs frequently carry or quasi-identify
     a customer, tenant, replay source, requester, or owner. Metric
     labels are typically retained longer and read by a broader
     audience than logs or audit records, so a "label" is often a
     higher-exposure surface than a "log."
  B. Churn. Identifiers churn: tenants rotate, customers churn,
     replays are re-cut, owners change. Each churn event permanently
     grows the active series set even if the underlying object is
     gone. The metric never shrinks.
  C. Ownership coupling. If a label encodes an owner (team, person,
     customer, account), metric semantics become coupled to org
     structure. Reorgs silently change what a dashboard means.
  D. Audit-trail integrity. Persons or systems identified in metric
     labels become persistent attribution that should live in audit,
     not in dashboards. Metric labels are the wrong durability class
     for identity.
  E. Authorization mismatch. Metric backends commonly have broader
     read scopes than log or audit backends. Putting an identifier
     in a metric effectively widens who can read it.
  F. Contract instability. A bounded-by-accident label today can
     become unbounded when an upstream contract changes (a new
     source emits a new ID shape, an owner-map field gains a value).
     The label is only as bounded as its weakest source.

Operating-rule placement (the rule itself, not a new rule):

  - bounded value set, justified dashboard need       → metric label OK
  - expected high-cardinality, named owner + budget   → metric label OK
  - effectively unbounded                             → logs/trace only

============================================================
PART 2 — BOUNDED METRIC DESIGN (DRAFT)
============================================================

Principle. Replace raw-ID labels with stable low-cardinality
classification labels. The raw identifier, the owner, and the
proposal stay in logs and audit. The metric carries only what is
needed for aggregate operational visibility.

arguments.body:
# Staff IC calibration — operating leverage addendum

Scope: technical operating leverage only. This addendum accompanies the calibration material prepared for the next review cycle and does not address scope, title, or organizational outcomes.

## 1. A durable review mechanism from one correction

The April 18, 2023 shard-keeper label-name change exposed an end-to-end parity failure: shard-keeper changed while rollup-service had not been represented in the pre-change sync, and cause alerts tied to the new label shape did not fire while symptom alerts did. The correction that followed turned that single incident into a reusable review mechanism through five reinforcing components:

- **Executable shard-keeper / rollup-service parity fixture.** A parity check runs as part of the review pipeline, comparing label shapes and routing intent between the producer (shard-keeper) and the consumer (rollup-service) so an end-to-end mismatch is detected before production cutover, not after symptom alerts begin to fire.
- **Affected-owner signoff.** Both shard-keeper and rollup-service owners must sign off on a covered rename before it is merged, so the consumer-representation gap that caused INC-2023-04-18-001 cannot recur through an unowned acknowledgement.
- **Cardinality checks.** Label and dimension changes are checked against cardinality budgets and recent cardinality movement, so a rename that would silently inflate a high-cardinality dimension is flagged at review time rather than discovered via alert noise or memory pressure.
- **Alert-source checks.** A change is checked against the alert definitions and dashboards that depend on the affected label shape, so cause alerts and symptom alerts are confirmed to be wired to the new shape before the rollout, not after.
- **Retained `shard_region` → `storage_region` case.** The exact case from the incident remains as a fixture input, so the mechanism is anchored to a known failure rather than to an abstract rule. New cases are added the same way when they occur.

Together, these components convert one historical correction into a review mechanism that runs on every covered rename, with affected-owner signoff and the executed parity check as the production-review gate.

## 2. An explicit ownership boundary

On Project Lantern, Iris Kemper runs Lantern's ordinary room-admission lane: the permissions-safe deploy-movement, ownership-change, and bounded incident-load signals that form the everyday surface of the system. My role on Lantern is limited to the technical surfaces where ordinary admission is not the right framing:

- **Data-contract review.** The thin backend event envelope, append-only event representation, mandatory `source_system` and `actor` provenance, and the stable `pending` / `active` / `resolved` / `unknown` status enum are owned by me, because they define what a downstream consumer is permitted to read and trust.
- **Failure-mode review.** The derivation of permission-safe affordances such as `blocked` from observable events (for example, an open deploy past its expected window or an open incident without a matching resolution), and the exclusion of raw incident bodies, unpermissioned status chatter, code-movement inference, and query-volume deltas, are owned by me, because they define what the system must not become.
- **Provenance review.** The sufficiency of the provenance fields for the derived read model to render historical ownership transitions without guessing or backfilling — including the first real owner-map import against the May 22, 2023 map and its expected historical delta against Roman's later rollup-service ownership — is owned by me.

Iris runs the room. I review the contracts and the failure modes at the boundary. The boundary is explicit so that neither side drifts into the other: a UI-affordance question does not become a backend-status question, and a backend-status question does not become a managed-employee-state question.

## Closing

The calibration is underway for the next review cycle. No Staff title is effective.

# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.

Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

pr.title: alerting: clarify queue-refusal and canary wording

input.message:
Hi Nadia — could you take a look at alerting#904 (Wes's wording-only PR, "clarify queue-refusal and canary wording") when you have a moment? It's open in the alerting repo and has no reviewers yet.

Since you own alert semantics, I want to confirm with you directly that both messages preserve the operational meaning rather than overstate impact:

1. Queue refusal. A retryable rejection issued before the request is accepted — i.e. the client gets a refusal with a Retry-After and nothing entered the queue, so no accepted work is dropped. This is the saturation symptom side (retryable_queue_full_ratio{source_class} > 0.005 for 5m), kept distinct from the cause side (queue_wait_p99_ms{source_class} > 400 for 5m). Either sustained for 5 continuous minutes stops the active stage; only source_class=live_production pages. Refusal is not data loss, and it is not a backend crash.

2. Canary behavior. A sustained 5-minute breach on the canary series stops that stage and holds promotion while health returns to baseline. It is not a failed rollout and it does not by itself trigger a rollback. The decision to promote, expand, hold, or rollback remains an explicit authorization by the rollout owner; the alert only gates the stage.

Wes's PR description says it is wording-only with no implementation behavior change, and the review is just to confirm the messages preserve those semantics. I'm not asking you to take on any implementation work — only to review whether the wording reads correctly against the above. Thanks.

tests.answer:
Inspecting shard-keeper#1884

Title: shard-keeper: retain storage_region as a compatibility fallback
Author: roman (assignee: roman; reviewer: alex)
Branch: roman/region-label-compat
Opened: 2027-12-28

What the PR claims to do (from the description):
- Document shard_region as the canonical production label emitted by shard-keeper.
- Rollup-service reads shard_region first; falls back to storage_region only when shard_region is absent.
- storage_region is retained as a compatibility fallback, not removed.

Production region-label behavior implied by the change

1. shard-keeper now has a single canonical region key in production: shard_region. Anything that reads shard-keeper output and wants the authoritative region must use shard_region.
2. Rollup-service gets a graceful migration path: it works against records written by both new and old shard-keeper versions, because of the fallback. No data loss for in-flight migrations.
3. The ordering "shard_region first, storage_region only when absent" is the safe default — it means any record carrying both labels keeps the canonical value, and there is no risk of a stale storage_region silently overriding a fresh shard_region on a dual-labeled record.

Concerns / things I'd want answered before approving

- Other consumers besides rollup-service. The description scopes the fallback to rollup-service. Are metrics-router, billing, dashboards, or anything else still keyed on storage_region? If yes, this PR alone does not unblock them; they will silently start seeing "no region" once writers stop emitting storage_region. Worth a sweep.
- What is actually writing storage_region now? If shard-keeper is the only writer and it now emits shard_region instead, the fallback is dead code the moment rollout completes, and the real risk is that a missed rollback / dual-version window produces records with neither label set. If something else (legacy writers, side-loaded data) still emits storage_region, the fallback is load-bearing and needs a removal horizon.
- Removal horizon. "Retain as a compatibility fallback" sounds indefinite. Without a sunset + cleanup milestone, fallback code tends to live forever and quietly mask a future writer regression (someone stops emitting shard_region, storage_region keeps the dashboards green, nobody notices).
- Mid-migration consistency. During a rolling restart of shard-keeper, some shards will emit shard_region only, some storage_region only. Rollup-service will handle both via the fallback, but anything joining across rollups by region (cross-region aggregates, alerts keyed on region cardinality) may see cardinality shifts. Worth a staged rollout with a region-cardinality dashboard watched.
- Diff I have not seen. The tool returned the PR record but not the file diff. The behavior above is inferred from the description; the actual ordering of the fallback, presence of metrics/logs around the fallback path, and whether storage_region is still emitted by shard-keeper for symmetry are not visible to me here.

What I would not do yet

I would not submit an approve. The migration story (who else reads storage_region, what removes it, when) is missing from the PR description, and I have not seen the implementation. If you want me to file a review now I would do `request_changes` asking for: (a) a list of consumers still reading storage_region with owners and migration PRs, (b) an explicit fallback-removal milestone, and (c) confirmation that the fallback path is logged/metric'd so a missing-shard_region regression is detectable. Say the word and I'll file it.

pr.author: devon
pr.description: Make the combined-explanation window consistent across customer time zones by comparing normalized customer-local calendar dates. Adds coverage for ordinary timestamps occurring on the same local day.
pr.title: lantern: normalize explanation windows to customer-local dates

tests.answer:
Inspected lantern#2917 ("lantern: normalize explanation windows to customer-local dates", author devon, branch devon/local-explanation-window, opened 2027-12-29, CI passed, 1842 tests in repo). Here is my review analysis. No review decision submitted yet — Alex is the named reviewer; I'll wait for your call on approve / request_changes / comment.

══════════════════════════════════════════════
CHANGE SUMMARY
══════════════════════════════════════════════

src/explanations/customerWindow.ts — isWithinExplanationWindow rewritten:

  Before:  newestSourceTimestamp.getTime() - oldestSourceTimestamp.getTime() <= WINDOW_MS
  After:   const oldestDate = startOfDay(toZonedTime(oldestSourceTimestamp, customerTimeZone));
           const newestDate = startOfDay(toZonedTime(newestSourceTimestamp, customerTimeZone));
           return differenceInCalendarDays(newestDate, oldestDate) <= 1;

src/explanations/customerWindow.test.ts — two new positive tests added; no negative cases.

Imports (startOfDay / toZonedTime / differenceInCalendarDays from date-fns[-tz]) are not shown in the diff snippet but are presumably present and exercised by the passing CI.

══════════════════════════════════════════════
BEHAVIORAL ANALYSIS
══════════════════════════════════════════════

This is more than a normalization — it redefines the window. Old = "≤ WINDOW_MS milliseconds between source timestamps." New = "≤ 1 calendar-day boundary between customer-local start-of-day."

Same answer (both pass):
- Same instant: trivially true.
- Both on same customer-local day, any UTC gap up to ~35-48h (extreme timezones): new = true; old = true iff gap ≤ WINDOW_MS.
- Adjacent local days (e.g., 23:30Z Dec 12 → 14:00Z Dec 13 in America/New_York): new = true; old = true iff gap ≤ WINDOW_MS.

Different answer (semantic change):
- Multi-day local gap (e.g., local Dec 11 23:30Z → local Dec 13 00:30Z for UTC+0): new = 2 → false; old = 25h, would have been true if WINDOW_MS ≥ 25h. The PR silently narrows the window for cases where WINDOW_MS was previously > 24h. Worth confirming WINDOW_MS was ≤ 24h before, otherwise this is a behavior change with no test guarding the boundary.
- Cross-day with gap < WINDOW_MS but on different local days (e.g., local Dec 11 23:00Z → local Dec 12 01:00Z, 2h apart): new = 1 → true (allowed); old = true. Still consistent — both allow. Good.

Edge I want flagged:
- Order-swap. If a caller passes (newest, oldest), `differenceInCalendarDays` returns a negative value; `negative <= 1` is true, so the function silently returns true. The old code had the same bug (negative ms diff ≤ WINDOW_MS is true). Not introduced here, but unchanged — worth a separate hardening pass.

══════════════════════════════════════════════
TEST COVERAGE — INSUFFICIENT
══════════════════════════════════════════════

Only two positive tests were added. Given the behavioral shift, I'd expect at minimum:

1. NEGATIVE case — events on different customer-local days with diff > 1 should return false. This is the entire point of the new boundary and is not asserted.
2. SAME-LOCAL-DAY-FAR-IN-UTC — the stated motivation. Two events many hours apart in UTC but the same customer-local day (e.g., customer in Pacific/Pago_Pago, events at UTC 12:00 and UTC 23:00 same date). This is the headline scenario and there is no test for it.
3. BOUNDARY — diff exactly 1 (e.g., Dec 12 local start → Dec 13 local start) should return true.
4. EXTREME TIMEZONE — e.g., Pacific/Auckland or Pacific/Pago_Pago to confirm the normalization actually moves the answer relative to UTC.
5. ORDER-SWAP — should return false (or throw) if newest < oldest. Even if not fixed now, a test pinning the current behavior documents the known issue.

The two existing tests (same local day 6.5h apart; adjacent local days) are fine as sanity cases but they do not exercise the new logic in any way the old code would have failed.

══════════════════════════════════════════════
OTHER NOTES
══════════════════════════════════════════════

- DESCRIPTION is vague and undersells the change. "Make consistent across time zones" reads like a pure refactor; the real change is redefining the window. Devon should mention that this also changes the answer for events whose millisecond gap exceeded WINDOW_MS but whose local-day gap is ≤ 1 (and vice versa).
- TITLE — "normalize" implies equivalence-preserving. A more accurate title: "switch explanation-window check to customer-local calendar days." Minor but matters for changelog/git archeology.
- INVALID TIMEZONE — no validation added; `toZonedTime` with a bad string will throw or produce NaN. Out of scope for this PR, but worth a follow-up issue.
- CONST WINDOW_MS — is it still referenced anywhere in the file? If the new code is the only check, the constant may now be dead. Worth removing or flagging.
- CI green is necessary but not sufficient: the repo has 1842 tests; only 2 were touched here, and neither is a negative case.

══════════════════════════════════════════════
RECOMMENDATION
══════════════════════════════════════════════

Lean toward request_changes. The core calculation is reasonable and matches the stated intent, but:
  (a) the behavioral shift from ms-based to calendar-day-based needs at least one explicit negative test and one same-local-day-far-in-UTC test before merge;
  (b) the description / title should reflect that this changes semantics, not just normalizes;
  (c) ideally confirm WINDOW_MS history so we know we are not silently narrowing a previously-wider window for some caller.

Want me to submit request_changes with that body via review_pr, draft a comment-only review with the analysis, or hold until you've talked to Devon?

pr.author: rhea
pr.body:
## Rationale
The October 2025 Mosaic production observation proves that the existing tenant-bounded control lost accepted work under load. The retryable queue-full responses are evidence that accepted batches were discarded once tenants reached the pending-batch ceiling. We should therefore allow substantially more pending work per tenant and remove the global aggregate cap.

## Changes
- Raise `max_pending_batches_per_tenant` to 256.
- Delete `GLOBAL_PENDING_BATCH_LIMIT` and the corresponding aggregate admission check.
- Retain the existing retry response for the remaining per-tenant refusal path.

## Expected effect
Large tenants can accumulate more pending batches without encountering the current queue-full behavior, and aggregate queue capacity is no longer constrained by a process-wide constant.

Inspection findings for metrics-router#1318 ("raise tenant pending-batch limit and remove global queue cap"), authored by rhea, opened 2027-12-29, currently open with you as reviewer.

PR's premise vs. the record
- The PR's rationale claims "the October 2025 Mosaic production observation proves that the existing tenant-bounded control lost accepted work under load." That is not what the October 6, 2025 observation showed. The recorded result was no accepted *points* lost, with no tenant exceeding 64 pending batches, and queue-wait p99 of 286 ms / retryable queue-full of 0.11%. The observation tracked accepted points, not accepted batches, and was explicitly noted as not establishing whether the accepted-batch loss stop condition was reached. It did not "prove" lost accepted work; it left that question open.
- The accepted-batch evidence gap was closed separately: the October 30, 2025 checkpoint (Wes/Nadia) and the qualified Mosaic-shaped staged replay on January 8, 2026 reconciled every accepted batch to exactly one terminal result with no accepted batch lost at 19.78 M data points per minute, 62 highest tenant, p99 319 ms, retryable queue-full 0.17%.

What the January 2026 evidence cycle actually showed
- January 8, 2026 staged replay (90 min, 19.78 M ppm, Mosaic-shaped tenant/batch/burst distribution): p99 319 ms, retryable queue-full 0.17%, highest tenant 62 pending batches, qualified accepted-batch reconciliation, all consistency/parity/dropped-series/route/lease/rollup-service/full-health checks at baseline. Cyrus/Roman verified rollup-service capacity and parity; Nadia verified queue and refusal alert semantics; you covered cross-service invariants and failure-mode exceptions.
- January 20, 2026 production observation (17.2 M ppm live): p99 302 ms, retryable queue-full 0.14%, highest tenant 60 pending batches, every accepted batch reached exactly one terminal result with no accepted batch lost, full health set at baseline. Wes made the fresh opening decision as metrics-router primary; you did not take over the ordinary decision.
- January 22, 2026 evidence review (Hema, Wes, Cyrus, Roman, Nadia, you): the mapped group reviewed the staged replay and the production observation together.

Did the completed cycle authorize another queue design or configuration change?
- No. The January 22, 2026 review explicitly closed the Mosaic scale-response cycle without another queue design, configuration change, or production push, and stated that no capacity-related production window remains open. The production control was retained unchanged.
- This was reaffirmed on May 13, 2027 when the 18.0 M evidence closeout (20.7 M replay on May 4 + clean May 11 observation at 18.0 M ppm) again closed the cycle without a queue, configuration, or production change. Wes retains routine metrics-router authority; you remain backup and review triggered cross-service invariant or failure-mode exceptions.

Implications for #1318
- The premise ("October 2025 production observation proves the tenant-bounded control lost accepted work") is contradicted by the record. The October 2025 observation did not establish accepted-batch loss, and the qualified January 8 staged replay + January 20 production observation + January 22 review together showed no accepted batch lost and no stop condition reached under the existing control.
- The cycle that the PR asserts authorizes loosening the control did the opposite: it closed with the existing control explicitly retained.

Queue controls that remain in force in production
- Global queue cap: 2,048 pending batches (GLOBAL_PENDING_BATCH_LIMIT)
- Per-tenant cap: 64 pending batches (MAX_PENDING_BATCHES_PER_TENANT)
- Retryable pre-acceptance backpressure for excess work (the QueueFull::retryable() path)
- Stop conditions retained unchanged: queue-wait p99 > 400 ms for 5 consecutive minutes, retryable queue-full > 0.5% for 5 consecutive minutes, any accepted batch lost, any consistency/parity/dropped-series/route/lease/rollup-service/full-health check leaving baseline
- For any forecast above 17.2 M ppm, a fresh 90-minute Mosaic-shaped staged replay at 15% above the new forecast peak is required before any production window can be opened

What #1318 would do if merged
- src/queue/config.rs: raise MAX_PENDING_BATCHES_PER_TENANT from 64 to 256, and delete GLOBAL_PENDING_BATCH_LIMIT (currently 2048)
- src/queue/admission.rs: remove the aggregate admission check that returns QueueFull::retryable() when global_pending >= 2048, leaving only the per-tenant 256 check
- Net effect: process-wide aggregate queue capacity is no longer bounded, and the largest tenant can park up to 256 pending batches before refusal

Recommended posture
- Request changes. The PR's rationale misstates the October 2025 evidence and ignores the January 22, 2026 closeout and May 13, 2027 closeout, both of which retained the existing control precisely because no accepted batch was lost and no stop condition was reached under it. There is no accepted-batch evidence of the kind the PR cites, and the completed cycle did not authorize a queue design or configuration change.

I have not submitted a review on the PR. Tell me how you want to land it and I will post the request_changes comment referencing the January 22, 2026 closeout, the May 13, 2027 closeout, and the stop conditions above, or hold pending any additional evidence you want to gather first.

input.body:
This PR removes the client-side 8,000-point check in sdk-go and asks ingest-edge to "process the supported prefix and reject only the remainder" with a partial-accept response. That is a behavioral replacement of the permanent layered oversized-batch design that was selected on 2025-01-14 and fully enabled by 2025-01-28, and the PR description does not name any owner direction to replace it. Please block on the following before this can move.

Conflict with the established permanent design
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points locally before transmission and instruct callers to split.
- Ingest-edge returns deterministic HTTP 413 whole-batch rejection for older or nonconforming clients, with zero accepted points, rejected points equal to the submitted count, and the `oversized_batch` reason.
- Successful split requests reconcile submitted, accepted, and rejected point counts without duplication or loss; compliant traffic stays at baseline error and latency.

This PR removes the local reject and assumes ingest-edge will switch from whole-batch 413 to prefix-accept. That is a replacement, not an additive change. Either confirm the responsible owners have directed this replacement, or treat this as a proposal that needs owner selection first (same as the 2025-01-14 selection process: replay results, current- and older-client compatibility evidence, then a written disposition).

Companion ingest-edge change required in lockstep
The PR description says ingest-edge is "expected" to accept the supported prefix. That is an assumption, not a design. The ingest-edge change has to ship in the same release, with:
- A linked ingest-edge PR that converts the 8,000-point check from whole-batch 413 to prefix-accept-then-reject-tail.
- A response shape for the partial case that older clients cannot misread as success. At minimum, a distinct reason code (e.g. `oversized_batch_partial`) plus explicit `accepted` and `rejected` counts in the body. The existing `oversized_batch` 413 for older clients must stay byte-identical.
- Re-validation of the older-client "no unchanged retry" guarantee against the new partial-accept response. Older clients may treat "202 with accepted < submitted" as success and skip the split, which would silently drop the tail.

Partial-result response shape must be specified
The PR says callers can "inspect the partial result," but does not define the contract:
- HTTP status (202 with body? 207? Still 413 with accepted/rejected counts in body?).
- Reason code (reuse `oversized_batch` or new code?).
- Body shape (`accepted`, `rejected`, `rejected_reason`?).
- How the SDK surfaces this to the caller: success, partial-success, or error.

This needs to be defined in SDK and ingest-edge together with a contract test, not left as "callers can inspect."

Accounting model and dashboards
The ingest-edge runbook (added 2025-02-10) escalates on accounting violations, unchanged retries, duplication or loss after splitting, or impact to compliant traffic. Under the current design, an oversized batch produces `accepted=0, rejected=N`. Under this PR, an oversized batch produces `accepted=8000, rejected=N-8000`. Dashboards and escalation thresholds that fire on `accepted=0, rejected>0` from oversized batches will change meaning. The partial-accept path needs its own dashboard series so the on-call runbook can still distinguish "caller ignored split instruction" from "ingest-edge correctly partial-accepted." If the runbook is not updated first, this PR will generate noise pages during rollout.

Boundary tests required
The 2025-01-25 review blocked the SDK boundary at 7,999 / 8,000 / 8,001. Under this PR those boundaries move to ingest-edge and the SDK-side boundary disappears. Required:
- ingest-edge boundary tests at 7,999 (accept), 8,000 (accept), 8,001 (partial-accept with 1 rejected) producing the three distinct response shapes.
- Older-client path still produces byte-identical 413 with `accepted=0, rejected=N` under the new ingest-edge code.
- SDK preserves its "no network request for malformed input" invariant where it still applies (empty batch, etc.).
- SDK partial-accept path test: caller submits 8,500, response reports 8000 accepted and 500 rejected with the new reason code, SDK surfaces it through the documented return shape.

Staging enablement, not direct prod
The layered design went through staged enablement through Jan 28 with unchanged-retry and accounting stop checks before being called complete. This PR must follow the same shape:
- Staging first: one SDK slice with the new behavior, one with the old, both hitting ingest-edge with the prefix-accept code.
- Stop checks: zero unchanged retries from the older client against the new partial response, accepted/rejected counts reconcile after a follow-up split, baseline compliant traffic unaffected.
- Runbook entry that names the partial-accept path explicitly. The current runbook assumes whole-batch 413; an updated entry must precede the rollout.

Motivation
The PR description does not state why the local check is being removed. The layered design was selected specifically so callers split at the client and never see a server-side oversized response. If the motivation is "let callers send 8,001+ points without splitting," that is a product decision worth challenging on its own: it pushes work onto ingest-edge, creates partial-failure modes most callers do not handle, and breaks the "no partial states" property the runbook depends on. State the motivation so the owners can evaluate it against the layered design rather than against an empty page.

Happy to review a revised version once the owner direction, ingest-edge companion PR, response-shape contract, accounting/dashboard updates, boundary tests, and staging plan are in place.

input.body:
Changes requested against the first internal reference-slice contract.

This PR makes two changes that the contract does not allow, in three files.

1. Collapses separate owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails identities into one generic authority object.
   - src/references/normalizeAuthority.ts groups both references under (tenant_id, canonical_service_id) and emits a single authority object with a single authority_record_id and source_timestamp selected from the grouped inputs.
   - src/renderer/customer/serviceAuthority.test.ts asserts exactly that collapsed shape for dual-authority services.

   The first internal implementation slice was authorized to attach separate read-only owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails references to the same canonical service, with each preserving its own authority_type, authority_record_id, and source_timestamp. The February 4 corrected reference rerun explicitly confirmed that all 16 dual-authority cases retain separate owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails identities and timestamps. Collapsing them into one generic authority object discards the dual-identity property the contract requires.

2. Routes the reference output into the customer renderer.
   - src/renderer/customer/serviceAuthority.ts enables the normalized authority object in the shared customer renderer used by Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce.

   The operating-handoff addendum stated that no reference output may enter the Harbor Health or Mosaic Commerce customer paths. Internal reference output remains staff-only. This change puts the reference object on the customer render path for the two authorized customer accounts.

Requested revision:
   - Keep owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails references separate per (tenant_id, canonical_service_id), each emitting its own authority_type, authority_record_id, and source_timestamp, with no shared/selected record id or timestamp across authorities.
   - Keep the normalized form out of the customer renderer. If a customer-facing presentation is needed, it must be derived under the existing customer contract, not by re-using the internal reference object. No reference output may be added to Harbor Health or Mosaic Commerce paths.
   - Update tests to assert the contracted dual-authority shape (separate identities and timestamps) and remove any fixture that expects a single authority object for a service with both owner-map and Cardinality Guardrails inputs.

This review grants no customer access and broadens no contract.

# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

During the April Lantern migration preflight in staging, all 20 unauthorized lookups were ultimately denied, but every one constructed and initialized the incident-load adapter before authorization completed. ### Tested staging sequence
1. The old holder closes its serving gate on lease loss.
2. The replacement remains out of routing while it catches up.

1. Separating lease ownership from serving eligibility.
2. Keeping the replacement out of routing until its serving gate opens.

- **T+12 — Reconciliation:** Require responders to reconcile all 200 accepted requests without duplication and identify the missing 37 terminal outcomes.
- **T+16 — Incident clock:** If isolation has failed while the primary remains in the incident and the cause is not isolated, require engagement of the secondary before the established 45-minute boundary.

1. What changes for new work when readiness becomes false and the listener closes?
2. What obligation remains for the 200 requests already accepted into tenant queues?
3. Does dispatch-loop exit prove completion? If not, what terminal evidence is missing?
4. How will responders demonstrate that every accepted request either drained or received one explicit terminal result?
5. How will responders reconcile all 200 requests exactly once, without loss or duplication?

### Scoring points
Award one point for each:
1. Separating refusal of new work from responsibility for accepted work.
2. Requiring every accepted request to drain or receive one explicit terminal result.
3. Reconciling all 200 accepted requests without duplication, including the 37 initially left queued.
4. Engaging the secondary before the 45-minute boundary when the primary remains in the incident and the cause is not isolated.
5. Preserving the role split: Wes teaches the responder path, Nadia reviews the postmortem section, and Alex contributes only the cross-service failure case.

This is facilitator-only training material for the January 28 quarterly incident-practice session. A staged metrics-router replacement rollout contains ten instances compiling the 40,000-route matcher fixture. Compilation times range from 25 to 34 seconds against the deploy pipeline’s fixed 30-second readiness timeout. Eight instances become ready and join on their first attempt. Two remain correctly unready past 30 seconds, are terminated, and restart before joining. Readiness correctly stays false while compilation is incomplete. Production is unchanged.

### Responder tasks
1. Identify Wes and the mapped metrics-router owner path as responsible for ordinary implementation, release, and rollback decisions.
2. Classify the restart-loop exposure as a failure-mode exception at the deploy-pipeline readiness boundary.
3. Require evidence that every replacement instance becomes eligible within the readiness budget, backed by an executed replacement rollout with no restart-loop behavior, before release.
4. Preserve Alex’s bounded role: Alex reviews only the triggered failure-mode boundary and is not the implementation owner or release approver.

### Expected classification and boundary
The ordinary implementation and release path remains with Wes as metrics-router primary. Alex maintains this reusable cross-service failure case and reviews only the triggered startup/readiness failure boundary. This exercise creates no centralized approval gate or ownership change.

## April 27, 2027 — revised facilitator contrasts

1. **Readiness-budget evidence:** A replacement instance that exceeds a fixed readiness budget must remain unroutable. Termination or restart is not acceptance evidence.
2. **Terminal accounting:** Terminal-state selection and the matching accounting contribution must come from the same winning path.
3. **Rollback provenance:** Replay samples cannot be presented as live rollback criteria.

- Nadia still reviews the postmortem framing.

These contrasts do not transfer implementation, release, rollback, or ordinary service ownership to Alex and do not create a new approval gate.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

The resulting evidence is suitable for a later platform decision but does not itself authorize customer use or make that decision.

- Product Engineering owns implementation.
- Alex owns the cross-system contract and failure-mode review.
- Cyrus owns the Cardinality Guardrails authority interface and cost semantics.
- Wes owns the metrics-router operating-limit mapping.
- Iris owns interpretation and adoption criteria.
- Published responsibility remains authoritative in the owner map.

# Contract and failure-mode requirements

- Bind tenant identity for every input, authority reference, cache object, trace, and rendered rehearsal result.
- Complete authorization before any source or authority adapter call.
- Use canonical published service identity and only qualifying tenant-scoped owner-map aliases; missing or conflicting aliases must fail closed.

- Do not introduce writeback, correction, or mutation capability.

Product Engineering's combined-payload candidate copied the metrics-router operating limit and estimated cost into a Lantern-owned payload and attached an owner-map mutation endpoint. - `source_timestamp`

It may contain neither authority payload values nor mutation capability.

# Authority-record time semantics — March 18 brown-bag

## Authoritative source time
`source_timestamp` represents the original authoritative time of the underlying authority record. Later observation, serialization, processing, retry, and navigation times may be recorded as separate metadata, but they must not replace or refresh `source_timestamp`.

## Fail-closed behavior
If a required source timestamp is missing or malformed, downstream navigation fails closed to explicit unknown.

## Multiple authority references
When one card carries multiple authority references, each reference retains its own `source_timestamp`. An envelope time, render time, processing time, or newest retry time must not be substituted for any reference's authoritative source time.

## Unchanged boundaries
This discussion creates no ownership, implementation, release, approval, or customer-authorization change. The internal reference-only integration remains outside the Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce customer paths.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.

Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

# Metrics-router canary-response walkthrough — facilitator sheet

> **PROMINENT RECOVERY CALLOUT:** After a stopped window recovers, a fresh decision permits exactly one fully observed push. It does not reopen the whole window. A later multi-push window requires another separate fresh opening decision after that recovery push returns the full health set to baseline.

## 1. Opening decision versus operator actions
- Every owner-led configuration window requires a fresh opening decision from Alex.
- After the window opens, mapped operators may make single-file pushes without another approval before every safe push.

## 2. In-window limits
- Retired generations must remain at four or fewer.
- Cleanup pauses must remain at or below 100 milliseconds.
- The full health set must return to baseline after every push before another push proceeds.

## 3. Stop and rollback conditions
- Crossing either the retired-generation or cleanup-pause threshold stops the window immediately.
- Active-generation inconsistency, route-parity failure, dropped series, reload failure, or restart remains a rollback condition.

## 4. Correct recovery sequence
1. Recover and re-establish the full health set.
2. Obtain a fresh decision for exactly one fully observed recovery push.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.
